issues.body:
## Current scope after the main-branch repair — October 13, 2026

[PR #168338](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/168338) is merged on main as [`45c7bc9e9ca9`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/45c7bc9e9ca9a838115d560ec13b67d287c3d2b4). It aligns admission with the final provider-bound projection and anchors estimation to matching provider-reported prompt usage, estimating only appended content while retaining conservative overflow recovery. The older unprojected-transcript complaint below no longer describes that path unchanged.

The maintainer [explicitly retained this issue](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/101929#issuecomment-6097100950) for the remaining conservative density estimate on newly appended tool results, and an independent reporter has [committed to retesting](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/101929#issuecomment-6125636471). Follow that existing owner/retest route rather than opening another overlapping fix.

The next useful evidence is `estimatedPromptTokens` beside the same provider request's `prompt_tokens`, from a build containing the merged commit, with both a fits-without-recovery case and a genuine-overflow control. The original 2.3–2.6x ratios and the maintainer's October 10 comparison are historical observations; this source-only update performed no model turn or new measurement.

---

### Bug type

Behavior bug

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

`context-overflow-midturn-precheck` estimates prompt tokens ~2.3–2.6× above provider-billed usage on tool-result-heavy turns, firing truncation recovery on turns nowhere near the context window.

### Steps to reproduce

1. OpenClaw 2026.6.10, model `openai/gpt-5.5` via Codex-compatible OAuth (`openai-chatgpt-responses`), `agents.defaults.compaction.midTurnPrecheck.enabled: true`, `agents.defaults.contextLimits.toolResultMaxChars: 16000`, default 200k context window, `compaction.reserveTokens: 50000`.
2. Run an isolated cron agent turn (`--session isolated --light-context`) that accumulates large tool results (in our run: ~250k chars of tool-result text across ~20 calls — a ~100KB JSON tool result plus several 10–15KB results).
3. Watch the journal: the precheck fires with `estimatedPromptTokens` far above what the provider bills for the same calls.

### Expected behavior

The precheck estimate approximates the real serialized outbound prompt (within tokenizer error), so recovery fires only when a turn genuinely approaches the window.

### Actual behavior

On a turn whose billed prompt (per-call `input + cached` from provider usage) ramped from ~47k to a 63–70k plateau (max 69,858 across 43 calls, deduplicated by response id), the precheck fired twice:

- fire 1: `estimatedPromptTokens=162262` vs the 63,292-token call billed immediately before it → **2.56×**
- fire 2: `estimatedPromptTokens=150348` vs 65,570 billed → **2.29×**

Each fire ran `route=truncate_tool_results_only` recovery, which rewrote the session file squeezing ALL prior tool results into a 16,000-char aggregate (`calculateRecoveryAggregateToolResultChars` returns `aggregateMaxCharsOverride ?? maxCharsOverride`, and this path passes no aggregate override; `RECOVERY_MIN_KEEP_CHARS = 0`), stubbing each result to ~70–99 chars ending in "rerun with narrower args if needed". The model then re-fetched the data it had already paid for (billed prompt drops 63,292→52,793 and 65,570→52,741 right after each recovery, then climbs back), the stub wording steered it into re-querying with narrower args in a loop, and after 371s a provider `server_error` ended the third attempt. Net: ~2.66M billed tokens, zero output delivered.

Mechanism (from reading the 2026.6.10 dist): `estimateLlmBoundaryTokenPressure` (attempt.tool-run-context / preemptive-compaction) counts tool-result text at `TOOL_RESULT_CHARS_PER_TOKEN = 2` chars/token — half the `ESTIMATED_CHARS_PER_TOKEN = 4` used for ordinary text — multiplied by `SAFETY_MARGIN = 1.2`, and it estimates over the **untruncated in-memory transcript**, while the actual outbound prompt gets per-result (`toolResultMaxChars`) + aggregate (×4) truncation applied by the stream-fn transform before send. Arithmetic on our run: the journal reports `toolResultReducibleChars=234607`, so tool results alone contribute ≈ 250k/2 × 1.2 ≈ **140k of the 162k estimate**, while the truncated wire prompt can carry at most 64,000 chars (~16k tokens) of tool results. That accounts for the entire overcount.

### OpenClaw version

2026.6.10

### Operating system

Ubuntu Linux (server); gateway runs as a systemd user unit

### Install method

npm package with the bundled Node runtime

### Model

openai/gpt-5.5

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw → codex-oauth → openai-chatgpt-responses

### Logs

```shell
# journalctl, gateway unit, 2026-07-07 (agent id redacted; rest verbatim)
11:35:54 [agent/embedded] [context-overflow-midturn-precheck] sessionKey=agent:<agent>:cron:367d6d6e-…:run:78a0bbc0-… provider=openai/gpt-5.5 estimatedPromptTokens=162262 promptBudgetBeforeReserve=150000 effectiveReserveTokens=50000 overflowTokens=12262 toolResultReducibleChars=234607 route=truncate_tool_results_only handled=true truncatedCount=5
11:35:54 [agent/embedded] [context-overflow-precheck] early recovery route=truncate_tool_results_only completed for openai/gpt-5.5; retrying from current transcript
11:38:07 [agent/embedded] [context-overflow-midturn-precheck] … estimatedPromptTokens=150348 promptBudgetBeforeReserve=150000 effectiveReserveTokens=50000 overflowTokens=348 toolResultReducibleChars=212104 route=truncate_tool_results_only handled=true truncatedCount=18
11:38:07 [agent/embedded] [context-overflow-precheck] early recovery route=truncate_tool_results_only completed for openai/gpt-5.5; retrying from current transcript
11:41:11 [openai-transport] [responses] … code=server_error requestId=6d29ab5b-e3d1-4356-ac89-d51ffedb7ccc
```

Billed usage for the same run (provider `usage`, deduplicated by response id): per-call `input + cached` = 47,263 → ramps to 63,292 by call 5 → oscillates 52–70k (dipping ~11–13k right after each recovery rewrite) → max 69,858. The estimator also does not count tool schemas while billed input does — so the per-content overcount is larger than the raw ratio suggests.

### Impact and severity

- Tool-result-heavy turns that are ~40% into the real window are treated as overflowing → destructive recovery on every affected turn.
- The recovery is a persistent transcript rewrite with very small stubs, so the model re-fetches everything it already had — call-count and token multiplication (~3× on our run), and long turns get exposed to transient provider errors.
- Frequency: deterministic for any turn whose tool results exceed roughly `(budget − prompt) × 2` chars — for us, every full work-queue digest turn until we mitigated.
- Mitigation we applied: `reserveTokens` 50k→30k (budget 150k→170k) and shrinking the turn's tool results — the estimator remains ~2.3–2.6× off.

### Additional information

- Closest existing report: #99843 (compaction trigger overestimate ~5.7× from usage-fallback cacheRead double-counting; fixed by PR #99864, merged 2026-07-05, **not in any published release** — latest `v2026.7.1-beta.2` predates the merge by minutes). Our defect is in the **midturn precheck's char-based estimator**, which looks like a different mechanism (chars-per-token ratio + untruncated transcript, not usage fallback) — but #99864 touches `packages/ai/src/utils/overflow.ts` and `src/cron/isolated-agent/run.ts`, so: **does #99864 also correct `context-overflow-midturn-precheck`'s `estimatedPromptTokens`?** Happy to re-test on the next release.
- Related: #97219 (same precheck, post-truncation abort), #74233 (prior art: precheck estimating from pre-assembly history), #85712 (sibling destructive-recovery hazard on the `compact_only` route — the `truncate_tool_results_only` recovery described above has the same "quietly degrade the transcript" character, plus the stub text actively instructs the model to re-query).
- Suggested direction: estimate over the post-truncation outbound prompt (or at least apply the same per-result/aggregate caps before counting), and use the ordinary chars-per-token ratio for tool-result text; alternatively reuse billed usage from the previous call as the baseline when available (as #99864 does for compaction).
- Config caveats for reproduction honesty: `midTurnPrecheck.enabled` is opt-in (we enabled it), and our 16,000-char recovery aggregate derives from our `toolResultMaxChars=16000`; with default caps the recovery budget would be 64,000 — larger stubs, same estimator defect.

issues.body:
### Summary
On the Telegram channel with the `claude-cli` backend and the default queue mode (`steer`), a message that arrives while a turn is running is sometimes **lost entirely**, not just delayed. When the queued message is drained, the gateway logs the **new** message's length but builds the prompt from the **previous** message's body. The new message is never sent to the model, and its ingress row is still marked `completed`.

This is different from #124731 / #156848 (steer silently degrades to a delayed followup) and #110727. Here the message never reaches the session at all.

### Version / setup
- OpenClaw 2026.9.6
- Agent runtime: `claude-cli`
- Channel: Telegram direct chat
- `messages.queue.mode` unset (defaults to `steer`)

### Evidence (5 drops between 2026-09-03 and 2026-09-28, all during an active turn)
- Case A: message A2 arrives mid-turn. After the turn ends, the gateway logs `[telegram] Inbound message … (86 chars)` (A2's length), but the prompt the CLI receives, per the Claude Code session jsonl, carries **A1's** text. A2 is absent from the native transcript (`transcript_events`), and A1 and A3 are present.
- Case B: the same off-by-one. The log shows a 520-char inbound (B2), and the prompt body is B1 (107 chars).
- Cases C and D: messages sent during the same long turn never produce any user turn.
- Case E: `Inbound message` is logged twice for the same message during a 23-minute turn, and still no user turn is recorded.
- Separately, 4 messages were delivered 75–81 minutes late (same condition).

In every case the ingress row in `openclaw.sqlite` is `completed`, so nothing retries.

### Expected
Every message received while a turn is running gets delivered, in order, after the turn ends. At minimum, the prompt body should match the message being logged and marked complete.

### Workaround being tested
`messages.queue.byChannel.telegram: "collect"`. I'll report back whether it avoids the drop.

I can share a small read-only detector script that cross-checks the Telegram message cache against both transcript stores, if that's useful.

issues.body:
## What Problem This Solves

In the documented Cloudflare Tunnel setup (docs/gateway/cloudflare-access.md, step 3), the Gateway runs on loopback with `trustedProxies: ["127.0.0.1", "::1"]`, `allowLoopback: true`, `userHeader: "cf-access-authenticated-user-email"` and `requiredHeaders: ["cf-access-jwt-assertion"]`.

Admission then checks only that the request comes from a trusted proxy address and that both headers are present. The JWT itself is never verified. So any process on the Gateway host can send:

```
cf-access-authenticated-user-email: attacker@evil.test
cf-access-jwt-assertion: totally-not-a-jwt
x-openclaw-scopes: operator.admin
```

and be admitted as that user with the scopes it asked for. A test harness against `/control/control-ui-config.json` got HTTP 200 and the operator-only config (including a private MCP server command) for both a garbage assertion and a well-formed but unsigned JWT with a fake issuer.

The docs already say this ("does not verify the JWT signature", "do not treat this setting as a defense against untrusted local code"). But the only boundary is then the host itself. If `trustedProxies` is set wider than loopback, or the proxy in front passes client-supplied `cf-access-*` headers through, the same forgery works remotely.

## Proposed fix

An opt-in setting that verifies the assertion. Existing configs keep working unchanged:

```json5
trustedProxy: {
  userHeader: "cf-access-authenticated-user-email",
  requiredHeaders: ["cf-access-jwt-assertion"],
  allowLoopback: true,
  cloudflareAccessJwt: {
    issuer: "https://example.cloudflareaccess.com",
    audience: "your-application-aud-tag",
  },
}
```

When it is set, the Gateway:

- verifies `cf-access-jwt-assertion` (RS256 only) against the team's keys from `<issuer>/cdn-cgi/access/certs`, cached and refetched on key rotation;
- checks `iss`, `aud` and `exp`;
- takes the user from the signed `email` claim and requires the user header to match it, since other code still reads that header.

Access service-token requests (nodes connecting through Access) carry no email claim and no user header. They keep today's outcome (`trusted_proxy_user_missing`, then the node's own credentials), so that flow does not change.

Failures get distinct reasons so an operator can tell them apart: `trusted_proxy_access_invalid`, `trusted_proxy_access_user_mismatch`, `trusted_proxy_access_keys_unavailable`.

## Evidence

- Forgery harness against the Control UI HTTP surface, documented config: garbage assertion and unsigned JWT both admitted (HTTP 200).
- Same harness with `cloudflareAccessJwt` on: garbage, unsigned, attacker-signed with the team's key id, and a real assertion with a forged user header are all refused (HTTP 401). A correctly signed assertion is still admitted (HTTP 200).
- With the setting off, behavior is unchanged.

## Open question

Should OpenClaw ever turn this on by default for the Cloudflare header pair? This proposal keeps it opt-in so no existing deployment changes, and leaves a default change for later.

Reproduced on a clean lampvm install of `6a60076`, running macOS 26.6.2 with an arm64, ad-hoc-signed debug build.

Launching OpenClaw immediately displays the macOS local-network permission dialog before the Welcome screen is visible or any onboarding action has been taken. Users are asked to allow network access before the app has introduced itself or explained the request.

![Local-network permission dialog before onboarding](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/9cd4c5819d6a2e4b98d5cf123fa47d7189096bf4/images/2026/11/a78ff3d3-6dd4-4f9a-81da-1e6a844761d4.png)

Network-related code paths to investigate, without attributing the prompt to either one:

- **Hostname lookup:** [Launch schedules `PresenceReporter.start()`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/6a6007663b36db8badd6967e7f2bed5c6b3a724e/apps/macos/Sources/OpenClaw/MenuBar.swift#L476). Its [first push reads `InstanceIdentity.displayName`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/6a6007663b36db8badd6967e7f2bed5c6b3a724e/apps/macos/Sources/OpenClaw/PresenceReporter.swift#L24-L44), whose [macOS implementation calls `Host.current().localizedName`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/6a6007663b36db8badd6967e7f2bed5c6b3a724e/apps/shared/OpenClawKit/Sources/OpenClawKit/InstanceIdentity.swift#L99-L109).
- **Gateway discovery:** [`GatewayDiscoveryModel.start()`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/6a6007663b36db8badd6967e7f2bed5c6b3a724e/apps/macos/Sources/OpenClawDiscovery/GatewayDiscoveryModel.swift#L106-L124) starts a [Bonjour `NWBrowser`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/6a6007663b36db8badd6967e7f2bed5c6b3a724e/apps/shared/OpenClawKit/Sources/OpenClawKit/GatewayDiscoveryBrowserSession.swift#L20-L42). The inspected [onboarding caller is page-gated](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/6a6007663b36db8badd6967e7f2bed5c6b3a724e/apps/macos/Sources/OpenClaw/OnboardingView%2BMonitoring.swift#L25-L36); the run did not establish whether browsing started before the dialog.

No log or trace tied the observed prompt to a particular call. The confirmed problem is the permission request appearing before onboarding context. The app should explain the request before triggering it.

### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

On a POSIX Git install, `openclaw update` to any main commit from 5a7d1718aa5 (#198661) onward fails at `preflight-build` with `Declaration input escapes checkout`, because the updater builds the target in a worktree nested inside the install and the target's declaration build now refuses type files read from the install's own `node_modules`.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Make a Git install at `v2026.11.4` (d843d6af39a4): `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm build && pnpm ui:build`. Plain macOS layout: no symlinked home, internal disk.
2. Stop the Gateway. Run `OPENCLAW_UPDATE_DEV_TARGET_REF=<target sha> node openclaw.mjs update --channel dev --yes --no-restart`.
3. Target 1c1814a0bf78 (parent of #198661): `preflight-build` passes.
4. Target 5a7d1718aa5 (#198661) or current main f947bdc9498: `preflight-build` fails and the install stays at d843d6af39a4.

### Expected behavior

The update builds the target and moves the install, as it does for 1c1814a0bf78 from the same install.

### Actual behavior

```
  ✓ preflight-deps-install (15.85s)
  ✗ preflight-build (23.11s)
    Failing check preflight-build (command-failed): Error: Declaration input escapes checkout: [redacted-path]
  ✓ preflight-cleanup (13.21s)
Failed: validating
```

The updater redacts the path. Building f947bdc9498 in the same nested layout by hand (`<install>/.artifacts/<dir>/worktree`) shows it:

```
Error: Declaration input escapes checkout: <install>/node_modules/undici/types/utility.d.ts -> <install>/node_modules/.pnpm/undici@8.12.2/node_modules/undici/types/utility.d.ts.
```

Cause:

- The updater puts its preflight worktree at `<realpath(install)>/.artifacts/.openclaw-update-preflight-XXXXXX/worktree` on POSIX (`src/infra/update-runner-git-commands.ts:104-113`, `src/infra/update-runner-git-preflight.ts:577,586`). That is three levels inside the install, whose root `node_modules` holds `undici`.
- `@anthropic-ai/sdk@0.137.0` `internal/types.d.mts` line 51 (also `openai` and `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk`) types `RequestInit` as a union of relative imports of `node_modules/undici` from 3 to 10 parent levels (`import("../../../node_modules/undici/...")` and longer). From the worktree's `.pnpm` layout, level 7 is the worktree's own `node_modules/undici` and level 10 is the install's.
- Since #198661, tsdown declarations come from one `tsgo -p <leaf> --listFiles` pass that reads the real filesystem, and every listed file must be inside the checkout (`scripts/lib/native-declaration-emitter.mts:377-386`, thrown at `scripts/lib/local-check-runtime.mts:166`). The API path it replaced denied reads outside the checkout, so the far union members did not resolve. #198661 lists this as intended ("Parent-install shadowing now fails loudly"), pinned by `fails closed when optional SDK relative imports reach a parent install` in `test/scripts/native-declaration-boundary.test.ts:239`. The updater's own nested worktree is a parent install in exactly that sense.

### OpenClaw version

From 2026.11.4 (d843d6af39a4) to main f947bdc9498. First bad target 5a7d1718aa5, last good 1c1814a0bf78.

### Operating system

macOS 27.2 (arm64)

### Install method

Git checkout (pnpm build), dev channel update

### Model

Not model related

### Provider / routing chain

Not provider related

### Impact and severity

- Affected: POSIX Git installs updating to a target that contains #198661. The preflight path does not depend on host layout; reproduced without a symlinked home or external disk. Windows builds in `C:\ocu` and was not tested.
- Severity: blocks the update. The install stays on its old commit and the Gateway starts on it again. No data risk seen.
- Frequency: 3 of 3 attempts from 2026.11.4 to main targets at or after 5a7d1718aa5 failed (5a7d1718aa5, 2516bca9fdb8, f947bdc9498). The update to 1c1814a0bf78 from the same build passed.
- Consequence: Git installs cannot reach current main. No release tag contains #198661 yet. A release cut after it would block Git installs on stable and beta the same way, since tag updates run the same preflight build.

### Additional information

Fix direction: keep declaration resolution inside the checkout when the checkout is nested in another install, for example by emitting through the bounded API filesystem when the command-line pass lists an input outside the checkout, instead of failing. Moving the preflight worktree out of the install would help only future updaters, since shipped updaters already pick the nested path.

issues.body:
## Title
`gateway status` takes 16–22s on Windows 11 — blocked in `spawnSync` → `tasklist.exe`

## Body

### Summary

On Windows 11, `openclaw gateway status` consistently takes **16–22 seconds**, while the Gateway itself responds in **149 ms**. The delay is a single synchronous child-process call that stalls under Node's `spawnSync` — the same `tasklist.exe` invocation completes in **70 ms** when run directly from the shell.

- OpenClaw: `2026.11.3` (847611d)
- Node: `v24.22.1`
- OS: `Windows_NT 10.0.28000 x64` (Windows 11)
- Gateway: local, `bind: loopback`, `auth.mode: token`, port 18789

### Measurements

| Command | Time |
|---|---|
| `HTTP GET 127.0.0.1:18789/health` | **149 ms** |
| `node -e "0"` | 65 ms |
| `openclaw --version` | 0.51 s |
| `openclaw gateway --help` | 2.31 s |
| `openclaw automations status` | 2.41 s |
| `openclaw sessions list` | 8.80 s |
| **`openclaw gateway status`** | **17–22 s** |
| **`openclaw gateway status --no-probe`** | **17.5 s** |

So the Gateway's request path is healthy; the CLI's service-inspection path is not. `--no-probe` roughly halves nothing — the probe is not the cost.

### Root cause

CPU profile of `openclaw gateway status --no-probe` (`node --cpu-prof`, 15,265 samples over 17.6 s):

```
  7959  52.1%  spawnSync @ child_process:1175
  3716  24.3%  (idle) @ (native):-1
   491   3.2%  compileSourceTextModule @ utils:316
```

The process is **not computing** — it is blocked waiting on a child. Watching child-process creation during the run identifies it:

```
[0.7s ] cmd.exe      ... gateway stat...
[15.s ] tasklist.exe C:\Windows\System32\tasklist.exe /FI "PID eq 8728" /FO CSV /NH
```

The Gateway PID lookup is done through `tasklist.exe` and it stalls for ~15 s inside `spawnSync`.

Critically, the identical command from PowerShell is fast:

```
tasklist.exe /FI "PID eq 8728" /FO CSV /NH   → 0.07 s
tasklist.exe /FO CSV /NH                     → 0.23 s
schtasks /Query /TN "OpenClaw Gateway"       → 0.05 s
sc.exe query                                 → 0.03 s
```

So this is not a slow OS query and not AV file scanning (adding `node_modules` and `node.exe` to Defender exclusions changed nothing: 16.4 s → 16.73 s). The same binary is fast when spawned normally and slow when spawned synchronously from this call site, which points at how the child is spawned/inherited (stdio wiring, job-object attachment, or console inheritance) rather than at `tasklist` itself.

### Suggested fixes

Ordered by effort:

1. **Drop `tasklist` for PID liveness checks.** Node can check a Windows PID without shelling out — `process.kill(pid, 0)` throws `ESRCH` for a dead PID, and on Windows throws `EPERM` while the process exists. That removes the child process entirely and turns a 15 s stall into microseconds. One caveat: PID reuse, so pair it with the existing start-time/heartbeat record rather than PID alone.

2. **If a child is required, stop using a synchronous spawn on a status path.** `spawnSync` blocks the event loop and gives no timeout control. An async `execFile` with `timeout: 2000` on the status path would degrade to "service state unknown" instead of a 15 s freeze.

3. **Add a timeout to the current call.** Whatever the underlying cause, a synchronous call with no timeout in a user-facing status command is a footgun. Even `spawnSync(..., { timeout: 3000 })` bounds the damage.

4. **Prefer native APIs for service state.** `sc.exe query` and `schtasks /Query` both measured ≤50 ms; the scheduled-task registration is readable through the Task Scheduler COM API without a child process at all.

5. **Report CLI-inspection time separately from Gateway health.** `gateway status` currently conflates "is the service running" with "how fast does the Gateway answer". A user with a healthy Gateway (149 ms) sees a 17 s command and concludes the Gateway is broken — I ran this investigation because of exactly that misreading.

### Reproduction

```powershell
# healthy gateway, still slow
curl.exe -m 5 -s -o NUL -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}s\n" http://127.0.0.1:18789/health
# → 200 0.149s

Measure-Command { openclaw gateway status }
# → ~17-22s

# the culprit, called out of the same context, is instantly fast
Measure-Command { tasklist.exe /FI "PID eq <gateway-pid>" /FO CSV /NH }
# → ~0.07s
```

### Impact

Any Windows deployment where an operator or an automation polls `gateway status` pays 17–22 s of wall clock and a blocked event loop per call. In my case a scheduled self-check treated this latency as a Gateway performance regression, which is a plausible failure mode for other users' monitoring too.

---

Filed manually after on-host diagnosis; happy to run further instrumentation against a patched build if useful.

issues.body:
### Summary

Add an opt-in Google Chat setting, `threadSessions` (default `false`), that keys each space thread to its own session when replies are threaded (`replyToMode: "first" | "all" | "batched"`). Existing configs keep today's one-session-per-space behavior.

### Problem to solve

With `replyToMode: "all"`, OpenClaw already replies inside the inbound thread, so a Google Chat space reads as one thread per question. But every thread in the space still resolves to the same session, `agent:<agentId>:googlechat:group:<spaceId>`. Here `<spaceId>` is the full resource name, for example `spaces/AAAA`.

When a bot is added to a shared space and several people ask unrelated questions in separate threads, this causes:

- **Context bleed:** an answer in thread B can draw on a different person's question and answer from thread A.
- **Serialization:** concurrent questions in different threads queue behind one session.
- **Disclosure risk for support-style bots:** one asker's thread content enters the context used to answer another asker.

**My use case.** We run OpenClaw as an internal consulting bot for our engineering team. The bot sits in one shared Google Chat space with `requireMention: true` and `replyToMode: "all"`, and answers from our service docs through memory search.

- Engineers from different teams @mention it to ask about a service: endpoints, deployment environments, alerting.
- Each question starts its own thread, follow-ups stay in that thread, and several threads are often active at the same time.
- We expect each thread to behave like its own conversation. Today it doesn't: every thread shares one session, so a follow-up such as "which of those is the health check?" can resolve against a different person's thread, and one asker's question becomes context for everyone else's answers.

The thread UI suggests isolation, but the session does not provide it. Mattermost, Microsoft Teams (`extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/thread-session.ts`) and Slack already key sessions by thread. Google Chat has no way to do this today.

### Proposed solution

Add `channels.googlechat.threadSessions` (boolean, default `false`; also per account under `accounts.<id>`).

- **Unset or `false`:** no change. One session per space, even with threaded replies.
- **`true`:** when the message is from a space (not a DM), `replyToMode` is set and not `"off"`, and the message carries `thread.name`, derive the session key with the existing `resolveThreadSessionKeys` helper from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/routing`:

  ```
  agent:<agentId>:googlechat:group:<spaceId>:thread:<threadId>
  ```

- **`replyToMode` keeps its meaning.** It still decides only where replies go. `threadSessions` adds nothing when replies are top-level, because there is no thread to key on.

Details:

- **One decision point.** The monitor already computes the effective reply thread (space message and `replyToMode` not `"off"`). The session key reuses it, so reply placement and session keying cannot drift apart.
- **Use the thread key everywhere.** It goes to access-policy context binding, `buildContext` (as `dispatchSessionKey`; `routeSessionKey` stays the space key) and `resolveTurn`.
- **Thread sessions start fresh: no `parentSessionKey` is passed.** This differs on purpose from Microsoft Teams and Mattermost room threads, which fork their base session.
  - In those channels the top-level post lands in the base session, and the thread inherits it to see the post it replies to.
  - In Google Chat, every space message, including the first one, already carries `thread.name`, so it goes straight into its thread session.
  - Forking would therefore add no thread context. It would only copy space history from other askers into each thread, which is the leak this setting removes.
  - This matches Slack's default `inheritParent: false`.
- **Thread ids use the default lowercase normalization.** Google Chat thread ids are mixed case. With a case-preserving `normalizeThreadId`, the dispatch key differed from the stored session key, and every reply failed with `Reply execution target differs from its captured source`.
- **Docs:** `docs/channels/googlechat.md` documents the setting, its dependency on threaded replies, and the fresh start.

**New config option:** following "ask before adding config options", I'd like maintainer approval for `threadSessions`. It is a separate option, not an extension of `replyToMode`, because reply placement and session scope are different concerns. Tying them together would silently change session behavior for every existing config that threads replies.

### Alternatives considered

- **Fork the space session into each thread** (`parentSessionKey`). This keeps prior space context but copies it into every thread, which is the leak this setting removes.
- **Use `replyToMode: "off"`.** This keeps one shared session but gives up threaded replies, so concurrent questions interleave at the top level.
- **`session.threadBindings` / thread-bound subagent sessions.** These solve a different problem (binding a spawned session to a thread), not per-thread routing of inbound channel messages.

### Impact

- **Affected:** Google Chat spaces with threaded replies, especially shared spaces where several people ask the bot questions at the same time.
- **Severity:** blocks workflow for shared or support-style spaces. It is a data-exposure risk there, because one person's question content can surface in another person's answer.
- **Frequency:** always, for every thread after the first in a space with threaded replies.
- **Consequence:**
  - Answers are wrong or confused because of unrelated context from other threads.
  - Concurrent askers wait on each other.
  - Operators must use one space per asker, or turn threading off, to keep conversations apart.
- **Behavior change for existing users:** none. The setting defaults to `false`. Turning it on starts every thread in a space with a fresh session.

### Evidence/examples

Prior art in this repo:

- `extensions/mattermost/src/mattermost/monitor-context.ts`
- `extensions/msteams/src/monitor-handler/thread-session.ts`
- `extensions/slack/src/monitor/message-handler/prepare-routing.ts`

Validation on a local build of `main` (`c8f87b2e516`) with the patch, running the Gateway in Docker against a real Google Chat app (Workspace add-on, webhook auth with `audienceType: "app-url"` and `appPrincipal`), `replyToMode: "all"`, `threadSessions: true` and `requireMention: true`:

1. @mention in a space: the reply posts in the inbound thread, and the session key is `agent:main:googlechat:group:spaces/<space>:thread:<threadId>`.
2. A follow-up @mention in the same thread uses that thread's earlier exchange.
3. A question in another thread cannot see the first thread's content.
4. `openclaw sessions` / the Control UI list one session per thread.
5. A message without an @mention gets no reply.

I repeated the same five checks with the patch applied to the `v2026.10.9` release tag, using the same setup and four concurrent threads. They gave the same results: four threads mapped to four thread sessions, and no shared space session.

Tests:

- New monitor cases cover `threadSessions` on/off with `replyToMode` `all`/`off`. The `threadSessions: true` + `replyToMode: "all"` case fails on `main` and passes with the patch; the unset case guards the default.
- `pnpm test:extension googlechat`, `pnpm test:contracts:channels`, `pnpm tsgo:extensions`, `config:channels:check` and `config:docs:check` pass, and `oxfmt` is clean.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself

### Additional information

- I have a branch ready: about 20 lines of source, one schema line plus regenerated config metadata, tests and docs ([compare](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/compare/main...maxence2997:openclaw:feat/googlechat-thread-sessions)). I'll open the PR against this issue if the direction is acceptable.
- While testing I found that Workspace Add-on apps need `botUser`: their mention annotations name the app by numeric `users/<id>`, so `requireMention` drops every message without it. The docs call `botUser` optional; the branch adds a one-line docs note. I can split that into its own PR if preferred.
- Related but distinct: #184592 (referenced-message context for thread replies). That issue notes that per-thread isolation and referenced-message content are separate requirements. This proposal covers only isolation and routing.

issues.body:
# Codex harness: thread stays "claimed by active work" after turn completes, wedging the session until gateway restart

## Summary

With the Codex agent harness, a session's Codex thread is not released after a turn finishes normally. Every following message to that session fails with:

```
Codex thread <threadId> is claimed by active work; stop it first.
```

The harness does not fall back (`Codex agent harness failed; not falling back to embedded OpenClaw backend`), so the agent stops replying entirely. Restarting the gateway clears it, but the next completed turn on the new thread wedges it again.

## Environment

- OpenClaw CLI: 2026.10.9 (8b18b55), Homebrew `openclaw-cli`
- `@openclaw/codex` plugin: 2026.10.9
- `@openai/codex`: 0.160.0 (darwin-x64 app-server)
- Node: v26.13.0
- macOS 15.8.2 (x86_64), gateway under launchd (`ai.openclaw.gateway`, port 18789)
- Channel: Discord DM, agent on Codex harness (`openai/gpt-5.6-sol`, fallback `gpt-5.6-luna`)

## Steps to reproduce

1. Run an agent on the Codex harness, bound to a Discord DM.
2. Send a message, and let the turn run tools and finish normally.
3. Send another message to the same session.

**Expected:** the second message runs a new turn on the thread.
**Actual:** it fails immediately with `is claimed by active work`. Every later message fails the same way, and each model fallback candidate fails too, until the gateway restarts.

## Evidence

The latest stuck thread is `01a19f8e-60b7-7fb1-b2ec-4689de6cc154`. Its rollout file shows the last turn ending cleanly:

```
2026-11-03T04:02:17.208Z  event_msg  task_complete  turn_id=01a19f90-5a8d-7000-8871-ed9011a6f36f
```

Three minutes later, the next inbound message was rejected:

```
2026-11-03T04:05:09.836Z  ERROR  Codex thread 01a19f8e-... is claimed by active work; stop it first.
```

Around turn completion, the log also has:

```
WARN agent/embedded  codex settled-turn finalization context is unavailable  reason=context_unavailable
INFO agent/embedded  codex app-server turn released after terminal dynamic tool result  tool=sessions_yield
```

The pattern repeats across gateway restarts (all times UTC, 2026-11-02 to 11-03):

| Thread | First error | Last error | Failures |
|---|---|---|---|
| 01a198bb-6040-70c1-8f60-2f24f2b70f2a | 13:30 | 01:59 | 35 |
| 01a19d4f-9fa8-7792-bc33-5b234394551a | 17:36 | 00:44 | 90 |
| 01a19f19-7e19-7430-9b32-49bc9ec81120 | 02:20 | 03:39 | 37 |
| 01a19f8e-60b7-7fb1-b2ec-4689de6cc154 | 04:05 | 05:06 | 29 |

The same error also appeared on 2026-11-01 for thread `01a198a5-3bd1-7250-af32-9f7e6d73e46d` (14 failures). Gateway restarts at 02:02, 03:44 and 03:53 UTC each cleared the wedge only until the next completed turn.

The claim doesn't appear in `state/openclaw.sqlite` (`state_leases` holds only `gateway-owner`) or in the agent's `openclaw-agent.sqlite`. It seems to live only in gateway memory, which would explain why a restart clears it. The error string comes from `@openclaw/codex/dist/.setup/thread-lifecycle-run-*.mjs` and `session-retirement-*.mjs`.

## Possibly related symptoms on the same gateway

- About 70 Codex app-server or code-mode-host processes (about 3.3 GB RSS) built up as children of the gateway within ~75 minutes of a restart. The gateway itself ran at ~150% CPU and 3 GB RSS, and CLI commands (`openclaw status`, `openclaw codex --help`) hung. After a restart, this dropped to one Codex process.
- A `memory-core` short-term workspace lock was held by a pid that no longer exists (`Timed out waiting for memory workspace lock ... held by 53114:...`).
- `memory session startup catch-up failed: Error: Agent database Worker owner is closed`.

## Related issues

- #188422: a sibling native child holds the parent, giving "claimed by active work". The shape is similar (the turn also ended through `sessions_yield`), but the stuck thread here made no native `spawn_agent` calls during its turns.
- #190932: the first dashboard reply hits the claimed-work guard on 2026.10.9. Here the first turn succeeds and every later turn fails.
- #172837, #182549, #181046: earlier claim, pin and fallback bugs.

## Suggested direction

The thread claim should be released whenever a turn reaches `task_complete`, including when settled-turn finalization hits `context_unavailable` or the turn ends through a terminal dynamic tool such as `sessions_yield`. A stale claim whose turn has already completed should also expire or be reclaimable, so the session doesn't stay dead until a restart.

issues.body:
## Feature request: one-way A2A dispatch that also suppresses failure receipts

Re-filing #44309 with current reproduction details, as the bot's close message instructed. The original was closed for inactivity on 2026-11-12, two days before we landed our third and strongest repro (2026-11-14).

Environment: OpenClaw 2026.11.4 (d843d6a), macOS, single Gateway, 11 agents.

## The gap

An agent cannot send a message to another agent without a reply coming back. Every `sessions_send` starts a turn on the target, and that turn's result is routed back to the sender as an inbound message. There is no way to express "this is one-way; nothing should come back."

This is not only inconvenient — it is the root cause of three distinct loops we have now hit in production.

## Three manifestations, all the same root cause

| # | Shape | Trigger | Fixable by policy? |
|---|-------|---------|--------------------|
| 1 | Agent echo | A dispatches, B replies, the reply re-enters A's turn, A replies again | Yes — a written rule ("stay silent on your own message routed back") handles it |
| 2 | Mandatory reply-back | Every dispatch must return a peer result, even when the dispatcher is fire-and-forget | No — this is the original report |
| 3 | **Failure receipt loop** | A failed send generates a receipt; the receipt re-enters the dispatcher as inbound; acting on it produces another send, which fails | No — new, detailed below |

## Repro for case 3 (the one the previous thread did not cover)

1. Configure a scheduled job that dispatches to an agent session.
2. Make that session unreachable — delete it, or restart the Gateway while a run is in flight.
3. `sessions_send` fails and the runtime produces:

```
sessions_send delivery to agent:<target>:main failed. The target may not have
received the message; retry or report the failure instead of assuming
delivery succeeded.
```

4. That receipt is delivered back to the dispatcher as a normal inbound message.
5. The dispatcher, following its own instructions ("do not assume delivery succeeded"), acts on it — which means another `sessions_send` to the same unreachable target.
6. That send fails, producing another receipt. Loop.

Observed: **11 receipts over roughly 6 minutes**, with no user input anywhere in the loop. It terminated only when we stopped answering and the target session was restarted.

Why the existing policy workaround fails here, specifically:

- **The receipts are generated by the runtime, not an agent.** Staying silent does not stop the next one; the failure that generates it is independent of whether the dispatcher answers.
- **Staying silent is the wrong response** — the receipt says delivery failed, so silence looks like ignoring a real error.
- **Answering makes it worse.** Acting on the receipt produces another send, another failure, another receipt. The only exits are "wait it out" or "restart the session", neither of which is a fix.

So this is not a discipline problem that belongs in user-land. It is the missing capability showing up in a place the original report did not anticipate.

## What the capability needs to cover

The acceptance contract for `replyExpected: false` should include delivery-failure receipts, not just peer results:

> **Delivery-failure receipts must honour the one-way flag.** If a dispatch was sent with no reply expected, a failure to deliver it should surface in the dispatcher's own error channel — a log line, a metric, a direct return value — not as a new inbound message that re-enters the turn loop.

Without that clause a reply-free dispatch still cannot be fire-and-forget: the moment the target is unreachable, the "no reply expected" promise is broken by the runtime itself.

## Concrete proposal

For `sessions_send` with `replyExpected: false`:

- **Success**: return `{ status: "accepted", runId, targetDisposition }`. No peer result, no receipt.
- **Failure**: return `{ status: "failed", error, targetDisposition }` **in the same synchronous return value**, and do not route a receipt back as an inbound message.
- **Retry policy, if any, belongs to the dispatcher.** The runtime should not self-retry into the same session and re-enter the loop.

Equivalent naming is fine; the contract is what matters.

## Why this matters beyond our setup

We can absorb this because our loop rate was low and the condition cleared. A dispatcher that retries automatically, or a busier schedule, turns the same bug into an unbounded message storm between runtime components with no human in the loop.

There is also a second practical consequence worth noting: a health-check style job that must notify on failure is exactly the pattern this blocks. The job needs to say "tell agent X, but do not start a conversation with it" — and today that is impossible without risking the loop above.

## What we already do instead

For anyone hitting this in the meantime, the workaround that has held for us:

1. A written team rule: on receiving your own message routed back, or an empty announce step, stay silent.
2. On a failure receipt: **do not answer and do not retry**. If a resend is genuinely needed, send once and then ignore all receipts.
3. Route unattended notifications through an external channel (we send email) rather than agent-to-agent dispatch, so no agent turn is created at all.

That last point is the real tell: to avoid a ping-pong we had to leave the agent system entirely.

Happy to test a preview build — this reproduces on demand by sending to a session that has been deleted or is mid-restart.

issues.body:
### Summary

The **memory forget index-planning path** in released **2026.11.4** and the current `main` source still binds an arbitrarily large `chunkIds` array directly into SQLite `IN (...)` predicates. For a single historical session with enough indexed chunks, the **read-only** `openclaw memory forget --dry-run --json` planning step can exceed SQLite's bind-variable limit before it produces a deletion report.

This is a **distinct query owner** from the session-memory origin-sync bind-limit bug fixed under #164283 / #167838. I have a historical real-world `too many SQL variables` failure consistent with this failure class, plus current-source evidence of the unbounded queries. **I have not executed a fresh production or synthetic runtime reproduction against 2026.11.4/main**, and cannot prove that these exact queries caused the 2026.9.3 occurrence.

### Source evidence on the released tag and current main

File: [`extensions/memory-core/src/memory-forget-index-read.ts` on v2026.11.4](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.11.4/extensions/memory-core/src/memory-forget-index-read.ts).

1. The reader collects all chunks selected for removal and constructs `const chunkIds = chunks.map((chunk) => chunk.id)` (around line 98).
2. **FTS row-count preview** contains the nested query `.where("id", "in", chunkIds)` (around line 112). In Kysely this expands the array into one SQL placeholder per ID.
3. **SQLite vec0 row-count preview** uses `.where("id", "in", result.value.chunks.map((chunk) => chunk.id))` (around lines 172–177), with the same unbounded shape.
4. [`memory-forget.ts`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/v2026.11.4/extensions/memory-core/src/memory-forget.ts) invokes `planMemoryIndex(...)` **before** the `if (params.dryRun ...)` return. Consequently `--dry-run` reaches these count queries.

The [current-main version of the same file](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/extensions/memory-core/src/memory-forget-index-read.ts) still shows the SQLite FTS and vec0 `IN` arrays (around lines 120 and 204). It uses `sqliteStringSet(chunkIds)` in a separate **PostgreSQL** branch, but not for these SQLite count queries. These statements do not bound the number of placeholders.

This is source-backed exposure, **not a claim of a measured current-main failure**.

### Historical field observation (2026.9.3)

- Ubuntu/Linux x64; npm-global installation; systemd-user Gateway; SQLite-backed `memory-core`; Ollama embeddings.
- A completed, no-longer-active historical session had approximately **627,049 transcript events** and **1.41 GB** of transcript payload.
- The agent SQLite database was approximately **4.7 GiB**, structurally healthy (`PRAGMA quick_check = ok`; zero foreign-key violations).
- `memory` + `sessions` indexing produced approximately **74,970 chunks in total**, **72,439** from session sources. The number of chunks selected for the single session was **not separately counted**.
- On that installation, the documented CLI command failed:

```console
$ openclaw memory forget --agent main --session <synthetic-placeholder> --dry-run --json
Memory forget failed: too many SQL variables
```

- We did not delete the original transcript. We eventually excluded session transcripts from memory indexing, reset **derived** memory indexes, compacted SQLite, and rebuilt the `memory`-only index. Gateway responsiveness recovered. This mitigation does **not** demonstrate that the forget bug was fixed.

No private session ID, session key, transcript, user identity, hostname, IP, bot details, or raw SQLite contents are provided.

### Synthetic regression requested

In a disposable fixture, populate enough `memory_index_chunks` associated with **one selected session** to exceed the runtime's SQLite `SQLITE_LIMIT_VARIABLE_NUMBER`, ensuring FTS and/or vec0 index tables exist. Then invoke the standard forget planner with that session under `--dry-run --json`.

Expected: the planner returns a bounded, nonmutating report, irrespective of chunk count. Ideally regression assertions separately exercise the FTS count and vec0 count branches, including counts **above** the effective SQLite variable limit.

Predicted from the current query shape: SQLite statement preparation can fail with `too many SQL variables` when the selected chunk-ID list exceeds that limit. The disposable fixture has **not** been run as part of this report.

### Expected behavior / suggested fix

Use a bounded set representation (e.g. the existing `sqliteStringSet(...)` / `json_each(?)` approach where supported) or bounded chunked counting for **both** SQLite count queries, preserving accurate FTS/vector row counts and read-only dry-run semantics. Do not loosen database ownership/maintenance guards.

An alternative is a set-oriented join / temporary read-only selection that avoids enumerating every chunk ID as a separate SQL parameter.

### Why this is not a duplicate

- **#164283 / #167838**: fixed the **session-memory synchronization and origin/tombstone lookups**, not this `forget-index-plan` FTS/vec0 count path.
- **#176243**: `memory forget` fails with **`ERR_WORKER_OUT_OF_MEMORY`** from large original transcript hydration; the reporter isolated a 512 MiB transcript reader limit. The error and proposed mitigation differ from the **SQLite parameter limit** here.
- **#181459 / #118885**: agent-DB size and repeated integrity-check performance, not forget-preview SQL parameterization.

### Impact / caveats

A single sufficiently large retained session may make the supported privacy/retention cleanup command unable to generate even a preview. Priority is a maintainer decision. This source examination does not establish current-runtime reproducibility, the exact historical failing statement, or any corruption or data loss.

I am reporting this without rerunning potentially expensive forget/index operations against a healthy production database. A disposable synthetic fixture is the next step.

issues.body:
## Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

## Beta release blocker

No

## Summary

With `appServer.sandbox: "workspace-write"` plus `appServer.networkProxy.enabled: true`, the bundled Codex plugin generates a permission profile whose filesystem map is only

```js
{ ":minimal": "read", ":project_roots": { ".": fileSystemMode } }
```

(`resolveCodexAppServerNetworkProxy` in `extensions/codex/src/app-server/config-security.ts`). There is no `":slash_tmp"` entry, so under bubblewrap the sandboxed command has no writable `/tmp`. Plain `workspace-write` without the proxy keeps `/tmp` writable (`codexSandboxPolicyForTurn` sends `excludeSlashTmp: false` unless `sandbox_workspace_write.exclude_slash_tmp` is set). Turning on the network proxy therefore silently removes `/tmp`, and none of the `networkProxy` options can add it back: they only shape the `network` block and the profile name.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure the bundled Codex harness:
   ```json5
   plugins: { entries: { codex: { config: { appServer: {
     sandbox: "workspace-write",
     approvalPolicy: "never",
     networkProxy: { enabled: true, domains: { "*": "allow" }, dangerouslyAllowAllUnixSockets: true }
   } } } } }
   ```
2. In a Codex turn, run `printf x > /tmp/t.txt`, or `soffice --headless --convert-to pdf --outdir /tmp /tmp/t.txt`.

## Expected behavior

The generated profile keeps the same `/tmp` access that `workspace-write` grants, for example by adding `":slash_tmp": fileSystemMode` unless `exclude_slash_tmp` is set (and honoring `exclude_tmpdir_env_var`). Alternatively, `networkProxy` could accept extra filesystem entries for the generated profile.

## Actual behavior

`/tmp` is not available inside the sandbox. Tools that hardcode `/tmp` fail; LibreOffice headless fails with `no valid pipe path found`.

## OpenClaw version

Observed on 2026.10.7. The generating code is byte-identical in `@openclaw/codex` 2026.11.1 through 2026.11.4 (`dist/.setup/config-security-BxV4sSRz.mjs`) and unchanged in 2026.11.5-beta.4 (now in `config-options-*.mjs`).

## Operating system

Ubuntu 26.04 (bubblewrap through the `bwrap-userns-restrict` AppArmor profile), Node 26.13.1.

## Install method

npm global install; Codex plugin installed with `openclaw plugins install codex`.

## Model

openai/gpt-6.1-sol

## Provider / routing chain

OpenAI (ChatGPT OAuth) → bundled Codex app-server harness (`@openclaw/codex` 2026.11.4, Codex CLI 0.164.0).

## Additional provider/model setup details

Gateway-side OpenClaw sandbox is off; Codex's own permission profile is the only sandbox.

## Logs

```
no valid pipe path found
```

## Impact and severity

Any agent that needs network through `networkProxy` loses `/tmp`, which breaks LibreOffice conversions and other tools that write there. We run a one-line local patch that adds `":slash_tmp": fileSystemMode` to the profile. When doing so, keep the gateway's own `/tmp/openclaw` (file logs) denied, e.g. `"/tmp/openclaw": "deny"`, if the host `/tmp` is shared with the gateway.

issues.body:
**Version:** OpenClaw 2026.11.3 Control UI (`control-ui-boot-shared-*.js`, dictation controller), iPhone, WebKit (Safari, home-screen web app, and WKWebView-hosted).

## Summary
On phones, composer dictation (hold the microphone button) loses a whole recording with no error and no retry in three common situations:

1. **Screen auto-lock / app switch during a recording.** `visibilitychange → hidden` calls `handleWindowBlur()`, which calls `stop({commit:false})`. That cancels the transcription session and throws away everything captured so far. A partial transcript is not kept.
2. **Lock or blur while the transcript is finalising.** File-based transcription runs when capture ends; we measured `talk.session.close` taking up to 20 s for a long note. If the page is hidden or blurred during that window, `retirePendingCommit()` cancels the pending commit. Nothing reaches the composer or the gateway.
3. **Any system dialog during the first press.** `window blur` also cancels, so the iOS/WebKit microphone permission prompt aborts the press that triggered it. The user has to allow, then press again.

Audio is streamed live with `talk.session.appendAudio` and is not buffered on the client (before the session exists it buffers only `BM = 10 s @ 8 kHz`). If the socket drops, there is nothing to resend.

## Repro
1. Open the Control UI on an iPhone with auto-lock set to 30 s, with dictation configured (`tools.media.models` audio).
2. Hold the mic and speak for more than 30 s without moving your finger. The screen locks and the note is lost; the gateway shows `talk.session.close` and no `chat.send`.
3. Or record a 60 s+ note, release, then lock the phone straight away. The transcript is lost.

## Expected
- While a recording is active (and while it is finalising), request a **Screen Wake Lock** (`navigator.wakeLock.request('screen')`, available in Safari 16.4+).
- When the page is hidden, **stop and commit** (`stop({commit:true})`) instead of discarding, or keep the partial transcript in the composer draft. Treat `blur` caused by permission dialogs as non-fatal.
- Keep the captured audio (or the finished transcript) on the client until the gateway confirms it, and show a visible **Retry** if it fails. The composer already has durable pending-input custody for typed text; dictation should end in the same custody.
- Offer **tap to start / tap to stop** as well as hold-to-talk. This is an accessibility need, and long holds are fragile on touch screens: `pointercancel` or a small finger slide outside the button bounds cancels the note. Today a short tap opens Talk or the picker instead.

## Workarounds today
- Raise Auto-Lock (Settings → Display & Brightness → Auto-Lock) to 2–5 minutes while dictating.
- Keep notes short and wait until the text appears in the composer before you lock the phone.
- Use the iOS keyboard's own dictation key in the composer. It is processed on the device and inserts text directly, so it survives a slow gateway.

issues.body:
### User-facing impact
When background work resumes the assistant, human corrections can sit queued until that work finishes. The assistant continues without the correction, so users cannot reliably redirect an ongoing task without interrupting it. Repeating the correction with an @mention did not help.

This is not just a delayed answer: **the running assistant does not receive the updated instruction.** Subsequent actions could therefore use superseded instructions. No destructive action or data loss is claimed here.

### Observed failure
On OpenClaw **2026.11.3**, Discord, macOS arm64, using the **built-in runtime, not Codex**, steering was rejected with `tool_authority_mismatch` during two completion turns from explicitly backgrounded exec listeners. Collaborative steering was already enabled.

Two corrections waited approximately **153 and 95 seconds** before being stored as follow-ups; response delivery was later still.

### Trigger sequence
1. Start exec work with `background:true` in Discord.
2. Let its completion notification resume the assistant and continue working.
3. Send a correction from the original allowed sender in the same conversation.
4. Observe rejection with `tool_authority_mismatch` and deferral instead of active-run consumption.

### Candidate-release finding
Official **2026.11.5-beta.3** includes requester retention (#185476) and required-answer promotion (#176245), but controlled compiled-module tests found a remaining conversation-identity gap:

- `buildSessionEventContext` omits `ChatId`; finalization leaves it absent.
- Run assembly copies that missing value into `conversationId`.
- Discord’s same-conversation authority projection requires a nonempty matching ID.

The actual builder/finalizer output could not preserve the unchanged authority snapshot. Supplying the matching conversation ID enabled that path.

**These are isolated tests, not a live beta Discord reproduction.**

### Expected resolution
Compatible human corrections should reach the active run at a supported boundary, without cancellation or expanded permissions. Preserve authenticated requester **and conversation identity** through completion handoffs, retain required human answers, and keep existing revocation and route/thread checks.

Please cover explicit-background completion followed by same-conversation human steering in a regression test.

Related: #170216. #196358 and #173360 concern other steering gates.

issues.body:
## Summary

Add a dispatch-only / handoff mode for agent-to-agent message delivery that drops a task into the target session without reply-back ping-pong or announce back to the requester.

## Problem to solve

Current `sessions_send` semantics are great for agent-to-agent conversation, but they are a poor fit for a very common controller/worker workflow:

1. Agent A chooses the next task and the responsible department/worker
2. Agent A sends a fully-formed task order to Agent B
3. The human then switches to Agent B's main session and continues there

In that workflow, Agent A's job should end after dispatch.

Today, `sessions_send` always carries the reply-back ping-pong + announce lifecycle. That creates several problems for pure handoff scenarios:

- the target agent's first reply is re-injected into the requester session as an `inter_session` message
- the requester agent may then respond to that injected message, creating an unnecessary extra loop
- the final announce step still runs even though the use case was dispatch, not conversation
- requester transcripts get polluted with worker-side acceptance / planning chatter
- in some UIs, the injected `inter_session` message can be visually confused with a user-authored message

This is not just cosmetic. It changes the workflow semantics. A one-way handoff ends up behaving like an internal conversation, which adds token cost, transcript noise, and routing confusion.

## Proposed solution

Add an explicit dispatch-only mode for A2A delivery.

Any of the following shapes would solve the problem:

1. Extend `sessions_send` with an explicit mode or flags, for example:
   - `mode: "dispatch"`
   - or `replyBack: false`
   - or `announce: false`
2. Or add a separate primitive such as `sessions_deliver` / `sessions_enqueue` with one-way semantics

Requested behavior for dispatch mode:

- persist the message into the target session
- let the target session continue normally from there
- do not run reply-back ping-pong
- do not re-inject the target's first reply into the requester session
- do not run announce back to the requester unless explicitly requested
- optionally allow a minimal structured ack if the caller wants delivery confirmation

This would cleanly separate two valid A2A patterns:

- conversation / coordination
- one-way dispatch / handoff

## Alternatives considered

- Using `sessions_send` as-is and relying on prompting to suppress reply/announce behavior is brittle because the current lifecycle is framework-driven, not just model-driven.
- Setting `timeoutSeconds: 0` is not enough because it changes waiting behavior, not the underlying reply-back / announce semantics.
- Hard-banning A2A for dispatch workflows is too restrictive because A2A conversation is still useful in other cases.
- Existing announce suppression requests help with one part of the problem, but they do not address the earlier reply-back reinjection into the requester session.

## Impact

Affected: multi-agent controller/worker setups, especially when one agent routes work to another agent's main session
Severity: Medium to High for orchestrated workflows
Frequency: Common whenever `sessions_send` is used for handoff instead of negotiation
Consequence: extra token usage, polluted requester transcripts, confusing turn ownership, and workflow drift from "dispatch" into "conversation"

## Evidence/examples

Observed behavior in the current flow:

1. Agent A calls `sessions_send` to Agent B with a fully-formed task order
2. Agent B replies normally
3. That reply is re-injected into Agent A's session as an `inter_session` user message
4. Agent A may respond to that injected message even though the handoff was already complete
5. The announce step then runs on top of that

Related issues that touch adjacent parts of the same lifecycle:

- #8299 `Feature request: config option to suppress sub-agent announce`
- #33478 `[Feature]: Structured Callback Actions and Thread Context Inheritance for Agent Handoffs`
- #39476 `A2A sessions_send: target agent can call sessions_send back, causing duplicate messages`

## Additional information

The current `sessions_send` behavior makes sense for agent-to-agent coordination. The missing piece is a first-class dispatch semantic for cases where the caller wants a clean handoff and does not want the requester session pulled back into the loop.

This should ideally be an explicit framework-level mode rather than something enforced through prompt conventions or magic strings.

### Bug type

Regression (worked before, now fails)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

In the macOS app on current `main`, the first chat message after a fresh onboarding fails with "This host is low on memory, so it could not start another session." The Mac has plenty of memory. The packaged Gateway runs on Bun, and under Bun `process.availableMemory()` returns only truly free pages, so the 1 GiB Claude CLI live-session guard trips on a healthy Mac.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Build the macOS app from `main` at d29fad4e3e687dedf683e38ec35b12cb85510637 (`scripts/package-mac-app.sh`, debug, arm64) and launch it on a fresh profile (`OPENCLAW_PROFILE=onboarding`).
2. Complete onboarding with a local Gateway, using Claude Code (`claude-cli/claude-opus-5-5`) as the AI.
3. Choose **Talk to my agent** and send `hi`.

### Expected behavior

The agent replies. The host was a 48 GB Apple silicon MacBook Pro, and `memory_pressure` reported "System-wide memory free percentage: 70%" at the time.

### Actual behavior

The turn fails before any model call. The chat shows "This host is low on memory, so it could not start another session. Try again after active conversations finish." with Try again / Report a bug.

Gateway log (`~/.openclaw-onboarding/logs/openclaw-onboarding-2026-11-16.log`):

```
lane task error: lane=cli:claude-cli:owner:… durationMs=5 error="Host memory is too low for another CLI live session."
cli terminal failure: provider=claude-cli model=claude-opus-5-5 durationMs=344 … error=Host memory is too low for another CLI live session.
model fallback decision: … reason=rate_limit status=429 code=cli_live_session_host_memory … fallbackStepFinalOutcome=chain_exhausted fallbackConfigured=false
Embedded agent failed before reply: Host memory is too low for another CLI live session.
```

The same Mac, measured with the bundled runtime and with Node at the same moment:

| Runtime | `process.availableMemory()` | `os.freemem()` | `os.totalmem()` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bundled Bun 1.4.4 (`~/.openclaw-onboarding/runtime/…/bin/bun`) | 548,831,232 (0.55 GB) | 548,831,232 | 51,539,607,552 |
| Node 26.12.1 | 19,644,563,456 (19.6 GB) | 548,831,232 | — |

Under Bun on macOS, `process.availableMemory()` is identical to `os.freemem()`. macOS keeps truly free pages low, so most Macs in normal use read below 1 GiB.

### OpenClaw version

main d29fad4e3e687dedf683e38ec35b12cb85510637 (2026.11.4, app build 2611160101)

### Operating system

macOS 26.5.1 (arm64)

### Install method

mac app (locally packaged from `main`, isolated `OPENCLAW_PROFILE`)

### Model

claude-cli/claude-opus-5-5 (shown in the UI as anthropic/claude-opus-5-5)

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw (mac app, local Gateway on Bun) -> claude-cli live session -> Anthropic

### Additional provider/model setup details

No fallback model configured (fresh onboarding default).

### Logs

See Actual behavior.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

Code at the tested commit:

- [`src/infra/host-memory.ts#L8-L14`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/d29fad4e3e687dedf683e38ec35b12cb85510637/src/infra/host-memory.ts#L8-L14): `readHostFreeMemoryBytes()` uses `process.availableMemory()` on darwin. Its doc comment assumes Node semantics ("Node's available-memory reading includes inactive and purgeable pages").
- [`src/agents/cli-runner/cli-live-session-registry.ts#L19`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/d29fad4e3e687dedf683e38ec35b12cb85510637/src/agents/cli-runner/cli-live-session-registry.ts#L19) and [`#L196-L224`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/d29fad4e3e687dedf683e38ec35b12cb85510637/src/agents/cli-runner/cli-live-session-registry.ts#L196-L224): `ensureCliLiveSessionMemory` throws `cli_live_session_host_memory` when that reading is below 1 GiB.
- [`src/agents/failover/user-copy.ts#L66`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/d29fad4e3e687dedf683e38ec35b12cb85510637/src/agents/failover/user-copy.ts#L66): user-facing copy.

### Impact and severity

- **Who:** every macOS app user whose first agent runs through the Claude CLI live session. The packaged Gateway always runs on Bun.
- **Severity:** blocks the first message after onboarding. The user is told their Mac is out of memory when it is not. The error is categorized as `rate_limit`/429, so it is retried or reported as capacity instead of a bug.
- **Release exposure:** the guard is on `main` only. It is not in v2026.11.1–v2026.11.3 or v2026.11.5-beta.1. It will ship in the next release cut from `main` unless fixed.

### Additional information

**Contributing changes.** Each change was reasonable on its own; the failure is in how they combine.

1. #161603 (merged 2026-09-30, first shipped in v2026.10.1) moved the macOS app's private runtime, including the local Gateway, to the OpenClaw Bun fork.
2. #144535 (merged 2026-10-10, shipped in v2026.10.10) added `readHostFreeMemoryBytes()` with a macOS branch that relies on Node's `process.availableMemory()`. The app had already been running on Bun for ten days. At that point the only effect was understated free memory in device/host stats.
3. #192534 (merged 2026-11-04, unreleased) added the blocking 1 GiB guard on top of that helper. Its description states the helper reads `process.availableMemory()` on macOS. Its proof simulated memory at the helper/`os.freemem` seam, so the packaged macOS app on Bun was never exercised.

**Process gaps:**
- Nothing tests the host-memory helper under the runtime the macOS app actually ships (Bun). Unit tests mock the reading.
- No packaged-app smoke test sends a first message after a fresh onboarding. A single "fresh install → first reply" check would have caught this before merge.
- The failure maps to `rate_limit`, which hides a local guard decision behind a provider-capacity category.

**Other callers with the same Bun-on-macOS assumption.** These are not user-blocking but read too low under Bun:
- `src/infra/worker-pool-sizing.ts` `resolveUpdateHashWorkerCount()` (`process.availableMemory()`; only Bun on Linux is special-cased).
- `src/commands/doctor-database-port-memory-concurrency.ts` (`readHostFreeMemoryBytes()` → undersized rebuild concurrency).
- `src/gateway/server-methods/system.ts` and `src/node-host/host-stats.ts` (reported free memory).
- `isConstrainedProcessLowOnMemory()` uses `process.constrainedMemory()`; verify its Bun/macOS behavior while fixing.

**Suggested direction:** on darwin, compute reclaimable memory independently of the JS runtime (Mach VM statistics: free + inactive + purgeable + speculative) or detect a Bun-equivalent reading. Cover it with a test that simulates Bun's `availableMemory == freemem` behavior. Optionally, stop classifying this guard as `rate_limit`.

Found during a fresh-install onboarding walkthrough of the macOS app.

issues.body:
## Problem

With `agents.defaults.compaction.notifyUser: true`, `runSessionCompactionIfNeeded` awaits `beforeCompaction` (the memory flush) first and only then calls `onCompactionStart` / sends "🧹 Compacting context...".

The flush is a full agent turn with a different system prompt and tool set, so a provider prompt cache keyed on the prefix usually misses and the flush re-reads the whole transcript. On a local model near a 256k window that is a cold prefill of several minutes. During it the chat gets no notice and the gateway logs `stuck session ... reason=active_reply_work`, so from the user's side the session looks hung. We observed a 5.5-minute flush on a 244k-token transcript followed by a ~20-second summary.

## Ask

Send the start notice (or a separate "saving memory before compaction" notice) before the memory flush begins, so `notifyUser` covers the whole maintenance window.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Crash (process/app exits or hangs)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

On 2026.10.10, Skill Workshop background experience-review preparation fails with ERR_WORKER_OUT_OF_MEMORY on a large session; the installed caller passes no limits to SessionManager.openModelContextAsync, and an isolated read of the retained database reproduces the worker OOM.

### Steps to reproduce

Observed production path:
1. Use 2026.10.10 with Skill Workshop automatic experience review enabled and a long-lived, tool-heavy main session.
2. Let a normal run finish and the built-in background experience-review preparation execute.
3. Observe "[skills/workshop] skill experience review failed ... ERR_WORKER_OUT_OF_MEMORY".

Isolated diagnostic reproduction already performed on a retained copy of the affected database (not a new production stress test):
1. Use the installed SessionManager.openModelContextAsync on that session in a network-isolated process, with cwd/signal but no limits.
2. It failed after 6172 ms with WorkerTaskError / ERR_WORKER_OUT_OF_MEMORY.
3. Repeat the native context read with bounded options. An 8 MiB / 20000-event experiment with toolResultOverflow:"omit" completed; the saved native-budget run returned 4473 events in 4938 ms.

This is a real-database diagnostic reproduction, not a portable synthetic fixture. The diagnostic called the reader directly; it did not run the complete scheduler/through-anchor/model-review lifecycle. Private transcript/database contents are not published. No known-failing production test was rerun for this issue.

### Expected behavior

Background review preparation should use bounded native context projection, preserve the latest relevant turn/tool pairs/compaction summary, and complete or report a deliberate size limit without exhausting its worker. The same retained database was readable through the bounded native path in the isolated check.

### Actual behavior

Repeated background review preparation errors; a directly invoked unbounded native context read reproduced JS heap exhaustion. The retained journal had 54 matching skill-review OOM log entries across Oct 28–Nov 3, with additional entries on Nov 4. These are log-entry counts, not 54 independently deduplicated model runs.

The installed 2026.10.10 caller (bundle experience-review-DgwNe5z2.mjs, source region src/skills/workshop/experience-review.ts) does:
const sessionManager = await SessionManager.openModelContextAsync(source, {
  cwd: workspaceDir,
  through: candidate.source,
  signal: abortSignal
});
No limits are supplied.

This concerns the transcript/model-context worker's 512 MiB old-generation heap, not the separate foreground SQLite session.actor.read failure in #191847 and not the memory index's input-byte limit in #192762.

### OpenClaw version

2026.10.10 (7dc3350); installed source and isolated saved-database test

### Operating system

Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS, x86_64; Node.js 24.22.2

### Install method

npm global; Gateway as a systemd user service

### Model

NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

### Provider / routing chain

Local Skill Workshop preparation -> SessionManager.openModelContextAsync -> transcript/model-context worker. The failing read precedes review-model inference; no external model/provider is involved in the isolated reproduction.

### Additional provider/model setup details

The foreground agent uses native Codex/OpenAI, but the effective background review model was not recorded in the diagnostic. It should not be inferred from the foreground model. The isolated reproduction disabled network access.

### Logs

```shell
[skills/workshop] skill experience review failed ... ERR_WORKER_OUT_OF_MEMORY

Saved isolated unbounded-read result (installation prefix/IDs omitted):
{"ok":false,"name":"WorkerTaskError","message":"Error [ERR_WORKER_OUT_OF_MEMORY]: Worker terminated due to reaching memory limit: JS heap out of memory","code":"unavailable","elapsedMs":6172}

Saved native-budget read result:
{"ok":true,"mode":"bounded","events":4473,"bytes":8392750,"elapsedMs":4938}

"bytes" is JSON serialization of the returned branch, including framing; it is not a measurement of peak worker heap.
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

A focused local candidate added only:
limits: { maxBytes: 8388608, maxEvents: 20000, toolResultOverflow: "omit" }
at the existing openModelContextAsync call, preserving through/cwd/signal and subsequent preparation-current checks.

Four isolated regression checks passed:
- short context retained;
- old oversized history bounded while latest turn retained;
- owned tool-call/result pairing retained;
- compaction summary retained.

Important limits: the full model-driven background review was not separately completed as an end-to-end acceptance test. The candidate was later reverted by operator choice; the installed review file returned to the original hash. We are reporting the failure and bounded-reader evidence, not claiming a deployed permanent fix. No heap cap was raised for this review experiment.

### Impact and severity

Affected: automatic Skill Workshop experience-review preparation on a large long-lived session.
Severity: blocks background review/learning for affected attempts; ordinary foreground conversations may still work.
Frequency: recurring matching error entries over multiple days; an isolated unbounded read reproduced the failure.
Consequence: automated review cannot reliably prepare its source context. This report does not establish a whole-Gateway crash, loss of existing skills, or private-data corruption.

### Additional information

Searched existing issues for experience-review, "experience review" with 512, review with OUT_OF_MEMORY, and review/memory in titles. #164279 describes broader review failure and #170101 pending-review scheduling/loss; neither establishes this bounded-context-read failure. #191847 is a different foreground actor/SQLite path. Please consolidate if there is a more specific existing issue.

First introducing version: NOT_ENOUGH_INFO (similar log entries predate the current 10.10 diagnosis). This report establishes the installed stable-version failure; no current-main or beta runtime was tested.

A useful upstream regression would exercise the production review-preparation caller with large retained history, verify the native limits are passed, preserve through-anchor/latest-turn/tool-pair/summary semantics, and separately verify review completion. Increasing all heaps or deleting chat history would not test that fix.

No credentials, account/chat/session IDs, host paths, raw configuration, database files or private conversation content are included.

## Follow-up to the review and candidate fix (Nov 5)

The reported 10.10 direct-reader OOM remains the original evidence. We subsequently verified the 11.5-beta.1 npm artifact against its published SHA512 and inspected its direct caller: it supplies 32768 bytes / 64 events / toolResultOverflow=omit. The newer current-main plugin/fork requester fallback described by the review is a separate preparation stage.

Maintainer PR #193544 now supplies evidence addressing the review's requested current-main regression and bounded requester lookup. The author reports a pinned-main real-worker OOM with 2,800 tool pairs and about 492 MiB of result text, followed by a bounded read preserving the through-anchor and requester/model boundaries. These are the PR author's results; our own tests remain the retained-database reader comparison described above.

At our latest check the PR was open, ready for review, unmerged, at head `2ea2054202cb960a38ac4a06e8cb24128accc055`. The revised PR body reports:
- the public SDK contract updated for both implicit-read ceilings and bounded-selection semantics;
- 99 focused tests, two Gateway sender/model/legacy policy cases, production build, typecheck and targeted formatting/lint checks passed;
- a real Gateway hook/scheduler/model review callback settled successfully with the worker's original heap limits;
- that live model attempted invalid skill drafts and ended silently, so the evidence covers review execution/settlement, not successful skill authoring;
- Linux coverage is left to PR CI.

The author has requested re-review. We have retained this issue and its original evidence while that review proceeds. Merge/release status and Linux acceptance remain to be checked; the Closes reference in an open PR is not a released fix. No competing PR, production update or private database upload was created by us.
