issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

`relocateCandidateRange` in `extensions/memory-core/src/short-term-promotion-rehydrate.ts` re-finds a stored recall candidate by scanning the whole live note for its snippet. It carries no prefix/suffix context, it accepts containment matches, and `normalizeRangeSnippet` compares the live range to the stored snippet after nothing but `trim()` and whitespace collapsing.

Two consequences, measured on one production workspace with all 512 live `short-term-recall` entries:

- **Ambiguous anchors:** for **89 of 512 candidates (17.4%)** the top-quality match occurs at more than one disjoint place in the file. The shipped tie-break then decides by line distance alone.
- **Fragment anchors after a normalization mismatch:** **22 candidates** relocate to a *fragment* of their stored snippet (quality 1), **14** resolve to nothing, 476 resolve at their stored range. All 22 fragment cases have an HTML comment inside the live range and none in the stored snippet. Stripping HTML comments from the live text restores containment for **22 of 22**.

In the worst three cases the stored 695-character snippet occurs **0 times** in the live note, while the fragment the promoter anchors on occurs **26 times**.

The W3C Web Annotation Data Model §4.2.4 introduces prefix/suffix precisely "to distinguish between multiple copies", and §4.2 requires a consuming agent to pick one when several sequences match. Brush, Bargeron, Gupta & Cadiz, *Robust Annotation Positioning in Digital Documents* (CHI '01, doi:10.1145/365024.365117) report that users preferred orphaning over partial-match repositioning (§5.3.3, §5.3.4).

### Steps to reproduce

1. Let memory-core record a `short-term-recall` candidate for a range in a memory note.
2. Add an HTML comment inside that range in the note, or let any tool that writes HTML comments do it.
3. Trigger rehydration for that candidate.
4. Observe the returned range: `normalizeRangeSnippet(lines, start, end)` no longer contains the stored snippet, so the scan falls back to a quality-1 fragment match and returns a different range, or `null`.

To reproduce the ambiguity independent of that cause, store a candidate whose snippet text also appears elsewhere in the same note and observe that the returned range is decided only by line distance.

### Expected behavior

- The stored snippet and the live range pass through the same normalization, so a note that only gained an HTML comment still resolves at its own range.
- When no unique match exists, the candidate is reported as lost (orphaned) instead of anchoring on a fragment that occurs many times in the file.

### Actual behavior

- The recorded snippet and the live range are normalized differently, so a range that merely gained an HTML comment stops matching.
- The promoter then anchors on a fragment and reports a relocation, or drops the candidate.
- Where several places match equally well, the pick is silent and distance-based.

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.4, and current `main` (`6a7b1e41`) is unchanged in this respect: `normalizeRangeSnippet` still calls only `normalizeSnippet`, which is `trim()` plus whitespace collapsing.

### Operating system

macOS 26.6.2 (arm64)

### Install method

npm global install

### Model

Not model-dependent. The measurement calls the shipped function directly; no model is involved.

### Provider / routing chain

Not applicable.

### Logs

No error is logged. The defect is silent: relocation and drop are ordinary outcomes of the scan.

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

The measurement is pre-registered and runs the shipped code rather than a paraphrase. Bytes 49203..59195 of `dist/short-term-promotion-Dn3jonZ9.mjs` (region SHA-256 `30c829d8e1641a38309f86c3e985b2c9b5b438cd770cad4f584d783c40a7151d`) were copied verbatim into a harness; only imports and an export were added. An instrumented copy with unchanged scoring collected every top-quality window; the shipped function's own answer was inside a top-quality place in 512 of 512 cases, so harness drift would have shown up as a mismatch rather than as a finding.

Population: all 512 live `short-term-recall` entries of one workspace (123 range entries, 389 claim entries), read read-only. Classification and headline numbers were fixed before the run.

| | n |
|---|---|
| resolved at the stored range | 476 |
| relocated | 22 |
| dropped (no match) | 14 |
| anchor matches more than one disjoint place | 89 (17.4%) |
| quality-1 fragment anchors | 22 (all relocated) |

A separate falsification inserted k lines above a stored range in memory only: two of three inspected candidates hold for k = 0, 2, 4 and jump to a different copy of the same boilerplate at k = 8, 16, 24. The third holds at every k tested, so the failure is data-dependent.

We can share the harness, the perturbation script and the anonymized census rows (ranges and outcomes only, no note text) if that helps.

### Impact and severity

Silent and latent rather than loud: a promotion anchored on a fragment can carry the wrong lines of the right file into a later turn, and there is no signal that it happened. It grows with note age, because every HTML comment written into a note after recording makes the stored snippet unmatchable.

### Suggested fix

1. Send the stored snippet and the live range through one shared normalization. This alone restores 22 of 22 cases in our data.
2. Treat a quality-1 fragment match as a lost candidate and report it, instead of promoting the fragment.
3. Require the chosen window to be unique in the file; otherwise orphan the candidate, or store prefix/suffix context so that the pick can be justified.

issues.body:
### Summary

`view_image` tool results are persisted verbatim into the agent transcript store, including the full base64 payload of every image. On a single agent this made **352 of 27,706 transcript events (1.3%) account for 451 MB of 564 MB total transcript data (80%)**, driving the agent SQLite database to 1.08 GB and turning routine session writes into 10+ MB synchronous SQLite transactions.

This is the underlying cause of the disk growth reported in #143524 and a major contributor to the main-thread write stalls that precede gateway unresponsiveness.

### Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.9.3 (1391f7c)
- Windows Server 2022, Node 24.18.0
- Gateway on loopback `127.0.0.1:18789`, single-node install
- Agent store: `%USERPROFILE%\.openclaw\agents\<agent>\agent\openclaw-agent.sqlite`

### Evidence

Event-size distribution across the whole `transcript_events` table for one agent (`javis`):

| single-event size | count | total | share of transcript bytes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| >= 5 MB | 12 | 112.5 MB | 20% |
| 1–5 MB | 122 | 225.8 MB | 40% |
| 256 KB – 1 MB | 218 | 113.1 MB | 20% |
| 64–256 KB | 161 | 25.6 MB | 5% |
| < 64 KB | 27,193 | 87.0 MB | 15% |

So **1.3% of events hold 80% of the bytes**, while the 27,193 ordinary conversational events total only 87 MB.

Every one of the largest events is the same shape — a `toolResult` from `view_image` whose `content` is raw base64:

```
--- 11.8MB session=c8b426bb seq=49 ---
{"type":"message","id":"75260f9f-...","timestamp":"2026-09-04T09:49:44.545Z",
 "message":{"role":"toolResult","toolCallId":"call_9vfbipmasjja4bn7j6emq9kx",
 "toolName":"view_image","content": ...
mid-payload sample: xsoB+oBfgF7WR20gANqGogc8/T3epIoeA9POnVANZ7gCGIA9NR8wfXzNcdZhbVIBxoBVtWq1wRdSx+us/S34...
```

Top offenders (same agent, all `toolName: "view_image"`):

| session | size | events | bytes/event | largest single event |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `c8b426bb` | 46.5 MB | 59 | 807 KB | 11.8 MB |
| `90a3362d` | 39.6 MB | 34 | 1192 KB | 11.3 MB |
| `17ab66fa` | 21.9 MB | 99 | 227 KB | 10.4 MB |
| `f6ff53d2` | 17.4 MB | 79 | 226 KB | 6.7 MB |

For contrast, a genuinely long text conversation in the same store is `967b2361` — 47.2 MB across **4,633** events (10 KB/event, evenly distributed). That is normal usage. The image sessions reach comparable size in **34–59 events**.

Reproduction is simply: send several images to an agent over Feishu/WeChat so `view_image` runs, then query the store:

```sql
SELECT session_id, COUNT(*) ev,
       SUM(LENGTH(event_json)) bytes,
       MAX(LENGTH(event_json)) biggest
FROM transcript_events
GROUP BY session_id
ORDER BY bytes DESC
LIMIT 10;
```

Each `view_image` call adds roughly (image bytes × 1.33) to the transcript, permanently.

### Impact

1. **Store size** — 1.3% of events produce 80% of the bytes. This is the mechanism behind the 1.4–2.8 GB WAL growth in #143524; the WAL is large because the rows being written are large.
2. **Synchronous write latency** — persisting a single 11 MB event is one synchronous SQLite transaction on the gateway's main thread. On this host that showed up as `slow SQLite transaction hold` warnings with `elapsedMs` from 1,205 up to 68,000, and correlates with the gateway going unresponsive while `node.exe` stays alive and the port stops accepting connections.
3. **Retention cannot recover it** — `openclaw sessions cleanup --enforce` with `pruneAfter=7d` / `maxEntries=2000` pruned 50 entries and freed **53 KB**, because the bulk sits inside recently-active sessions protected by `preserveRecent`. Deleting five image-heavy sessions removed 135.8 MB of transcript data (564.0 → 428.2 MB) but the file grew 1075.9 → 1084.3 MB with only 72.8 MB freelist, so reclaiming it further requires offline `VACUUM`.
4. **`VACUUM` is not a remedy** — a full offline `VACUUM` before any deletion took **406 s** and recovered **4 MB** (1079.3 → 1075.4 MB, freelist 0). The data is live, not fragmentation.

### Expected behaviour

Image payloads should not be stored inline in the transcript. Reasonable options, roughly in order of preference:

1. **Store by reference.** Persist images as content-addressed blobs on disk (the `sessions/` directory already holds per-session artifacts) and keep only a path/hash plus metadata in `transcript_events`.
2. **Cap persisted tool-result size.** Truncate any single tool result above a configurable threshold (e.g. `session.maintenance.maxEventBytes`) when writing to the store, keeping the model-visible payload in memory for the current turn only.
3. **Strip base64 on persist.** The base64 is only needed for the in-flight model call; after the turn completes it has no replay value that a stored file path would not serve better.
4. **At minimum, make it visible.** Emit a warning when a single transcript event exceeds a few MB, and count inline-media bytes in the `diskBudget` report so operators can see where the growth comes from.

### Related

- #143524 — WAL growth on agent SQLite (this issue is the likely root cause of the volume)
- #143757 — Windows scheduled-task config prevents headless gateway start (separate defect on the same host)

### Notes

Happy to run additional queries against this store — it still contains 428 MB of transcript data with the pattern intact, and the deleted sessions are preserved as `.zst` archives under `agents/javis/sessions/` if a before/after comparison is useful.

issues.body:
## Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash). Whether it is a regression is unknown: no earlier version was tested.

## Beta release blocker

No

## Summary

The `pdf` tool has no path at all for a **scanned PDF** (image-only pages, no text layer) once no vision-capable model is available: the tool is gated on a PDF model *before* it ever looks at the document, so "there is no model" and "this document needs a model" collapse into the same hard failure.

Two gates, both in `src/agents/tools/pdf-tool.ts` (`origin/main` @ `9b350d9e933`):

1. Registration — `createPdfTool` returns `null` when model resolution yields nothing (`pdf-tool.ts:396`, `:410`), so on a host with no PDF-model candidate the tool is not registered at all.
2. Execution (deferred discovery, the path the production caller uses) — the handler throws before any document is loaded:

```ts
      const pdfModelConfig =
        registrationPdfModelConfig ??
        resolvePdfModelConfigForTool({ ... });
      if (!pdfModelConfig) {
        throw new ToolInputError("No PDF model configured.");
      }
```
(`pdf-tool.ts:475-482`; the runtime-generation variant is `:207`.)

The result is that **text extraction from a scan is treated as a model capability**, even though it is not: reading characters off a raster page is extraction, not comprehension. The document-extract plugin already detects exactly this case — a near-empty text layer plus rendered images — and already owns bounded page rendering, but that signal is only consumed *after* a model call, so it is unreachable when there is no model to call.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Configure an agent with no vision-capable model available to the `pdf` tool (no configured PDF model / all candidates unauthenticated).
2. Give it a scanned PDF (raster-only page; `pdftotext file.pdf -` returns empty).
3. Ask it to read the document.

## Expected behavior

With no vision model, a scanned PDF is either read by a host-side extraction path (where one is available), or refused with an error that distinguishes "no model configured" from "this document needs one" — not silently unreachable at registration time.

## Actual behavior

- No PDF model candidate → the tool is absent from the toolset (registration `return null`), so the agent has no failure to report and no capability to name.
- Deferred discovery → `ToolInputError: No PDF model configured.` thrown at `pdf-tool.ts:481`, before the file is opened. The document is never inspected, so the existing scan signal in the extraction plugin never runs.

## Environment

- installed: `openclaw@2026.8.1` (npm global, Linux LXC, `node v22.23.2`), verified against `origin/main` `9b350d9e933`
- models: Anthropic + OpenAI via provider profiles; failure reproduces whenever the PDF-model resolver returns null

## Model

n/a: the failure happens before any model call, when the PDF-model resolver returns null. The exact models configured on the agent at the time of the report are unknown.

## Provider / routing chain

agent tool loop → `pdf` tool (`createPdfTool` at registration, or deferred discovery at call time) → `resolvePdfModelConfigForTool` → null → tool not registered, or `ToolInputError: No PDF model configured.` before the file is opened. The ask is the ordering of this gate; OCR ownership stays with the document-extraction capability.

## Impact and severity

A scanned invoice/statement — the normal shape of a Brazilian bank or utility PDF — is unreadable by an agent whose model set is otherwise fine, with a message that points at configuration instead of at the document. Time-to-notice is immediate but the diagnosis is not: the operator reads "No PDF model configured" on a host where models *are* configured but the resolver produced no PDF candidate.

## Note on prior art

We opened PR #142253 (local `pdftoppm` + `tesseract` fallback inside the pdf tool) and closed it unmerged: automated review flagged it as the wrong ownership boundary — the recommendation was to keep OCR in the document-extraction capability with a narrow core change for model-free tool availability — plus P1 findings on cancellation propagation and raster pixel budget. This issue records the capability gap on `main` independent of that implementation; we are not carrying a local patch for it.

issues.body:
### Summary
On OpenClaw 2026.11.1, parent agents resumed after native helper completion lose execution authority during ordinary work. Failed continuations can then leave background work attached, blocking subsequent human messages.

### Impact and severity
**High: blocks ongoing work and subsequent user requests.**

This is repeatedly breaking two independent Discord conversations. From the user’s perspective, sessions seem to break every few minutes; that is the reported experience, not a measured failure interval.

This makes the whole assistant experience unreliable. Delegating work becomes an exercise in babysitting broken sessions: work stops, follow-ups fail, and recovery does not prevent recurrence. It is not a cosmetic error or an isolated failed tool call—it defeats the point of having an assistant carry a task through to completion.

### Observed failure sequence
1. A native helper finishes and the parent resumes.
2. The parent successfully posts a progress message with `final=false`.
3. Approximately 20 milliseconds later, that same tool call reports:
   ```
   agent tool caller authority is no longer active
   ```
4. Subsequent cleanup also fails.

The clearest observed incident occurred on November 6, 2026, at approximately 17:19:18 America/Los_Angeles.

In another affected conversation, the next human request was rejected after a five-second cleanup wait because the session “still has background work.”

### Code-level finding
Inspection of the installed code found:
- `agent-harness-completion-recovery.ts` captures the transcript write counter/version and rejects changes when validating continuation authority.
- `source-reply-mirror.ts` records successful progress messages in that transcript, including messages marked `final=false`.
- Recording those messages increments the counter being checked.

This strongly suggests self-invalidation: a legitimate progress-message write changes the transcript state used to validate the running continuation.

**Evidence limit:** this is an observed incident plus code inspection, not a newly executed deterministic reproduction. The exact invalidating write has not been isolated for every affected run.

### Expected behavior
A legitimate progress message must not revoke the active continuation’s authority. A failed continuation must not leave background work blocking subsequent user requests. Existing authorization boundaries should remain enforced.

### Environment
- OpenClaw: 2026.11.1
- `@openclaw/codex`: 2026.11.1
- macOS; Discord conversations
- Related prior report: #166964

### Additional diagnostic problem
The generic authority error obscures which validity check failed. Logging the invalidation reason would make these recurring failures substantially easier to diagnose.

### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

The download button (or hover action) for files in the Control UI file browser does not render, despite having valid session files, correct origin configuration, and no known config flags blocking downloads. The localization strings `downloadFile` and `downloadAsImage` exist in the compiled UI bundle, but the UI element is never shown.


### Steps to reproduce

1. Setup OpenClaw Gateway to run in a container
2. Setup Cloudflared tunnel to run in a container, using different public domains for `*` and `/webhooks/*` routes (same Docker network as gateway)
3. Configure OpenClaw to use token auth (not `trusted-proxy`)
4. Verify `publicOrigin`, `controlUi.allowedOrigins` are consistent and that `trustedProxies` includes cloudflared container docker IP
5. Open the Control UI at `https://<ui-domain>/openclaw`
6. Navigate to a session that has file attachments/uploads
7. Open the file browser panel
8. Observe that no download button, link, or hover action is visible for files

### Expected behavior

A download button or hover-activated download option should appear next to each file in the file browser, allowing users to download session attachments.


### Actual behavior

The file browser shows files but provides no download mechanism — no button, no icon, no context menu option.


### OpenClaw version

2026.11.3

### Operating system

Ubuntu 26.04

### Install method

docker container using 2026.11.3-browser container

### Model

N/A (but, Qwen 3.6, gemma4, embeddinggemma2 all running locally)

### Provider / routing chain

N/A

### Additional provider/model setup details

All other aspects of OpenClaw Control UI and webchat function as expected when accessed at `https://<ui-domain>/openclaw/`

Both OpenClaw Gateway and `cloudflared` run as separate Docker containers on the same Linux host:

```
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Cloudflare Network                │
│                                                │
│  <ui-domain> ──────────────────────────────┐   │
│  <wh-domain> ──────────────────────────────┤   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┼───┘
                                              ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      Host OS                             │
│                                                          │
│  ┌──────────────────────┐    ┌────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Docker: cloudflared  │    │  Docker: OpenClaw      │ │
│  │                      │    │  Gateway               │ │
│  │  Tunnel agent        │    │  (port 18789)          │ │
│  │  Authenticates to    │    │                        │ │
│  │  Cloudflare account  │    │  - auth: token         │ │
│  │                      │    │  - bind: lan           │ │
│  │  Publishes:          │    │  - publicOrigin:       │ │
│  │  • <ui-domain>       │    │    https://<ui-domain> │ │
│  │  • <wh-domain>       │    │                        │ │
│  └──────────┬───────────┘    │  - trustedProxies:     │ │
│             │                │    <tunnel-proxy-ip>   │ │
│             │ docker network │                        │ │
│             └────────────────┤                        │ │
│                              └────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Control UI** served from `https://<ui-domain>/openclaw`
- **Webhooks** routed via `https://<wh-domain>`
- Both subdomains are published by the same `cloudflared` container, which routes to the OpenClaw Gateway container on port 18789
- The two containers share a Docker network; the tunnel proxy IP (`<tunnel-proxy-ip>`) is configured as a trusted proxy
- Auth mode: token-based

## Configuration

Relevant `openclaw.json` settings (sanitized):

```jsonc
{
  "gateway": {
    "mode": "local",
    "port": 18789,
    "bind": "lan",
    "publicOrigin": "https://<ui-domain>",
    "trustedProxies": [
      "<tunnel-proxy-ip>",
      "127.0.0.1",
      "::1"
    ],
    "controlUi": {
      "enabled": true,
      "basePath": "/openclaw",
      "allowedOrigins": [
        "https://<ui-domain>",
        "https://<wh-domain>"
      ]
    },
    "auth": {
      "mode": "token",
      "token": "${OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN}"
    },
    "uploads": {
      "enabled": true
    }
  }
}
```

- `controlUi.allowedOrigins` is **explicitly set** to both domains — verified via gateway logs that it hot-reloaded successfully with no errors
- `uploads.enabled: true` — the only config flag that gates both uploads and downloads
- No other download-specific configuration keys exist in the documented config reference

## Investigation Performed

### Origin / CORS — ruled out

- `publicOrigin` matches the URL loading the Control UI
- `controlUi.allowedOrigins` explicitly includes both subdomains
- Gateway logs confirm hot-reload of `allowedOrigins` with no errors
- **Conclusion:** Not an origin mismatch

### Config gating — ruled out

- Searched full documentation for any `allowDownloads`, `disableDownloads`, `fileDownload`, or similar config keys — none exist
- The only gate is `uploads.enabled` (which is `true`)
- **Conclusion:** No config key is blocking downloads

### UI bundle — download code exists

- Compiled UI bundle contains localization strings `downloadFile` and `downloadAsImage`
- RPC endpoints are registered: `sessions.files.list`, `sessions.files.get`, `sessions.files.set`
- **Conclusion:** Download code is present in the bundle

### Web search — no prior reports

- Searched GitHub issues, Reddit, and general web for "download button missing", "file browser download", "Control UI file download"
- No matching bug reports found
- Closest issues are all about missing Control UI assets from npm packaging (different problem)
- **Conclusion:** Appears to be isolated to this deployment or a very recent regression



### Logs

```shell
None relevant
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

_No response_

### Impact and severity

- Affects: all users
- Severity: blocks workflow
- Frequency: Always
- Consequence: Cannot download workspace files for use in other apps

### Additional information

_No response_

### Bug type
Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker
No

### Summary
Detailed, non-native Slack progress cards emit raw read filenames in a Block Kit mrkdwn field, where filename characters are formatting syntax rather than literal text.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Use this existing configuration:
```json
{"channels":{"slack":{"streaming":{"mode":"progress","progress":{"style":"card","toolProgress":true,"nativeTaskCards":false}}}}}
```
2. Emit an ordinary prepared read-tool item with args.path set to /tmp/demo *literal* _under_ ~strike~ `ticks` & <@U123> report.txt.
3. The regression fixture is included in the accompanying prepared fix: [dispatch.preview-fallback.test.ts](https://github.com/ooiuuii/openclaw/blob/codex/slack-progress-literal-tool-arguments-20261104/extensions/slack/src/monitor/message-handler/dispatch.preview-fallback.test.ts). Apply that test change alone to base 80c59348c20aef94a53a7ee963f54b0856c64c23 and run:
```sh
pnpm test extensions/slack/src/monitor/message-handler/dispatch.preview-fallback.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```
The fixture exercises the production prepared-item projection, progress compositor, detailed card presentation, and draft update payload. Its transport is local and mocked; it does not contact Slack or an inference provider. The baseline run fails the literal-row assertion while the other 96 dispatch tests pass.

### Expected behavior
Raw argument text is represented literally in the card, including *, _, ~, and backticks. Authored commentary, links, and inline code retain their existing formatting behavior. Slack distinguishes plain_text from mrkdwn text objects: https://docs.slack.dev/messaging/formatting-message-text/ and https://docs.slack.dev/reference/block-kit/composition-objects/text-object/.

### Actual behavior
The captured baseline payload contains a section text object of type mrkdwn with the filename's formatting characters unchanged. For example, *literal* remains formatting syntax in that field. The payload evidence establishes the serialization defect; no live Slack UI rendering was tested.

### OpenClaw version
Source checkout at 80c59348c20aef94a53a7ee963f54b0856c64c23.

### Operating system
Linux 7.0.0-38-generic, x86_64 local sandbox fixture.

### Install method
Source checkout; repository test runner through pnpm test. Final proof uses the already-cached, checksum-verified OpenClaw Bun fork 1.4.4 (revision 1.4.4-canary.1+191755ec1), selected by the normal runner.

### Model
None. Synthetic tool activity; no inference call is needed.

### Provider / routing chain
None. Prepared read-tool event → production Slack progress compositor/card → local draft transport fixture.

### Additional provider/model setup details
No live Slack send or paid provider call was made for this reproduction.

### Logs
Baseline command exit: 1 (1 failed literal-row regression, 96 passing controls). The captured section was:
```json
{
  "type": "section",
  "text": {
    "type": "mrkdwn",
    "text": "Read from /tmp/demo *literal* _under_ ~strike~ `ticks` & <@U123> report.txt — running"
  }
}
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence
Serialized before/after payloads were captured in the local fixture; no downloadable bundle is claimed here. The reviewed final candidate retains a plain_text raw tool row with emoji=false, while the fallback still escapes mention-shaped text. Final focused proof passes 138 tests. This is payload proof, not live Slack UI rendering.

### Impact and severity
Display correctness in explicitly enabled detailed Block Kit tool progress. A filename can look different from the argument actually supplied to the tool. There is no evidence that this changes tool execution or the actual filename. Quiet/default progress and native task-card behavior are outside the changed presentation lane.

### Additional context
Reported by @ooiuuii. No prior known-good release was established, so this is not labeled a regression. The proposed repair does not restore unsupported backslash escaping.

issues.body:
### Summary

In `openclaw onboard` with Custom setup and discovery on, onboarding exits with code 1 right after "Set up memory embeddings?". Setup has already installed and started the Gateway service by then. The next step imports memories from other AI tools, and it refuses to run while a Gateway owns the state:

```
◇  Set up memory embeddings?
│  No
Cannot admit migrate for migration providers in state root ~/.openclaw: This operation requires exclusive offline state ownership. No local mutation was attempted. Inspect openclaw gateway status. This command is offline-only. To run offline, stop the Gateway through its service owner, wait for ownership to release, then rerun this exact command.
```

The rest of onboarding (app recommendations, the browser or TUI handoff) never runs, and memories from Claude Code are never offered.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Fresh macOS user with no `~/.openclaw`, and Claude Code installed.
2. Run `openclaw onboard`, choose **Custom setup**, accept the security prompt, then pick **One agent** and **Full access**.
3. Pick the detected AI and let the connection check pass. Setup installs the LaunchAgent and reports "Gateway: running at ws://127.0.0.1:18789".
4. Answer **No** to "Set up memory embeddings?".

Expected: onboarding offers the memory import (or skips it when there is nothing to import) and continues.

Actual: the error above, exit code 1.

### Cause

`runGuidedOnboarding` (`src/commands/onboard-guided.ts`) runs `importMemories()` after setup apply has started the Gateway service. `runSetupMemoryImportStep` goes through `withPluginMigrationProviders`, which calls `runWithLocalStateOwner` with `onForeignOwner: "refuse"`. It throws as soon as it finds the running Gateway, before it looks for any memories.

### Environment

- OpenClaw `main` at 7de4434e211, built from source
- macOS 26.6 test VM, Node 24.21

In the Android client (`apps/android/app/src/main/java/ai/openclaw/app/ui/SidebarContent.kt`), the "New session" action in the drawer header is rendered as an unadorned monochrome `IconButton` with `Icons.Default.Add` tinted with `palette.text`. By comparison, the Web Control UI elevates "New chat" into a primary visual action by giving it a highlighted rounded container with filled brand/accent color (coral/salmon) and centered plus icon. - Style the button with an accent filled container (e.g., brand coral/accent background using `ClawTheme.colors`).
- Apply rounded container styling (squircle / rounded rectangle) consistent with the Web rail new chat button.
- Maintain appropriate padding, touch target (48dp), and semantic accessibility descriptions (`"New session"`).
- Keep the existing `CircularProgressIndicator` state when `sessionCreating` is true.

### Alternatives considered

- Keeping the plain monochrome `IconButton`: Weak because New Chat is the primary workflow entry point, but currently lacks hierarchy next to utility actions (search, close).
- Adding full text label ("New Chat") in the top bar: Consumes too much horizontal space in the drawer header alongside the Agent picker and Close button.

prs.title: fix: show the real group activation in session status
prs.body:
Closes #200429

## What Problem This Solves

In a group or channel set to answer every message (`requireMention: false`), asking the agent for its session status says `Activation: mention`, so the status card claims the bot needs an @mention when it does not. Native slash `/status` gets it wrong the other way: it says `always` in groups that do require a mention.

## User Impact

User impact: the status card's `👥 Activation` line now matches how the conversation is really gated, in the `session_status` tool, text `/status` and native `/status` alike. An explicit `/activation` override still wins.

## Why This Change Was Made

The text `/status` command already used the reply path's default (the channel/account/group `requireMention` resolution). The `session_status` tool hard-coded `mention` and the native `/status` fast path hard-coded `always`. Both now use the same resolver as replies:

- `resolveSessionDefaultGroupActivation` in `groups.ts` rebuilds the conversation from the stored session route the way event turns do (`prepareReplyConversation`) and runs `resolveGroupRequireMention`. `session_status` calls it for group/channel sessions (the group check moved into `session-status-session-resolve.ts` with it, keeping the tool under the max-lines budget).
- The native fast path resolves the conversation from the command context, as its continuation path already does, and passes the result to both status call sites.

Related: #5940 (same symptom on Discord, closed as stale).

## Evidence

**Live, isolated Gateway** (branch build, throwaway Mattermost 11.7.15 in Docker on 127.0.0.1, mock model). Config: `groups: { "*": { requireMention: false }, "<gated-channel>": { requireMention: true } }`, `groupPolicy: "open"`.

| Session | Real gating | `session_status` on `main` | `session_status` on this branch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| always-on channel, thread session, no override | replies without @mention | `mention` ❌ | `always` |
| always-on channel, no override | replies without @mention | — | `always` |
| always-on channel after `/activation mention` | — | `mention` | `mention` |
| mention-gated channel | no reply without @mention; replies with it | `mention` | `mention` |

<details><summary>Captured terminal output (ids redacted)</summary>

```
$ node drive.mjs always "hello from the always-on channel"
posted always: "hello from the always-on channel" id=<post:1>
bot: "Protocol note: acknowledged. ..."          # mock model reply, no @mention needed
```

prs.title: fix: show the whole reply when you reopen a TUI session
prs.body: Closes #200408 ## What Problem This Solves In `openclaw tui`, a reply longer than 8,000 characters is complete while it streams, but after you close and reopen the session it stops mid-sentence with `...(truncated)...`. The full reply is stored, yet the TUI gives no way to see the rest, so it looks as if the model stopped early or text was lost. ## User Impact User impact: reopening a TUI session (Gateway or `--local`) shows long replies in full again. If the full text cannot be loaded, the preview stays and says so instead of ending silently. ## Why This Change Was Made The Gateway caps text in `chat.history` to keep history pages small. The Control UI already loads capped rows in full through `chat.message.get` (#122207); the TUI took the capped text as it came. The TUI now does the same as the Control UI: after loading history, each assistant row marked `truncated: true` / `reason: "display-cap"` is replaced by the stored message, newest first, four reads at a time. History pages stay bounded, and no protocol or schema changes. If a read fails or the message is unavailable (for example on a Gateway without `chat.message.get`), the capped text is kept and its marker becomes `...(truncated; the full reply could not be loaded)...`. Local mode (`openclaw tui --local`) had the same cap. It now reads the stored message in-process the same way the Gateway's `chat.message.get` handler does. ## Evidence Live check, Windows 11, against a running 2026.11.5-beta.4 Gateway: the session from #200408 holds an 11,532-character reply that `chat.history` returns as 8,018 characters ending `...(truncated)...`. - Before (installed 2026.11.5-beta.4 TUI, session reopened): the reply stops mid-sentence at "forest ecology", followed by `...(truncated)...`. - After (this branch built from source, same session reopened): the whole reply is shown, ending with `THE END`. Before: After: Focused tests: - `src/tui/gateway-chat.test.ts`: two new cases. A capped row is replaced by the `chat.message.get` result (fails on `main`, passes here). When the read reports unavailable or the request is rejected, the preview is kept with the "could not be loaded" marker (fails on `main`, passes here). - `src/tui/embedded-full-message-reader.test.ts` (new): the same for `--local`, including an oversized stored message. - `gateway-chat.test.ts`, `embedded-backend.test.ts` and the new file: 170 passed. `pnpm check:changed`: typecheck, lint, format, line-cap and mock-export ratchets pass. The dead-export scan reports three exports in untouched files that are already on `main` (`approval-shared.ts`, `spawn-broker/host.ts`, `system-agent/operation-types.ts`). Not exercised live: `openclaw tui --local` (covered by the unit tests above). In local mode the full text is loaded before the existing per-message and page byte budgets are applied, so a very long session can keep fewer older rows than before.

prs.title: fix: keep archived usage path resolution asynchronous
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Reading archived transcript usage uses an async API, but resolving the transcript filename still performs synchronous filesystem calls on the Gateway thread. The existing zero-sync-filesystem regression reproduces this on main.

## User Impact

Archived usage reads no longer block the Gateway thread during transcript path resolution. Candidate ordering, restored-root and sibling-agent fallback, and existing synchronous callers retain their current behavior. No configuration or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

One shared path policy now accepts synchronous or asynchronous filesystem probes, rather than maintaining two containment implementations. Transcript candidate planning is likewise shared. The async usage reader selects the async resolver.

Compatibility review also found that native async realpath handles a symlink followed by a parent segment differently from the existing resolver. Normalize the input before resolving it and retain a regression proving sync/async agreement.

## Evidence

- Original public async usage entry reproduces synchronous realpath calls before the fix (1 failed, 27 skipped). Generated, relative and absolute filenames now retain usage results with zero observed synchronous filesystem calls.
- A separate symlink/parent-segment regression fails before the normalization correction and passes with it. Existing sibling symlink replacement, restored-root, unsafe-path and fallback cases exercise both resolvers.
- Final Node focused consumer proof: 83 tests pass across five files (usage, path policy, shutdown draining, history revocation and filesystem helpers).
- Final Bun proof: 41 tests pass across usage and path policy. Canonical five-file type-aware lint, core typecheck, formatting and diff checks pass.
- No native Windows execution was available; Windows coverage remains with PR CI. No timeouts or assertions were relaxed. Independent review was explicitly waived by the maintainer; local simplification and compatibility review completed.

prs.title: fix(ui): show dictation progress and preserve pending transcripts
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Dictation can disappear without progress or an error, and starting another recording can discard text that is still being transcribed. When earlier recordings are still transcribing, a new recording can also open the microphone and capture audio that the Gateway then refuses to transcribe, because each connection holds at most two transcription sessions.

## User Impact

The composer shows "Transcribing…" when recording has stopped and text is pending, and shows an error when dictation finishes without text.

![Composer error after a recording finishes without text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/81e55d2508955d7e309d0ddd68cfc316893de622/images/2026/11/c4501593-373b-49cc-b345-18a758130ad1.png)

Users can keep typing or record again while stopped recordings finish. Their text enters the draft in recording order, even if a later transcription finishes first, without committing an active recording's partial preview.

Dictation claims its Gateway session before the microphone opens, so starting takes one Gateway round trip longer. If both of the connection's sessions are still transcribing earlier recordings, the microphone stays closed and the composer says "Dictation is busy finishing earlier recordings. Try again in a moment."

Normal start: the microphone opens once the Gateway accepts the session.

![Composer listening after a normal dictation start](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/81e55d2508955d7e309d0ddd68cfc316893de622/images/2026/11/506f767a-9f6d-4ede-b9d6-cfb2f9610967.png)

No free session: two stopped recordings are still transcribing, so a third start shows the busy message and does not open the microphone.

![Composer showing the dictation busy message while earlier recordings transcribe](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/81e55d2508955d7e309d0ddd68cfc316893de622/images/2026/11/56ba9505-36a5-4ce0-91af-f09b2602a0ee.png)

## Why This Change Was Made

Stopped recordings stay pending independently of microphone capture, and the draft beneath an active preview is preserved. Cancelling or switching drafts still discards pending results. On New Session, a failure arriving while another microphone is opening stays visible.

Admission belongs to the Gateway, which already limits transcription sessions per connection. The composer creates the session first and opens the microphone only after it is accepted, which also removes the browser's buffering of audio captured before a session existed. The Gateway reports a full connection with a `TALK_SESSION_CAPACITY` error detail (code `UNAVAILABLE`, retryable), so the UI does not read error text. Transcripts and stopped recordings exist only after the lazy capture module has loaded, so the ordered queue, the draft placement (insertion helper and captured-versus-live selection policy, shared by the chat composer and direct dictation through the owner's `placeTranscript`, which reaches it through the stopped-recording queue) and the busy copy load with it; the composer owner keeps the commit decision, playback and cancellation listeners. This keeps the composer's boot bundle within its budget.

Scope is composer dictation status, error reporting, pending transcript handling and session admission. Waveform drawing, animation, sizing, layout and audio retention are unchanged. Realtime Talk keeps its existing order (microphone first, then provider session).

Related: #195982, #196063.

## Evidence

Validated local head: df6237948874.

- Real run of this head in a disposable macOS VM (lampvm clone, destroyed afterwards): built inside the VM, an isolated Gateway with its own state and no provider keys, the built Control UI in headless Chromium with a synthetic microphone tone, and a configured CLI transcriber (first run returns no text, the next two take 45 seconds). The empty recording showed the transcription error; a normal start listened after the Gateway admitted the session; with two stopped recordings still transcribing, a third start got `TALK_SESSION_CAPACITY` from the real relay, showed the busy message and never opened the microphone; both texts then arrived and the draft read "First words Second words". Screenshots and details are in the evidence comment.
- Tests: 609 passed across 26 files, including (composer-dictation, chat-composer, chat-composer-actions, chat-composer-suggestions, chat-composer-sizing, composer-direct-dictation, New Session composer, new-session-page, split Talk, gateway-errors, optional English loading, Gateway file transcription, Talk relay, transcription relay). The dictation status UI e2e file is included. A new test (a provider error during the microphone permission prompt stops startup) fails on 4a319c61dd15 and passes here. The two new admission tests (microphone waits for the Gateway; busy without opening the microphone) fail on ce03a6211412, and the new Gateway capacity test fails there without the typed error. The earlier ordering regression tests produced 7 failures on 6864cdac.
- Control UI performance, measured on 4a319c61dd15 (this head changes only lazily loaded dictation code) merged into main bd614490e566 (and the same sizes merged into d0daf88ab13): chat boot JS 1324112 B (that main 1324449 B, -337 B), new-session boot JS 815714 B (that main 815670 B, +44 B), largest JS within its cap; the remaining violations (largest CSS, chat boot request count) are already present on main.
- UI and core typecheck, scoped lint, formatting, import-cycle and madge checks, the Control UI controller guard, `ui:i18n:verify`, the test-line budget (+302 of 400) and `git diff --check` passed.

Before: only the second recording remains.

![Before: first recording's text is lost](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/d7d3655a4fad311e3e73136339d895ec9eb462a5/images/2026/11/af980603-cbc2-4b37-8383-bbde05db8704.png)

With this change: both recordings remain in order.

![After: both recordings' text is preserved](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/d7d3655a4fad311e3e73136339d895ec9eb462a5/images/2026/11/ad86d1d5-ea96-4b9b-99d8-c8026e23e117.png)

Real transcription providers and the full test suite were not run.

prs.title: improve(ci): prepare Watch companion during build
prs.body:
## Summary
- Start the selected Watch simulator's actual paired-phone preparation alongside the existing foreground Xcode build/settings work, then join before any Watch boot/install/test operation.
- Preserve the selected pair, all five test selections, existing Xcode product resolution, independent build/boot failure status, and cleanup on early exit. No new jobs, setup steps, cache, planner, or concurrency-cap changes.

## Why and expected effect
In CI run [43995805967](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43995805967), iOS job [133747919619](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43995805967/job/133747919619) took 80m53s with ~2s queue time. The Watch step took ~940s. Its paired-phone boot occupied **75.803s** (02:34:32.572358–02:35:48.375373 UTC), after ~106s of build/settings work. Overlapping only those independent operations offers an ideal **~76s iOS-branch saving**, not 940s. Watch boot/test remains unchanged. Actual native overlap timing is not yet measured; simulator/compiler CPU and I/O contention can reduce or erase the gain.

This is **not a measured whole-FRV speedup**. Parent [43995308737](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43995308737) finished in a failed 93m34 diagnostic envelope: CI ended 02:50:43, but candidate checks' final receipt was 02:56:29. That sample's downstream barrier means the proposed iOS saving alone would yield **zero parent wall-time benefit**. It targets native-dominated cycles without adding runner queue/setup or changing other branches. It should not land if native qualification shows a regression.

## Historical constraint
Commit [56c643947272575869cb051d020a7fc419eb8ac0](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/56c643947272575869cb051d020a7fc419eb8ac0) intentionally prepared the paired phone to fix Watch XCTest startup timeouts. That requirement is retained: the paired phone may differ from IOS_SIMULATOR_ID, and its successful preparation still precedes Watch operations. This is scheduling, not removal of the prerequisite. Existing build-product reuse is retained.

## Proof and limits
- Actual workflow-shell regression: base fails the overlapping-operation handshake; patched workflow passes. No timing-threshold assertion and no production test hook.
- All 78 iOS workflow tests pass, including unpaired destinations, actual companion selection, exact boot-failure status, product-resolution failures, and foreground-build failure cleanup. Final simplified run: 78 passed in 4.84 s.
- Focused TypeScript check, type-aware lint, formatting and git diff --check pass. Pinned actionlint, zizmor and the workflow scanner pass.
- CI caught an introduced workflow-size regression: 480,295 > 480,000 bytes. Removing redundant exit-status bookkeeping in favor of existing set -e and the EXIT trap reduces it to 479,980 bytes; the actual size guard now passes without changing its limit. The independent private-UI ownership assertion still fails on extensions/openclaw-id-access/browser/recovery-uses.e2e.test.ts. Its source/test/planner inputs are unchanged from base, and the same assertion reproduces locally. No baseline changed.
- **Native qualification remains blocked (November 17, 2026).** Run [44008458145](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44008458145) targets prior head `881ead0778835f1b0718d0d2249c216d0ee3497b`, not the final settlement simplification. Its [ios-build (tests) job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44008458145/job/133790080755) is terminal **cancelled**, completed at 05:48:40 UTC; the earlier focused iOS lifecycle step failed. Watch-step metadata remains incomplete despite the terminal job, and the retrieved log ends before that step. Neither native Watch success nor comparable timing/cleanup proof is established. Ordinary PR CI does not execute this release-only Watch step. No rerun or new runner allocation was started during recovery.
- Current-head CI [44009289838](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44009289838) is complete with the independently reproduced private-UI inventory failure plus aggregate gate failure; it is not all green. [Hosted ClawSweeper](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/200380#issuecomment-6937399148) reviewed `5d6e495179adba91891bdc8ef591ac054d013a0c`: no code findings, but an explicit before-merge requirement for native qualification and comparable baseline/candidate Watch timings remains. **Not RFR.**

## Simplification
Move existing pair discovery; background one existing command; join and clean up its PID. No helper or alternate execution path. Against merge base: workflow +22/-12, tests +32/-1. Against the first revision: workflow +7/-10 and 315 fewer bytes; tests unchanged. Best-effort termination covers the owned bootstatus client; normal runner cleanup remains responsible for the simulator service/process tree. No claim that terminating the client rolls back a partially booted simulator.

Managed update finalization logs expected plugin deferrals at WARN, once per plugin and again when Doctor warning snapshots repeat. Embedded JSON makes these notices harder to read and obscures actionable warnings.

## User Impact

Expected parent-held package deferrals produce one INFO summary with a plugin count and explain that plugins will converge after the parent releases install records. Security and unresolved migration warnings remain at WARN; failed phases remain at ERROR. No user action or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The finalize lifecycle recognizes Doctor's existing parent-held package-deferral wording when rendering warning snapshots. Other step records use structured logger fields and readable stderr progress. Persisted diagnostics, receipts, convergence, and settled-warning retirement are unchanged.

The summary counts the first complete Doctor warning batch; later snapshots do not repeat it. Unrecognized deferral wording continues to warn. prs.title: feat(control-ui): give composer actions the pane draft
prs.body:
## Problem

Control UI composer actions (`host.ui.registerAction({ placement: "composer" })`) cannot see or change the draft they sit next to. Their `run` context has `sessionKey`, `agentId`, `session`, `host` and `signal`, but no draft. Only a full composer replacement receives `draft`/`setDraft`, so a plugin that wants a "rewrite my draft" button must replace the whole composer.

## Solution

Composer actions now receive `composer` in their `run` context, bound to the pane that invoked them:

```ts
run: (context: BoardGetParams & {
  session?: ControlUiSession;
  host: ControlUiHost;
  signal: AbortSignal;
  /** Composer placement only: the invoking pane's live draft; retires with `signal`. */
  composer?: { readonly draft: string; setDraft: (text: string) => void };
}) => void | Promise<void>;
```

- `composer.draft` reads the pane's draft at call time (`getDraft()`, falling back to the rendered `draft`), not a snapshot from the click.
- `composer.setDraft(text)` goes through the pane's existing `onDraftChange`, the same owner the composer replacement uses.
- Once the invocation retires (signal aborted, pane session/agent changed, pane no longer presented, or the registration withdrawn), both throw `This plugin UI view has ended.`, matching retired composer-replacement operations.
- Header and session actions are unchanged and get no `composer`.

The chat footer passes its props into `openclaw-plugin-contributions` as a new `composer` bridge property; `runControlUiPluginAction` wraps it into the scoped handle. Docs: `docs/plugins/feature-plugins.md` has the contract and an example.

## Impact

- Additive, optional field on an experimental SDK type; no export added or removed.
- No CSS, i18n or Gateway changes.
- Production delta: +~37 lines across 5 files; one focused test.

## Evidence

- Unit: `ui/src/plugins/control-ui-contributions.test.ts` "binds composer actions to the invoking pane's live draft until the pane retires": the draft read is live, `setDraft` updates the pane draft, and after the pane's session changes both `draft` and `setDraft` throw and the pane draft is not touched.
- Control UI e2e on real isolated Gateways (dist builds, Playwright Chromium), base = merge base `8f0d03fe9c46`, head = this branch. A scratch local plugin (not committed) registers a composer action "Shout draft" that uppercases `context.composer.draft`. Draft typed: `please fix the flaky login test`.
  - Head: the draft becomes `PLEASE FIX THE FLAKY LOGIN TEST`; the run context keys are `agentId,composer,host,session,sessionKey,signal`.
  - Base: the draft is unchanged; the run context keys are `agentId,host,session,sessionKey,signal`, and the action reports "run context has no composer".
- Gates: `pnpm check:test-types`, `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:ui`, oxlint and oxfmt on the changed files, `ocx test ui/src/plugins/` (19 files, 154 tests), `pnpm plugin-sdk:check-exports`, `pnpm plugin-sdk:surface:check`: all pass.

prs.title: fix(update): keep openclaw runnable when an npm update is killed while publishing the package
prs.body:
Related: #200366, #200273

## What Problem This Solves

When an ordinary `npm install -g` installation updates, the updater moves the installed package aside and only then moves the new one into place. If the updater is killed in between (SIGKILL, power loss), there is no `openclaw` at all until the managed helper, if it survived, or a recovery command printed earlier finishes the job.

That gap was not short. On `main` it spans the move itself, two directory syncs, the preservation of local `dist` edits, a recheck of the new package and a journal write: 7 of the 37 filesystem and journal steps of one update.

## User Impact

User impact: on macOS, and on Linux with a system perl (x64, arm64) or Node 26, a normal npm update now publishes with one atomic exchange. The package path names a complete package at every instant, also when the updater, its helper or the machine dies. A killed update leaves either the old version running or the new one, never neither.

Where no exchange is available (no tool, a filesystem that refuses the call) the update installs with the previous two moves, and the existing recovery covers the gap as before. One thing differs from before in that fallback: the journal records the `publish` intent and tries the exchange first, then records `displace` and runs the old sequence. The `package-swap` step text says which ran: `published by an atomic exchange (perl)` or `published by two moves (atomic exchange unavailable: <reason>)`.

Things to know:

- A kill in the short stretch before the exchange leaves the old version running and the journal open. The next update, and `openclaw update repair`, refuse with `Package publication is incomplete` until the printed recovery command runs `repair` (which aborts the update) and `retire`. That is how an interrupted publication that had not touched the package already behaved.
- Local `dist` edits are captured from the old package at its path just before publication, not after it has been moved aside. A publication that is then refused still leaves that recovery bundle behind.
- No change to the journal's schema, version or stored fields, to any SQLite schema, config, protocol or dependency.

**Update behavior.** The installed version's updater publishes, not the candidate's. An installation on a published release that updates to a build with this change is published by that release's code, with the two moves. The first update the new build runs itself uses the exchange. The recovery helper for an update is sealed from the updater that starts it, so the helper always knows the layouts its own updater can leave.

## Why This Change Was Made

A journaled publication now records its `publish` intent, gives the candidate the name `previous` inside the journal's recovery directory, and exchanges that name with the package path in one call (`exchangePaths` from #200273). After the exchange the layout is exactly what the two moves produced: new package installed, old one under `previous`. Everything that runs afterwards (launchers, verification, rollback, settlement, retirement) is unchanged, and so is everything an older release might read after the update.

The alternative was to exchange the package path with the candidate's own name and move the old package to `previous` afterwards. I did not take it, because its in-between state has the new package installed. Any release can be the new package, including an older one after a downgrade, and none of them knows that layout. With the order chosen here, the one new state has the old package installed, and that is the build whose updater wrote the journal.

**The one new state.** Journal `publishing` / `publish`, package path holds the previous package, `previous` holds the candidate, `candidate` is absent. It is accepted only with that recorded intent and the recorded identities of all three directories. The owner returns the candidate to its own name before it classifies anything, so no other reader had to learn the state.

| State | Journal | Package path | `candidate` | `previous` | Who handles it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| prepared | `prepared` | old | new | – | unchanged: repair, the helper and rollback abort |
| intent recorded | `publishing` / `publish` | old | new | – | repair, the helper and rollback abort, as for the untouched `displace` state before |
| **candidate waiting (new)** | `publishing` / `publish` | old | – | new | the owner's `restore` returns the candidate, then as the row above. Admission, `update repair` and remount settlement refuse it as incomplete, as they refuse the row above |
| exchanged | `publishing` / `publish` | new | – | old | unchanged: identical to the state after the second move |

When the exchange is unavailable the candidate returns to its name, that return is synced, and the old sequence runs from its first step.

**Who can read a journal in the new state.**

- The updater that wrote it, its managed helper, and the recovery helper sealed from it: all this code.
- `openclaw` at the package path: in the new state that is the old package, the build whose updater wrote the journal. A candidate is never installed in that state, so a downgrade cannot put older code in front of it.
- Older code can meet it only when the updater ran from somewhere else (for example a checkout updating an npm prefix that holds an older release), or after someone installs another version by hand. I read the published sources for that: 2026.11.4, 2026.11.5-beta.4, 2026.10.9, 2026.9.37 and 2026.9.9. In each, the publication owner compares the identity of `previous` with the recorded previous package before it does anything and refuses; admission and settlement decide from the phase and the installed identity and do not look inside the recovery directory. No release restores, deletes or completes anything from that layout.
- Three things older releases do without inspecting it, for any unfinished publication and not only this state: 2026.10.9's explicit repair after a device remount closes the journal and moves the whole recovery directory aside as evidence; several releases do the same after a manual install over the package; and 2026.11.5-beta.4 may clear group/other write bits on the installed package before it refuses.

`package-update-publication-owner.ts` sits at the 700-line lint limit, so the exchange lives in a new module, `package-update-publication-exchange.ts`, and the owner gains six lines.

## Evidence

**What was checked.** A real journaled update runs in a child process to the end, then once per boundary with the child SIGKILLed right after that boundary. A boundary is one completed filesystem mutation, one journal commit, or the start or end of the exchange tool. After each kill the package path must hold a complete package; then recovery runs on every killed installation.

Before, on `main` (`f52f728d341`, production code untouched): 7 of 37 boundaries leave no package.

| # | Boundary | Journal | Package path |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1–23 | preparation, intent `displace` recorded | up to `publishing` / `displace` | old |
| 24 | old package moved to `previous` | `publishing` / `displace` | **missing** |
| 25–29 | local `dist` files preserved (5 steps) | `publishing` / `displace` | **missing** |
| 30 | intent `publish` recorded | `publishing` / `publish` | **missing** |
| 31–37 | candidate moved into place, launchers | `publishing` … `publication-complete` | new |

At 24–30 admission refuses the next update, and only `repair` restores an installation, by publishing the candidate.

After:

- None of the boundaries leaves the path without a package. The old package serves until the exchange tool has ended and the new one from then on.
- Recovery from every killed run: a run killed before the exchange ends `aborted` with the old package and the candidate back under its own name; a run killed after it ends `publication-complete` with the new one. A second `repair` leaves the same layout (after an abort it refuses with `Forward publication is disarmed (aborted)`), `retire` removes the recovery directory, and publication admission accepts the next update.
- With every exchange tool failing to start, the update takes the two moves and exactly two boundaries have no package: the move to `previous` and the commit that records `publish`. `repair` publishes forward from both. This is the negative control. It was seven on `main`; the five steps that preserve local `dist` files now run before the first move on macOS and Linux, whichever way the package is then published.
- Rollback after a failed verification restores the old package on both methods, and retirement removes the rejected candidate.
- The managed helper, after a real SIGKILL with the candidate waiting, rolls the update back and restarts the old version.
- A candidate under `previous` without the recorded `publish` intent (no intent, or `displace`) is still refused with `Package publication object changed`, journal untouched.
- A publication stopped with the candidate waiting: admission and `update repair` refuse, the transaction's rollback restores the layout and aborts.
- If an exchange tool that outlived its updater publishes while recovery runs, recovery reads the publication as published and completes it.
- A sync failure after the exchange keeps the callback from running and the journal at `publish`; `repair` refuses until the sync works, then completes.

**Docker, Linux** (image `node:24.22.1-trixie-slim`, aarch64, perl 5.40.1).

- `published-driver` cell with the `launcher` follow-up, candidate built from `c4b45d3f668`: passed. Published 2026.11.4 installs the candidate with its own updater and its two moves. The candidate's updater then runs the follow-up update, a plain package directory published through the journal. The cell now asserts that this update printed `Package publication recovery:` and that its `package-swap` step names the exchange. The step read `replaced openclaw; published by an atomic exchange (perl)`.
- `package-installed-recovery`, cut `anchor-before`, candidate built from `835b005e905`. This lane kills the installed updater between the two moves, so its fault preload now also keeps the exchange tools from starting for that cut; the run reported `exchange-tool-withheld` and then the kill in the displaced state. The lane does not pass, on this branch or on `main`, for two reasons this change does not touch:
  1. The lane expects recovery to clear all group/other bits (`mode & 0o7700`). #193272 changed recovery to clear only write bits (`0o7755`). The first tree comparison fails with `mode 755 -> 755 (expected 700)`.
  2. With that expectation aligned locally (not committed), the whole `anchor-before` row passes: displacement kill, status, `repair` twice, killed and resumed retirement, completed status, archive. The lane's final `openclaw update` is then refused with `Update <id> has unfinished recovery; reconcile it before starting another update.`

  A package built from this branch with the three production files taken from `main` gives the same row, field for field, and the same refusal. Both failures need their own fix.

<details>
<summary>Commands, counts, review and test audit</summary>

Base for the reproduction: `origin/main` at `f52f728d341`. Branch created from `origin/main` at `df78722789e`; `origin/main` merged in three times since, last at `8f0d03fe9c4`. None of that movement touches the publication owner, the swap or the exchange. The last merge brought two commits (Codex app-server tests, model registry sources) after the Docker cell and the test runs; nothing was rerun for them.

**Reproduction and red/green**

- Sweep harness: `src/infra/package-update-release-switch.process.test.ts`, layout `journal`. The child is a real updater process that runs `swapStagedPackageInstall` with a prepared journal and is SIGKILLed after one boundary.
- With the three production files from `main` (`package-update-publication-owner.ts`, `package-update-swap.ts`, `package-update-swap-publish.ts`): the four journal test files fail 9 of 101, and `update-managed-service-handoff-interrupted.test.ts` fails 1 of 17 (the new `exchanging` cut).
- On this head: all pass (below).

**Tests** (macOS arm64)

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run <86 files>` on the local default runtime (pinned Bun 1.4.4, exchange route `osascript`): 6 shards passed. unit-fast 3 files / 15 tests, unit-fast-isolated 2 / 18, tooling 7 / 334, infra 55 / 762 passed and 1 skipped, cli-process 5 / 102, cli 14 / 206. Run on the first merge of `main`; the four journal files edited afterwards were rerun: 4 files / 101 passed. After the last merge of `main`, the two listed tests it changed and the script tests (`update-restart-module-outcome`, `eager-import-closure`, `pr-wrapper-source-closure`, `vitest-worker-artifacts`) were rerun: 6 files / 137 passed.
- `OPENCLAW_VITEST_RUNTIME=node` (Node 26.12.1, exchange route `node:ffi`), the seven journal and exchange files: 7 files / 129 passed.
- The 86 files are every `src/infra/package-update-*` and `package-activation*` test, the `src/cli/update-cli*` tests that publish or recover a package, `path-exchange.test.ts`, both `update-managed-service-handoff-interrupted*` tests, and `test/scripts/update-restart-module-outcome.test.ts`, `eager-import-closure.test.ts`, `pr-wrapper-source-closure.test.ts`, `vitest-worker-artifacts.test.ts`, `check-deadcode-exports.test.ts` and the two CI test-plan tests.
- Left out: `src/cli/update-cli/update-command-handoff.test.ts` fails 3 of 14 on this machine with and without this change (its fixture guard under Bun).

**Checks**

- `pnpm tsgo:all`: passed.
- `oxfmt --check` and `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` on the 17 changed code files: clean.
- `OPENCLAW_CHECK_CHANGED_SKIP_DEADCODE=1 node scripts/check-changed.mjs`: exit 0.
- `pnpm check:test-lines-ratchet`: net +400 of 400. `pnpm check:test-mock-exports`: OK.
- `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/check-session-identity-ratchet.mts --base origin/main --no-merge-base`: OK, 1672 files, 6576 grandfathered pins.
- `pnpm format:docs:check`, `pnpm docs:check-links`, `pnpm docs:check-mdx`: clean (1434 files formatted, 16716 internal links with 0 broken, MDX check passed).
- `git diff --check`: clean.

**Review**

The autoreview helper does not run on this machine, so a fresh read-only agent that had not seen my reasoning reviewed the diff against the contract, and a second one audited every touched test file in full. Findings and what changed:

- The `package-installed-recovery` Docker lanes need the two-move window: their fault preload now withholds the exchange tools for the displaced cut.
- The candidate's return to its own name (after an unavailable exchange, and in recovery) was not synced: it is now, before the journal moves on.
- Recovery could race an exchange tool that outlived its updater: after returning the candidate it rechecks identities, puts the previous package back if the tool published meanwhile, and reads the publication as published. Test added.
- Parent syncs after the exchange were unproven: rows added to the existing parent-sync test.
- An assertion that could pass on an empty match now requires the match.
- The sweep runs about forty updaters one at a time because they share one lease database: explicit 300 s test timeout with the reason, not a retry.
- "First package rename refused" had drifted onto the waiting-candidate rename on macOS and Linux: it refuses the displacement again, behind a refused exchange.
- The manifest-read counts in the digest-reuse test depended on a tool being present: hosts without one are pinned to the two moves.

**Test files read in full**

`package-update-release-switch.process.test.ts` and its child fixture, `package-update-publication-boundary.test.ts`, `package-update-publication-durability.test.ts`, `package-update-activation-durability.test.ts`, `package-update-activation-recovery-command.test.ts`, `package-update-swap.assertions.test-support.ts`, `update-managed-service-handoff-interrupted.test.ts` and its two fixtures. No test was removed, skipped or loosened. Existing tests that inject a fault into one of the two moves now state which publication they exercise (`publishWithoutPathExchange()` or `refusePathExchange()`), so they still run the path they were written for.

</details>

**Not proven.**

- Linux under a kill. The kill sweep ran on macOS (`osascript` under Bun, `node:ffi` under Node 26). On Linux the perl route ran only to completion, in the Docker cell. No Docker lane kills the updater around the exchange.
- Power loss. SIGKILL is not a power cut. The directory syncs are proven by fault injection, not by a crash-consistency test.
- Older releases meeting the new state. That answer comes from reading the five published sources, not from running them against such a journal.
- A reboot that clears the temporary lease database while a publication waits before the exchange. The old package keeps serving and the journal stays open, as it already does for an interrupted publication that had not touched the package. Not changed and not tested here.
- An exchange tool that outlives its updater and publishes after recovery has already aborted. Only the case where it publishes during recovery is covered.
- Rollback through the package transaction from the "intent recorded" state. The sweep recovers that state through `repair`; the transaction rollback test starts from the waiting-candidate state.
- With the exchange tools missing, the sweep recovers only the two runs that have no package, not every killed run.
- The `package-installed-recovery` lane does not pass on `main` (see above), so it is not a passing lane here either. Only its `anchor-before` cut ran.
- Windows and FreeBSD keep the two moves. Only their existing unit tests ran, on macOS.
- The full test suite and the dead-code scan were not run.

prs.title: fix(crabbox): join heartbeat cleanup before replacement
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Strict plugin replacement can finish while a Crabbox heartbeat process is still alive. [Scheduled main CI](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44032222298/job/133867332542) reproduces this in the existing real-process replacement test; the same assertion failed in an earlier full run.

## User Impact

Crabbox heartbeat retirement waits for its command cleanup before replacement completes. An uncertain cleanup is reported through the retained stop/dispose promise rather than silently releasing the heartbeat owner.

## Why This Change Was Made

The command runner intentionally permits a bounded return during startup cancellation while retaining physical cleanup separately. Heartbeats previously joined only the bounded result. Run each heartbeat in the existing command scope and retain its completion promise. Schedule retries after that scope settles, outside its async context, so the next heartbeat does not inherit a closed scope.

This changes only the heartbeat lifecycle; the command runner contract and provider protocol stay unchanged.

## Evidence

- Existing replacement test fails on Linux/Bun with its child still alive after strict stop (37 ms and 65 ms in two runs).
- Candidate overlay passed 94 existing tests across the real-process replacement, command-scope settlement, heartbeat, stop-lifetime and command suites in a qualified macOS/Bun lab. Relevant source and runtime files match the branch base; the lab source was restored afterward.
- Independent P0–P2 review found no actionable defects.
- Draft pending native exact-head lint/type checks and Linux CI. The local pass does not establish that the original Linux failure is fixed.

The Lobsterdex has no lobster from Latin America yet.

User impact: a new rare lobster, the Clawlombian, can visit and fill a 52nd slot in the Lobsterdex. Lobsters already found stay in the dex.

The Clawlombian is a coral lobster in a cream sombrero vueltiao with black braided bands and a zigzag hatband. prs.title: fix: keep slash commands in ordinary prose from executing
prs.body:
Related: #199841

## What Problem This Solves

Quoting slash-command instructions in an ordinary message can silently switch the session model, change runtime settings, or run a command instead of discussing it. For example, `Send /model to choose another model.` can select a fuzzy-matched model and lose words from the prompt.

## User Impact

Slash commands, directives, and shortcuts are interpreted only when the canonical sender text begins with `/`, allowing leading whitespace and channel-owned bot addressing. Mid-sentence commands and examples stay ordinary text across the shared Gateway/channel reply path. Explicit native commands, leading commands, chained directives, and `$skill-name` references retain their existing behavior.

**Control UI dependency:** #199841 fixes the separate Enter-time command extraction that happens before Gateway ingress. This backend PR alone does **not** complete the requested all-surfaces behavior until that companion lands. It was verified open at `00e64bab02267db85170b9ad0ffd48ec652e7adf`; its UI implementation is not duplicated here.

**Compatibility:** integrations that supply only a generated envelope/sender label in `Body` must instead provide clean `CommandBody` or `BodyForCommands`. Plain slash-leading `Body` remains supported. Once a message starts with `/`, existing chained parsing remains; this is not Markdown-aware quote parsing inside an admitted command message. No configuration or state migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared reply owner captures directive admission before stripping spans. Reset/general-command preparation and early abort, native-command, bash, and compaction paths now use canonical sender text rather than turning bracketed examples or sender labels into commands. Feishu also stops treating arbitrary plaintext `@name` as removable addressing; its normalized transport mention markup keeps its existing behavior.

The inline directive parser handles model/profile/runtime selection, thinking/fast/verbosity/trace/reasoning controls, elevated/exec settings, queue behavior, and status shortcuts. General slash-command dispatch and explicit skill references remain separate. No new parser, helper, state, configuration, or public field was added; the seven production files have a combined net growth of five lines.

## Evidence

- The exact fuzzy-model sentence failed on base with a synthetic visible catalog entry and passed with the fix. Canonical-admission owner regressions produced 14 intended failures before repair; 282 core owner/consumer tests passed. A required test-only extraction then moved the command-source contract into a coherent sibling suite; the original and new session suites passed 95 tests afterward.
- Feishu plaintext mention regressions produced two intended failures before repair; its command, sequential-key, and ingress suites pass 29 tests across three files, including actual transport-mention controls.
- Shared downstream command tests cover Discord, Slack, Telegram, WhatsApp, Signal, iMessage, and WebChat. Representative Discord, Slack, and Telegram adapter suites passed 47 tests; unchanged-input adapter proof was retained rather than restarted.
- After the canonical cutover, Gateway ingress and prompt-prefix stability suites passed 42 tests across two files. The ingress table exercises Control UI/WebChat and macOS/iOS/Android client identities with ordinary slash prose and leading-command controls.
