prs.title: fix(update): keep openclaw runnable when a pnpm or Bun update is killed while replacing the package
prs.body:
Related: #200273

## What Problem This Solves

If an update is killed (SIGKILL, power loss) while it replaces the installed package, `openclaw` can be left with no package at all and no longer starts. This fixes that for pnpm and Bun installations, and for npm installations whose update runs without a package-publication journal.

That swap moved the installed package to a backup name, preserved or replayed local `dist` edits, and only then moved the new package into place. The package path did not exist for that whole stretch. No journal records this swap, and `openclaw update repair` cannot run without a package.

**Not fixed here.** Most npm updates on macOS and Linux publish through the package-publication journal, which has the same missing-path window between its two moves. That path is unchanged. "The journaled path" below says why and lists the options.

## User Impact

User impact: on macOS, and on Linux with a system perl (x64, arm64) or Node 26, these swaps publish with one atomic exchange. The package path names a complete package at every instant, also when the updater is killed, and nothing needs manual recovery.

This covers pnpm and Bun global projects, and npm when the journal is not used: `--reapply-local-overrides`, a release replaced in place behind its package link, a target without delegated post-core execution, or an update with no executor fence.

Where the exchange is unavailable (no tool, a filesystem that refuses the call, a stage on another filesystem) the update installs with the previous two moves. The `package-swap` step text says which method ran: `replaced openclaw; published by an atomic exchange (perl)` or `...; published by two moves (atomic exchange unavailable: <reason>)`.

Behavior changes to know about:

- Local `dist` edits are captured from the old package at its path immediately before publication, instead of after the old package moved to its backup. This holds on macOS and Linux for every swap without a journal, including the two-move fallback, where it shortens the missing-path window to the two moves themselves. Capture still follows service drain.
- An updater killed just before the exchange leaves the new, unpublished package under `.openclaw.package-backup-<pid>-<time>` beside the old package, which keeps serving. A later verified in-place swap removes it with the other historical backups.
- One new way to fail: if the exchange is unavailable and the rename that returns the staged package to its stage then fails, the update fails with the installed package untouched and names where the staged package is. The forward rename has just succeeded, so I do not expect this in practice.

Windows, FreeBSD, and npm package links to a checkout are untouched. No config, schema, protocol, journal or dependency changes.

**Update behavior.** The installed version's updater performs the swap, not the candidate's. An installation on a published updater that updates to a build with this change gets the published updater's swap, as before. The first update that such a build runs itself uses the exchange. The change adds no marker and no state. The one new leftover is the backup-named directory above, which any updater treats like every other historical package backup.

## Why This Change Was Made

POSIX `rename` cannot replace a non-empty directory, so two moves always leave a window. `exchangePaths` from #200273 closes it with one call (`renameat2(RENAME_EXCHANGE)` on Linux, `renamex_np(RENAME_SWAP)` on macOS).

The staged package first takes the backup name beside the package path. One exchange then leaves the new package on the package path and the old one under the backup name: the same two names the backup and activation moves produce. Nothing has to follow the exchange, so rollback, retirement, the transaction and the launcher steps are unchanged, and no step after publication can fail and strand the old package. That is why the candidate takes the backup name first, instead of exchanging stage and package path and moving the old package afterwards.

Local override capture and replay move before publication, because the old package no longer moves first. The replay helper then runs from the installed package at its own path.

`package-update-swap.ts` sits at the 700-line lint limit, so the unjournaled publication moved into a new module, `package-update-swap-publish.ts` (165 lines). It holds the two-move sequence unchanged and the exchange in front of it. The swap itself grows by 7 lines.

<details>
<summary>Kill states, and how existing readers treat them</summary>

Unjournaled swap with the exchange. `backup` is `.openclaw.package-backup-<pid>-<time>` beside the package path.

| Killed after | Package path | `backup` | Stage | What a later run sees |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| launcher backup, override capture | old | absent | new | Unchanged from today before the swap. |
| staged package took the backup name | old | **new** | empty | New state. The old package serves. A later verified in-place swap removes `backup` as a historical backup (tested). |
| exchange tool started, not confirmed | old or new | the other | empty | The call is atomic: the row above or the row below. |
| exchange | new | old | empty | Today's state after the activation move. |
| launcher steps | new | old | empty | Unchanged from today. |

Fallback on macOS and Linux when the exchange is unavailable: the candidate returns to the stage (the first row again), then the old package moves to `backup` (package path **missing**, old intact under `backup`, new in the stage), then the new package moves into place. That is today's window minus the override work.

- **Activation journal, its recovery and `openclaw update repair`.** This path runs only when no journal was prepared. No record exists, so admission, repair and the sealed helper have nothing to interpret, and no record needs a change.
- **Rollback closures.** Before the exchange nothing is registered and nothing has moved. After it the old package is under `backup` and the new one on the package path, the state `restoreNpmPackageRoot` and the native restore already handle. Rollback itself still uses two moves.
- **Historical backup retirement** removes a leftover `backup` after a later verified in-place swap, whatever it holds. A release switch does not retire historical backups, so on an OpenClaw-owned prefix the leftover stays inside the release it was left in.
- **The npm destination gate from #198673** acts only on an empty package path and only on a link, so it ignores the leftover directory.
- **Stage cleanup** finds no package root in the stage, as after any activation.

Two outcomes that are not a clean exchange get explicit handling. If ownership is lost after the candidate took the backup name, nothing more moves and a warning names where the candidate is. If another writer leaves the two paths in neither state, the swap claims nothing: rollback reports the installation as unverified and completion retires nothing.

| Variant | Window before | After this change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| npm directory, no journal | yes, including override work | closed with the exchange; two moves otherwise |
| pnpm, Bun (`native`) | yes, the whole global project is missing | closed with the exchange; two moves otherwise |
| npm with a journal | yes, between displacement and publication | unchanged |
| npm package link to a checkout (`rootLink`) | yes; the next update from the checkout restores the link (#198673) | unchanged |
| staged package that is a link to a checkout | yes | unchanged |
| Windows, FreeBSD | yes | unchanged; no exchange is attempted |

The package link keeps two moves because its lifecycle proves ownership on the moved entry and refuses without touching the package path. An exchange would publish before that proof.

</details>

### The journaled path

A journaled npm update moves the old package to `<anchor>/previous`, then moves `<anchor>/candidate` onto the package path. The journal records each generation under a fixed name, and every reader throws `Package publication object changed` or `generation roles are ambiguous` when a name holds the other generation. Publication permutes those three names cyclically, so any single exchange leaves one of them holding the wrong generation for one state. The schema would not have to change, but the recovery interpretation would, and helpers and CLIs sealed before such a change would refuse that state. I stopped there, because the journal is the most recovery-critical owner in the updater.

Options, for a maintainer decision:

1. Leave it (this PR). The managed update helper, when it survives, or the printed recovery command finishes a killed journaled publication.
2. Teach the journal owner an exchange publication in its own PR: no schema change, one new durable state, and every recovery, settlement and remount reader has to learn it.
3. Skip the journal where the exchange is available. Smallest code, but it drops standalone publication repair for most npm updates.

## Evidence

**What was checked.** A real package swap runs in a child process once to the end, then once per boundary with the child SIGKILLed right after that boundary. A boundary is one completed filesystem mutation or the start or end of one exchange tool. After each kill the package path must serve a complete package.

- Before the fix, 6 of 16 boundaries leave no package: the backup rename and all five steps of preserving local `dist` files. The next boundary publishes.
- After the fix, none of the 17 boundaries does. The old package serves until the exchange tool has ended, and the new one from then on. The override capture finishes before the candidate moves, and the recovery bundle holds the old package's files.
- With every exchange tool failing to start, the swap takes the two moves (20 boundaries) and the same sweep finds exactly one boundary without a package, the backup rename. The test then restores the installation by renaming the backup back. This is also the negative control: the sweep fails for a publication that backs up before it publishes.
- Rollback after a failed verification restores the previous package, its files and its launcher on both methods, and leaves neither backup nor rejected candidate behind.
- A swap killed with the candidate under the backup name still serves the old package, and a later verified swap removes the leftover.
- pnpm: the whole global project is exchanged, the step names the exchange, and rollback restores the previous project.

**Docker, Linux.** `published-driver-release-in-place` (published 2026.10.9, then the candidate's own updater replaces a release in place, which runs without a journal). Image `node:24.22.1-trixie-slim`, aarch64, perl 5.40.1.

- As committed, on `8b2ce35c5b5`: `PASS published 2026.10.9 → candidate 2026.11.4 (8b2ce35c5b5...)`. The candidate's `package-swap` step reads `replaced openclaw; published by an atomic exchange (perl)`. The cell now asserts that text.
- The published 2026.10.9 updater's own step in the same run reads `replaced openclaw` and prints a `Package publication recovery:` command: that update is journaled, and this change cannot alter it.
- An earlier run on a base before #200321 stopped at `Installed candidate tree exceeds the release budget (52228 entries)`. With that one assertion bypassed in a local, uncommitted edit it passed with the same step text. The bypass is not in this PR, and the run above did not need it.

<details>
<summary>Commands, counts and checks</summary>

Red, then green. Command: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/infra/package-update-release-switch.process.test.ts src/infra/package-update-swap.test.ts src/infra/package-update-swap.forward-authority.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`

- First reproduction, production code untouched at base `51ceecd7aeb`, with the first version of the sweep: 4 failed, 6 passed. The sweep names the six boundaries above.
- Final tests with `package-update-swap.ts` and `package-update-local-overrides.ts` from base: 10 failed, 26 passed.
- Head: 36 passed on Node 26.12.1 (route `node:ffi`), macOS 27.2 arm64. With Node 24.22.1 first on `PATH`, those files plus `path-exchange.test.ts`: 40 passed, and the fixture run directly on that Node reports `published by an atomic exchange (osascript)`.
- On `b0f1596dd94`, those files plus `path-exchange.test.ts`, `package-update-swap.windows.test.ts` and `package-update-steps.native-transaction.test.ts`: 6 files, 65 passed.

Affected tests: every `src/infra/package-update-*`, `package-release-*`, `package-local-overrides*` and `path-exchange` test, plus every test that imports the swap or its fixtures, directly or through a shared fixture: 134 files.

- Infra project on `a08d6c94d0f`, the same change before `main` was merged in: 84 files, 1290 passed, 11 skipped, 2 failed. Both failures are `update-command-database-rollback.test.ts` cases that hit the 120 s test timeout while 84 files ran in parallel. Run alone, that file passes 18 of 18, and its `package` case takes 28.5 s here against 28.2 s with the swap from `main`.
- The other 50 files all passed: 8 unit and tooling files on `a08d6c94d0f` (58 passed), and 42 daemon, CLI and commands files on `8b2ce35c5b5` (682 passed, 8 skipped).
- `update-command-handoff.test.ts` is excluded from those lists: 3 of its 14 tests fail on this machine with `Fixture handoff escaped its private lease database`, identically with the swap from `main`.

`main` was merged in three times while this ran. Those merges touch none of the changed files, the swap, its callers or its fixtures.

Checks on `b0f1596dd94`: `oxfmt --check` and `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` on the changed files, `pnpm tsgo:all`, `pnpm check:test-lines-ratchet` (+364 net test lines, allowance 400), `pnpm check:test-mock-exports`, `pnpm format:docs:check`. On `8b2ce35c5b5`: `OPENCLAW_CHECK_CHANGED_SKIP_DEADCODE=1 node scripts/check-changed.mjs`, and before it `docs:check-links` and `docs:check-mdx`. The dead-export scan exits 1 with two entries, in `extensions/slack` and `ui`. Neither is touched here.

On the pushed head `37922d1585c`, which adds two unrelated commits from `main`: `git diff --check` and `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/check-session-identity-ratchet.mts --base origin/main --no-merge-base` (`Session identity ratchet OK: 1673 files, 6584 grandfathered pins`). The diff adds no identity comparison and none of the counted phrases.

CI on `37922d1585c` failed one job, `checks-node-compact-small-2`: `test/scripts/update-restart-module-outcome.test.ts > retains package backups after unverified post-swap module failures`, with `Unexpected package dependency`. Its fixture `scripts/tests/update-restart-swap-fixture.mjs` names every production module it runs and rejects any other import, and it did not name `package-update-swap-publish`. The follow-up commit `test(update): load the swap publication module in the restart swap fixture` adds the module. The fixture's context reports a fixed `linux` platform whatever the host is, so it sets `supportsPathExchange` to false: it keeps exercising the two moves, which is what it tested before, and can never make a host exchange call under a platform that is not the host's. Red without the fixture change and green with it, same command: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/update-restart-module-outcome.test.ts`. Also run on that commit: `test/scripts/ci-changed-node-test-plan.source-owners.test.ts` and `test/scripts/eager-import-closure.test.ts` (2 files, 100 passed), `oxfmt --check`, `run-oxlint.mjs`, and the session identity ratchet (OK). The fixture file was read in full; nothing was removed.

Test audit. Files read in full: `package-update-release-switch.process.test.ts`, its child fixture `package-update-release-switch.process.test-support.ts`, `package-update-release-switch.test-support.ts`, `package-update-swap.test.ts`, `package-update-swap.forward-authority.test.ts`, `package-update-swap.windows.test.ts`, `package-update-swap.assertions.test-support.ts`, `package-update-steps.native-transaction.test.ts`, `update-command-terminal-outcome.test.ts`, `update-command-mutable-signals-compensation.test-support.ts`.

- Nothing was deleted or weakened, and no timeout or retry was added.
- Existing cases that inject a fault into the two-move sequence (a denied backup rename, the Windows rename retries, a signal between the moves) would no longer reach that sequence on macOS and Linux, so they now select it: `publishWithoutPathExchange()` turns the platform predicate off, as on Windows, and the signal fixture makes the exchange tools fail to start.
- One case asserted the old window (override work that loses authority leaves the package moved away). It keeps that assertion for the two-move sequence and gains a counterpart for the exchange, where nothing moves.
- The cross-device stage case now refuses every rename out of the stage, which is what a real cross-device stage does, so it also covers the fallback from an unavailable exchange.
- The child fixture counts `mkdtemp` and `writeFile` as boundaries too, which adds boundaries to the two existing adoption sweeps without changing what they assert.

Review. The autoreview helper cannot run on this machine. Two fresh read-only agents reviewed the diff, the second after the fixes for the first. Resolved: an exchange that ends in an unknown state no longer reports a verified rollback or retires anything; ownership is checked again right before the exchange; the sweep asserts every boundary; the non-clean outcomes and pnpm have tests; the signal fixture restores `execFile`; the docs name the pnpm and Bun recovery target, the in-place retirement condition and the remaining rollback window. Not changed: a failed return of the candidate to its stage still fails the update (see User Impact).

</details>

**Not proven.**

- The journaled npm path, linked roots, Windows and FreeBSD keep their window. None of them was changed.
- An updater killed while the exchange tool is still running: the tool can finish the one system call afterwards, which leaves either valid state. Reasoned and documented, not tested. The fixture cuts before it starts the tool.
- Whether signal compensation can start while an exchange tool is still running was not traced beyond the existing signal tests, which pass.
- pnpm and Bun were exercised through the fixtures, not through a real global project, and not in the kill sweep.
- No run on a native x86_64 host, on Bun as the running runtime, or on filesystems other than APFS and the Docker volume.
- Only the in-place Docker cell was run. No published-driver cell covers pnpm or Bun.
- The full affected set was not rerun after the merges of `main`, only the six focused files.
- The full affected set was not rerun after the fixture commit below; only the tests it names were.

prs.title: fix(ui): guide Chat to setup when no model is connected
prs.body:
Closes #200323
Closes #200325

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Chat shows an unconfigured default as selected and sends messages into a misleading authentication failure when no model is connected.

## User Impact

Chat points fresh installs to model setup, keeps unsent drafts, and leaves model-independent commands available. No configuration migration or new setting is required. Existing configured, local, restricted, and worker-owned inference paths remain available.

## Why This Change Was Made

A built-in default name is not evidence of a usable model. The picker and composer now use completed catalog and authentication state to recognize the no-model case and reuse the existing setup flow. Pending or failed discovery is not treated as proof that credentials are absent.

This prevents the unconfigured send path in #200325; it does not rewrite general provider errors or historical failures. No native onboarding files are changed.

## Evidence

### Test-fixture typecheck follow-up

The added closed-picker regression omitted the required `selectedSession` prop. The fixture now passes the selected row from the same `createSessionsListResult` instance used by `sessionsResult`; all profile-read and rendered-heading assertions remain unchanged. This changes one test file only (3 added lines, 1 removed), with no production, budget, or timeout changes.

- Reproduced TS2322 at `fdd249e` using `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs --noEmit -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.ui-chat.json`; the identical command now passes with exit 0 and no diagnostics. The earlier UI-only typecheck did not cover this test configuration.
- Reran the PR's focused tests: **202/202 unit tests (12 files)**, **38/38 browser tests (2 files)**, and **8/8 bundled E2E tests (2 files)**. The repaired closed-picker test, inline-output, tool-icons, all seven composer-catalog cases, and unconfigured-model E2E pass. Bundled E2E reuses the unchanged, previously measured production build.
- Targeted lint, formatting, and diff checks pass. The `pr-simplify` pass keeps one shared session fixture and adds no helpers, casts, suppressions, or assertion changes. This follow-up adds 0 production lines and 2 net test lines; whole-PR delta against pinned main `53278c3` is +67 production and +282 test lines.
- `checks-node-compact-small-1` / `runtime-process-build-graph.test.ts` was left alone: no edits or manual reruns. Previous production-size evidence below is unchanged; this does not claim new-head CI has finished.

CI repair acceptance: compare pinned main `53278c30303fd9609599a123160469724370cf26`, PR head `857339f59972b394158cb3ce9a6d96d8734f500c`, and the candidate with identical production-build inputs and hash-normalized gzip measurement. The largest JS asset must be at most 572,440 bytes without raising budgets or regressing configured/unconfigured model flows. The unchanged inline-output browser test is compared repeatedly on both pinned heads.

The current repair moves account-heading preparation out of Chat boot and into the existing lazy-loaded picker panel. It adds no loader, changes no budget, and preserves account aliases, selected profiles, locale updates, configured auth-cold rows, and phantom-default filtering.

- Largest JS gzip: **572,485 → 572,278 B** (**−207 B**, **162 B below** the 572,440 B limit). The unchanged PR reproduced its exact CI size locally. Pinned main measured 572,349 B in this paired local build (main CI reported 572,352 B). The base-relative performance check passes with no violations. Largest CSS remains 59,191 B and Chat boot remains 21 JS requests on both main and candidate; those inherited overruns were not changed.
- Final candidate: **202 unit tests / 12 files**, **38 browser tests / 2 files**, and **8 bundled E2E tests / 2 files passed**. This includes all 7 chat-composer-catalog E2E cases, the unconfigured-model E2E case, and the unchanged chat-pane-tool-icons test. UI typecheck, targeted lint/format, and diff checks pass.
- The new lazy-work regression fails on pinned main with 2 profile reads while the picker is closed; the candidate performs 0 until opening and then renders the account heading. Existing locale/account-selection and favorites assertions remain intact.
- The reported inline-output expected-1/got-0 failure was **not reproduced**: 5/5 PR runs passed, and main had 5 passing runs plus one earlier fixture failure (`onTestFinished() can only be called inside a test`, during first-run dependency optimization). The final candidate also passes. No causal PR regression or definitive flake root cause was established; no event handling, assertion, or timeout was changed. This is not a claim that the original CI failure was fixed.

<details>
<summary>CI repair commands and measurement scope</summary>

Builds use the performance comparison script's fixed branch, commit, timestamp, build ID, release flag, and settings-plugin inventory. The main-archive wrapper could not extract into the sandbox temporary filesystem; instead the same toolchain built the existing clean pinned-main worktree, and `pnpm ui:check-performance --base-dist <pinned-main>/dist/control-ui --json` compared it to the candidate. Test runs used the CI Bun selection and Chromium. Browser proof uses synthetic Gateway responses, not live provider authentication. Existing Solid untracked-read warnings were present; passing counts do not claim a warning-free log. New-head CI is still required.

</details>

Both bugs were reproduced in a real run of the macOS app on a fresh install at main commit 9a6a00e3, with screenshots in the linked issues.

Fix verification uses the actual Control UI in Chromium with synthetic Gateway responses, not live provider authentication:

prs.title: fix(whatsapp): normalize hosted JIDs consistently with Baileys
prs.body:
## Problem and solution

WhatsApp address handling disagreed across target normalization, ingress, allowlists, mentions, approvals, sessions, and quote lookup. Hosted and device-qualified JIDs could identify the same sender differently at each boundary.

Use one typed classifier backed by Baileys. Preserve hosted routing and device normalization, and keep PN and LID identities distinct without a verified mapping. Carry observed alternate identities through receive and cached quotes without optional discovery on the receive path. Setup auth inspection stays dependency-light.

Doctor migrates shipped LID allowlist entries only with account-local mappings that agree across every account inheriting the policy. Unresolved entries remain unchanged with a warning. Mapping reads reject contradictory forward/reverse entries. That rejection now survives receive and approval fallbacks: only genuinely missing mappings may use Baileys lookup. Equivalent LID target expansion uses the same resolver.

Rebased onto `f17c94115978d10e0702dd48170464a1f4c84dc0`, preserving main's durable receive admission, send IDs, delivery recovery, socket authority, and runtime-scoped quote cache. No core or Plugin SDK production changes. Net scope: production +949 lines; tests/support +1,201, plus one test-tooling prerequisite registration. The allocation covers 794 lines above the standard test budget for distinct protocol, authorization, migration, setup, receive, quote, and delivery regressions.

## Review findings addressed

- **P1, receive fallback:** preserve an explicit rejected-mapping result. Real Baileys storage reproduces its stale reverse mapping; receive admission and approval resolution both reject it without calling that fallback. Both regressions fail before this repair and pass afterward. The replacement identity remains accepted, and missing-map lookup remains covered.
- **P2, unused identity path:** remove `knownE164`, its branch, and its test. Quote identity stays owned by the existing cache.
- **Timeout test:** remove the forwarding-only case. Remove the duplicate recorder-only case too. The existing late-accepted socket scenario now checks PN-target quote lookup for a LID-routed send after its mapping file is removed.
- **CI fixture ownership:** keep reusable real Baileys test support inside the WhatsApp plugin. The core CLI test uses public Baileys key persistence directly. Bind the typed lookup method without an untyped forwarding callback.
- **Cold Doctor setup:** register this fixture with the existing Control UI prerequisite owner. The admission regression fails before the registration and passes afterward; Doctor starts only after asset preparation completes.
- **Stored-data compatibility:** the built CLI runs Doctor against persisted Baileys mappings and legacy account `allowFrom`/`groupAllowFrom` entries, verifies the saved phone policies, preserves the mapping file, reloads it through Baileys, and passes `config validate`.

## Evidence

- Signed head: `d7a1f1f6931f3a682406bc8d5eaeb5d1c1a81729`.
- 140 focused tests passed across seven affected suites before the duplicate recorder case was removed. After fixture relocation, the boundary and both fixture consumers passed (67 tests). The prerequisite correction passed 371 build-admission, runner-outcome, and CI-shard tests.
- WhatsApp package, extension-test, and tooling-test typechecks passed. Targeted lint/format, plugin import boundary, mock-export guard, whitespace, and exact test budget passed. Independent reviews of the production repair and final fixture correction found no P0–P2 defects.
- Crabbox full `pnpm build` and built-CLI compatibility test: payload exit 0, [run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43794012236), source `41015db0c2c920554982f6f586680c73e28a73af`. Product code is unchanged afterward. Crabbox repeated `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` and the revised compatibility fixture: exit 0, [run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43796460906), source `1b83b77c3665178e79fb3813b67a46cec93cbbc7`. Both owned leases were stopped; their lifecycle cancellation during cleanup is separate from the successful payloads.
- The [remote artifact build for the final head](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43797629127) passed.
- Final-head CI passes both import boundaries, all typechecks, ratchets, WhatsApp test bundles, and the [built-CLI Doctor lane](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43797629388/job/133070685840). The log shows matching Control UI assets prepared before workers, then the migration test passes in 17.5 seconds.
- No local full build or full test suite was run.

## Remaining CI failure

[CI run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43797629388) has one underlying failure: [core lint stripe 2](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43797629388/job/133071672686) rejects `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(...))` at `src/agents/tool-search-prepared-catalog.ts:118` under `unicorn/prefer-structured-clone`. The file is absent from this PR branch and its pinned base. CI merges the PR into newer main `ef8d709a05a391011ccb1dd1b2c931d0cf7e8095`; that parent and merge `a512ea23ea0ed3e5a36103f639eac50969f38f09` contain the identical file blob `5226ae58848652825503bb9c0558b70b73c7baf0`. The aggregate gate is red because of this inherited main defect.

## Remaining proof

Live WhatsApp receive/reply/approval proof is deferred until an isolated test account is available, as requested. The persisted-data compatibility test does not claim a full upgrade from a published release.

prs.title: fix: let interrupted Control UI builds recover on restart
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Restarting a source Gateway while its first Control UI build is running can leave a build claim behind even after the compiler has stopped. The next build then refuses the retained artifact lock, leaving the UI unavailable.

## User Impact

User impact: on POSIX, a normally canceled cold UI build can finish cleanup and a restarted Gateway can build and serve the UI. Unknown or unjoined shutdown still retains the lock and staging for inspection; this does not reclaim locks based on PID death. Windows keeps the existing conservative child-owned claim behavior. No configuration or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Bind each managed build invocation to the existing artifact owner, which retires its claim only after the existing managed-child runner verifies completion. Route UI build steps and Settings generation through that operation, stop admitting steps after cancellation, and allow the source builder 15 seconds to settle its existing 5-second grace plus 5-second drain before escalation. No new ownership manager or cleanup protocol is introduced.

## Evidence

The original real-process reproduction showed a joined cancellation returning `ABORT_ERR` while its old child-owned claim prevented reacquisition. The repaired operation releases that claim after join and permits reacquisition. A separate abrupt-termination probe preserves the claim, lock, and unjoined marker while a descendant can still write.

On this mainline port, a real isolated Gateway cold build was interrupted with SIGTERM, left an empty artifact lock and no staging, then restarted, rebuilt, and served the UI with HTTP 200 (41.923-second test). The 130 affected consumer tests passed (105 tooling + 25 infra), including real signal-death/still-writing regressions, existing SIGKILL/unknown ownership cases, and UI publication consumers. Scripts and tooling-test typechecks, targeted typed lint, format, and diff checks passed.

The first mainline Gateway run overlapped a validator in the same checkout: its global empty-lock assertion observed that validator's legitimate owner after the UI joined. The owner PID was identified as the task's typed linter. After all validators exited, the unchanged cold-build proof passed alone; no production change or weaker assertion was used.

The release-preparation source snapshot was `97b800653691637437f0d28f12d6e94ad3a6b2d0`; this port is based on main `687dc6c99a32714473a646942382ebcd7f5e6552`. The historical failed CI build lacks its original builder log, so this demonstrates the deterministic interrupted-build defect, not a proven attribution of that historical CI failure.

Review: self simplification/source review and parent source inspection completed without substantive findings. At the requesting maintainer's explicit direction, no local reviewer/model or nested review agent was run; these inspections are not claimed as independent review. Hosted/native enforced review, security, and CI gates remain applicable.

Limitations: Linux runtime proof only; Windows automatic cancellation recovery is not claimed. The real UI cancellation proof covers verified join; unknown-shutdown retention is covered by ownership siblings and the abrupt managed-child probe, not by injecting an unknown Vite termination. No visual UI changes or provider/model calls are part of this repair.

prs.title: fix: agents' first Knowledge saves and lookups fail because the prompt never shows their call shapes
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: agents' first `knowledge_remember` call is often rejected, and some `knowledge_lookup` calls too, because the Knowledge memory prompt describes the arguments in prose and never shows the call shape.

## User Impact

User impact: agents see the exact `knowledge_remember`, `knowledge_lookup` and `knowledge_grep` call shapes before their first call. This should remove most rejected first calls. Tool schemas and validation do not change.

## Why This Change Was Made

On one host, between Oct 4 and Nov 16:
- **`knowledge_remember`:** 200 of 1,097 calls were rejected (18%), and 131 of 240 sessions had their first remember call fail. The usual mistake was `items[].claim` where the schema wants `items[].text` + `items[].kind`. Others were `items[].type`, wrong `kind` values, a top-level `claims`, and slug `requestId`s.
- **`knowledge_lookup`:** 87 of 764 calls were rejected (11%), mostly `{ key }` or `{ title }` where it wants `{ query }`.

The prompt said "an items array (not claims) holding one claim per item" without naming `text` or `kind`, which pushed agents toward `{ claim }`. It never said lookup and grep take `{ query }`, and the Knowledge Index line ("accepts a listed title or aka") pushed agents toward `{ title }`.

Changes:
- The remember guidance now shows `knowledge_remember({ requestId, attribution, excerpt, items: [{ kind: "fact" | "preference" | "decision" | "commitment" | "event" | "belief", text, subject?, about? }] })`.
- The recall and lookup lines show `knowledge_grep({ query })` and `knowledge_lookup({ query })`. The Knowledge Index line names `knowledge_lookup({ query })`.
- A new test parses those shapes out of the rendered prompt and checks them against the real tool schemas: every named key exists, required keys are present and not marked optional, and the `kind` values match. The prompt therefore cannot drift from the schemas, and the test doesn't depend on the compact-hint code.

With every Knowledge tool enabled, the prompt grows by about 141 bytes. There are no argument aliases and no schema changes.

The related compact-hint fix in core is a separate PR: #200064.

## Evidence

- `memory-prompt.test.ts` fails when a shape names an unknown key, marks a required key optional, or lists the wrong `kind` values. A mutation that renamed `about?` made it fail.
- Focused tests pass: `memory-prompt`, `memory-provider-entry`, `conversation-grants`, `memory-index`, `memory-index-hook`, `recall-gate`.
- `pnpm check:changed` passes, except the unused-export scan, which fails only on files this PR does not touch, inherited from current `main` (`compaction-floor.ts`, `replay-session-state.ts`, msteams test-support files and others).
- A pre-PR Astra review found the drift test skipped the final item key. That is fixed.
- Gap: there is no live-model before/after run yet. The first-call rejection rate should be measured again after this ships.

prs.title: fix: stop retrying worktree cleanup that cannot preserve data
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Managed checkout cleanup keeps retrying snapshot refusals that require human repair. Nested repositories, unavailable Git objects and unreadable files remain safely preserved, but indefinite retries waste snapshot work and hide why disk space is not being reclaimed.

Related: #189288, #200299. Integrated with the landed checkout-custody changes in #200335.

## User Impact

User impact: administrators can see why cleanup retained a checkout and when automatic retries have stopped. Nested repositories are preserved immediately; missing/corrupt objects and permission failures receive three attempts with 2h/4h backoff, then remain preserved. After repair, run `openclaw worktrees gc --retry-deferred` to reopen cleanup, including when capacity is exceeded.

Preserved files still occupy disk until an operator resolves them. These safety refusals also prevent force removal. No schema, migration, configuration or cache is added. The existing cleanup receipt stores the typed reason and terminal retry state; CLI status and administrator Gateway results expose the outcome.

## Why This Change Was Made

The retry owner capped delays but never capped attempts. Typed snapshot refusals now reach that owner through the existing worker error transport. Both direct removal and capacity eviction record the outcome while holding checkout custody; automatic cleanup honors it before inspecting files. Explicit retry clears an obsolete receipt so a repaired checkout is not permanently blocked by an earlier failure.

Terminal preservation is the bounded option for nested Git repositories: a lossless nested snapshot would also need to preserve their refs, unreachable objects, alternate stores and linked worktrees. No checkout is removed without preserving its content.

## Evidence

Real service/Git/registry regressions fail before the fix and pass afterward for nested preservation, capped missing-object/permission retries, and force-removal safety. The integrated focused worktree suites pass **78 tests**. Wrapper closure and unreadable-path CLI regressions pass; affected CLI/Gateway mappings and UI browser/e2e consumers were checked. Codex autoreview is clean through P2 on the integrated diff.

A synthetic latest-stable `2026.11.4` CLI upgrade preserved the existing registry row, inner Git history and file hashes. Fresh CLI processes retained terminal receipts; automatic GC above capacity made no repeated attempts; after repair, explicit retry safely removed the selected checkout, and restore recovered its tracked content. The sibling's unsaved files remained intact. Doctor used the existing backed-up migration and skipped service management for the isolated state/config. No live deployment or user data was used.

Production-shaped synthetic btrfs proof uses 62,000 files / 1.1GB, 5,000 sessions / 35.11GiB DB, A/A controls and five interleaved A/B pairs. For missing objects, six failing baseline attempts become three attempts followed by unchanged terminal receipts. Late-sweep medians: wall **1804→753ms**, process CPU **1993→953ms**, main allocation **24.83→4.81MB**. CPU excludes Git children; allocations exclude worker isolates; the DB is size-shaped with sparse transcript content. A/A wall3059/2592ms shows substantial host/cache noise, so operation counts are stronger than a production speedup claim. Nested late-sweep medians are **1055→719ms**, CPU **1215→941ms**, allocation **6.30→6.13MB**; its baseline already avoids repeated snapshots through GC preflight, while the candidate records a durable typed terminal state. Runtime delta against the integrated baseline is +162 lines, covering typed outcomes, bounded persistence, recovery and status visibility.

[Exact-head CI run](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44007250774) is red only for the existing capacity concurrency test (`service.capacity.test.ts:469`, expected one successful create, received zero) and its aggregate gate. It reproduces on exact integrated main parent `9f441adc`; the immediately preceding commit passes all24 tests. The introduction is #200335 (`9f441adc`), which narrowed allocation custody. The precise CI main parent `6ba51132` also reproduces the identical assertion in a bounded repetition of the original case, with unchanged production sources. Both requests reject at the4GiB safety reserve. The remaining repeats were stopped after two reproductions; passing isolated replays are not treated as a fix. The test and four allocation owners are byte-identical between main and the tested merge. This is an inherited main regression requiring follow-up, not a waived PR failure. Security-fast and all other selected jobs pass.

Final narrow `pnpm check:changed --base 9f441adc` passes every scoped gate (format, types, lint and structural/database ratchets); the full command exits1 only for six inherited dead-export diagnostic entries. All are also present on the exact main baseline, with no new entries. ClawSweeper's final-head re-review has **zero open items** and accepts the shipped-entry-point/upgrade proof. Native landing uses the explicitly authorized, pinned inherited-failure route and retains both red results honestly.

prs.title: fix(ios): keep conversation history visible during agent discovery
prs.body:
Related: #159404

## What Problem This Solves

An already displayed conversation can become empty while iOS resolves its default agent or replaces a presentation alias with the same canonical conversation.

## User Impact

Previously displayed replies remain visible during a verified same-conversation handoff. Unknown or different Gateway, account, agent, or conversation identities still clear the old display, and fresh empty history removes retained rows.

## Why This Change Was Made

The iOS presenter verifies matching Gateway/account/ingress inputs. The transcript owner compares the canonical key and agent recorded by accepted history with the resolved destination. Only display rows survive; live authority, cursor, run ownership, outbox mappings, permissions and capabilities do not transfer. Drafts and durable outbox entries retain their existing owners. No schema, configuration, dependency, or animation change.

The maintainer integration preserves current main's asynchronous history decoding, synchronous foreground question expiry, run-scoped streaming retirement, local-send revision and attachment/question authority guards. Only the display handoff is added to those current owners.

## Evidence

- The current six-file integration (dcdd2dedec3, based on main 53278c30303) passed the iOS app build and all 4 ChatSendHydrationTests cases. The shared package passed 211 tests in 5 suites (245 expanded parameterized cases), covering transcript cache, outbox, agent navigation, input history and foreground/history handling. The package manifest was intact: no test exclusions or overlays.
- Strict SwiftLint and configured SwiftFormat pass all 6 touched Swift files. A fresh independent P0–P2 review of the complete integration and owning source found no actionable issues. All 6 files in the tested native checkout match the current candidate byte-for-byte.
- Earlier paired native iOS execution reproduced the visible alias handoff failure: the base clears the conversation to “Loading chat,” while the candidate retains the two displayed replies until replacement history arrives. A subsequent authoritative empty history clears both versions. These screenshots use synthetic conversation data.

### Before / after: canonical-alias handoff

These captures are from base 0633f256350b and the original candidate d240ab4b9b55 with the previously recorded mechanical repair. They are not new runtime captures of the integrated published head.

![Before: alias handoff clears the displayed conversation](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ce481889-9f09-4e07-a6e1-adfade86283c)

![After: the same conversation remains visible while history is pending](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/5fef74d4-ac6d-467e-b313-f9ceeccb9fc0)

### Proof limits

Fresh late-agent/config launch hydration and a real different-owner runtime control were not completed; the owner and history tests cover those contracts. This PR does not claim scroll-position continuity across presenter replacement or CPU, memory, or latency improvements. It keeps transcript rows visible, not the separate reader-position state.

## Contributor credit

- @mikengyn
- @vyctorbrzezowski

## Work sessions

Linked for team reference; these sessions aren’t public.

- [Original discussion](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/dashboard/6b98dedd-1923-4f79-837e-5d48ac84b6c4)
- [Implementation and verification](https://team.openclaw.ai/chat/roboclaw/~key/subagent/770b2d9e-2050-41a7-8af9-aa202b8a46f6)

prs.title: fix(deps): update Undici to 8.12.4
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Updates the six direct Undici pins from 8.12.3 to 8.12.4: the root package and the Anthropic Vertex, Browser, Discord, Slack, and Telegram plugins. The matching lockfile resolutions and integrity were regenerated with pinned pnpm 12.15.0.

## User Impact

Once released, these packages resolve Undici 8.12.4. No configuration change or user action is needed.

The existing Undici 8.11.2 through `mailauth@7.3.1` remains outside this direct-pin update. Moving to mailauth 8 requires separate major-version compatibility qualification.

## Evidence

The final head is `ec91c38213002f9226bc58742fa14930963ef4a3`. Its tree is identical to the previously reviewed `6e04bb3d` tree; the commit message was reworded. Inspection found only six manifest pin updates and matching lockfile substitutions, with no production source changes.

- The frozen lockfile, direct-pin consistency, registry integrity, and unchanged Node requirement were verified. `git diff --check` passes.
- Current-head [artifact build](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44004200307) and [dependency/security review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44004200395) passed.
- Current-head [provider shard](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44004200721/job/133776295492): 49 files passed / 1 skipped; 615 tests passed / 1 skipped, including affected Anthropic Vertex transport, discovery, policy, and region coverage.
- Earlier affected-plugin suites and static checks are recorded in the PR history. The existing independent review of the identical tree found no actionable findings. Local autoreview could not authenticate.

### Final CI and inherited failures

[Run 44004200721, attempt 1](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44004200721) completed on this head: 141 jobs succeeded, 22 were skipped, six test jobs failed, and the aggregate gate failed. `security-fast` passed. The automatic comparison has no matching scheduled-main jobs; the following attribution comes from inspected source, mocks, logs, and baseline execution.

- **Discord custody** ([job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44004200721/job/133776295225)): `retains ambiguous Discord announcement custody after an unidentified send` timed out waiting for ambiguous announcement settlement. The exact CI baseline `4cbd215a` reproduced the same timeout at test lines 636/1208 in an isolated UTM VM with a frozen install resolving Undici **8.12.3 at all six direct sites**, using CI's pinned Bun revision. This is a real baseline failure; its underlying announcement/queue defect remains uncorrected.
- **FaceTime collection** ([job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44004200721/job/133776295590)): the baseline child-process mock exports only `spawn`, while unchanged runtime initialization requires `execFile`. Collection fails before HTTP executes.
- **Package harness** ([job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44004200721/job/133776295542)): the trusted-checkout fixture omits the module now statically imported by baseline `npm-command.ts`. Module resolution fails before argument parsing or HTTP.
- **Browser CLI output** ([job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44004200721/job/133776295400)): the Gateway and exit paths are mocked; the observed output mismatch has no Undici transport. It matches prior identical-tree CI. Isolated passing replays did not establish a repair.
- **Codex context persistence** ([job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44004200721/job/133776301726)): the unchanged test expects zero `markSentToProvider` calls, while the baseline persistence notifier invokes it. Its synthetic harness performs no Undici request.
- **Codex auth queue** ([job](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44004200721/job/133776301516)): refresh and workspace assertions fail inside mocked credential/native-client boundaries. No token endpoint or Undici request executes. The exact scheduling cause remains unresolved.

The actual CI checkout was merge `21ddc754` with ordered parents `4cbd215a` and this PR head. Its baseline-to-merge delta is exactly the seven dependency files. The named failure inputs are unchanged. Landing uses the supported inherited-failure exception; the failed CI is not represented as passing.

prs.title: feat(update): capture PostgreSQL stores while the Gateway serves
prs.body:
Related: #196154

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: an update of an install with PostgreSQL stores keeps the Gateway down for the whole run, because the PostgreSQL rollback capture needs exclusive state ownership and a Gateway the updater does not manage has to be stopped before the update starts.

## User Impact

User impact: PostgreSQL stores are captured while the Gateway still serves, and after the stop only the stores written since their capture are captured again. With the new opt-in `--wait-for-gateway-stop <seconds>`, an update on a Gateway the updater does not manage (custom service, foreground process) prepares while it serves and asks the operator to stop it only for the swap, migrations and restart. On the real install below the Gateway was down about 287 s instead of 941 s. SQLite stores are captured after the stop as before.

## Data-model compatibility

This change adds no store schema and no migration. The only persisted shape change is an optional `sourceDigests` field in the update backup record; records written without it still parse.

Existing data, end to end, on a real Git install with every store family on PostgreSQL 17.11 (macOS, private cluster, foreground Gateway). Data is written on the base `2516bca9fdb8`, the base updater moves the install to this head `7da4339c06f7`, the head reads it back, and then the head's updater runs again into a target whose Doctor throws after the stop, so the database rollback has to restore it.

Data written on the base, with the Gateway serving:

```text
$ openclaw automations create "0 0 1 1 *" "proof acknowledged write" --name occ-proof-written-on-base --agent main --json
{
  "id": "32f86522-2a99-45f6-8a3f-7aca56342499",
  "agentId": "main",
  "name": "occ-proof-written-on-base",
  "enabled": true,
  "schedule": { "kind": "cron", "expr": "0 0 1 1 *" },
  [... cut ...]
}
$ psql -qAt -d openclaw -c "INSERT INTO \"$AGENT_NS\".cache_entries (scope, key, value_json, updated_at) SELECT 'occ-proof', 'k' || g, json_build_object('n', g, 'text', repeat(md5(g::text), 12))::text, 1 FROM generate_series(1, 2500000) g"
```

`$AGENT_NS` is the idle agent's PostgreSQL schema (1.5 GB after the insert). Each check below reads the automation back through the Gateway with `openclaw automations list --json` (count of entries named `occ-proof-written-on-base`) and counts the rows with `psql -c "SELECT count(*) FROM \"$AGENT_NS\".cache_entries WHERE scope = 'occ-proof'"`.

Hop 1, base updater with the Gateway stopped (`openclaw update --channel dev --yes --no-restart`, dev target pinned to `7da4339c06f7`):

```text
23:48:31 base data: seeded rows 2500000, automation written on base present 1
23:48:32 hop 1: gateway stopped; base 2516bca9fdb8 updates itself to 7da4339c06f7
Update mode: git
Update target: 2026.11.4 (7da4339c)
00:05:04 hop 1: update exit 0
00:05:18 hop 1: gateway ready on 7da4339c06f7; down 1006.1 s
00:05:19 hop 1: read back on the head: seeded rows 2500000, automation written on base present 1
```

Hop 2, this head's updater (`openclaw update --channel dev --yes --no-restart --wait-for-gateway-stop 600`) into `28745954995a`, which is `7da4339c06f7` plus a Doctor that throws once the harness creates a flag file:

```text
00:05:20 hop 2: 7da4339c06f7 to 28745954995a (Doctor fails after the stop)
16:13:55.288   ✓ database snapshot (Gateway serving) (91.16s)
00:13:56 update asked for the stop after 516.1 s of preparation while serving
00:13:57 acknowledged write: automation occ-proof-between-capture-and-stop created through the Gateway
00:13:57 armed forced Doctor failure
00:13:57 gateway stopped
16:14:30.024   ✓ database snapshot (17.63s)
16:15:03.268   ✗ openclaw doctor (30.09s)
16:15:03.268     Failing check openclaw doctor (command-failed): proof: forced Doctor failure after the Gateway stopped
16:17:31.123   ✓ database rollback (147.3s)
16:18:18.445 Warning: Kept the capture taken while the Gateway served: <state>/agents/probe/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite
00:18:32 update exit 1
00:18:42 gateway ready on 7da4339c06f7; down 284.7 s
00:18:43 acknowledged write present after the update: 1
00:18:44 after rollback: seeded rows 2500000, automation written on base present 1
```

Result: the automation and all 2,500,000 rows written on the base are read back on this head through the Gateway and in PostgreSQL. After the forced failure, the rollback restores them, and the idle store that holds the rows is restored from the capture kept from while the Gateway served. The write made between that capture and the stop is also present. `HH:MM:SS` lines are the harness in UTC; `HH:MM:SS.mmm` lines are the update output in local time.

## Why This Change Was Made

This answers the three open questions on #196154:

- **Capture generation.** Each PostgreSQL store is captured from its own `REPEATABLE READ` snapshot. Inside that same snapshot the capture records the store's existing generation fingerprint and a reuse digest: catalog facts, sequence allocations, and per table `count(*)` plus `sum(hashtextextended(row_to_json(t)::text, 0))`, computed on the server. After the stop, under exclusive ownership, the update reads the digest again. Equal: the capture is kept with its recorded generation. Different or unreadable: that store's capture is dropped and it is captured again exactly as today. A write acknowledged after the capture therefore always lands in the rollback point.
- **Shutdown handoff.** Managed services keep today's drain and stop. For a Gateway the updater does not manage, `--wait-for-gateway-stop` prints one line asking the operator to stop it, then polls for state ownership until the bound. The updater never stops, signals or starts that Gateway. On timeout it drops the captures it took, changes nothing, and refuses with `database-engine-preflight` as today.
- **No acknowledged write lost, including the updater's own writes.** The update writes its run record and plugin cohort reservation to the shared state store before the capture under ownership, so that store is normally captured again; idle stores keep their capture. A capture that fails while serving falls back to the capture after the stop.

The digest is not a new generation format. Restore checks keep using the existing fingerprint, recorded from the capture snapshot itself. Accepted edge case: two different row multisets with an equal row count and an equal 64-bit hash sum read as unchanged (about 2^-64 per changed store). Cost on one 1.27 GB table on PostgreSQL 17.11: digest 1.36 s, in-database copy 6.13 s.

Signals considered and rejected: `pg_stat` counters (asynchronous, resettable, miss `TRUNCATE`), `xmin` plus row count (PostgreSQL 16+ opportunistic freezing hides updates), WAL position (cluster wide), logical decoding (needs `wal_level=logical`), and change-marker triggers in every store (a schema change and a cost on every write).

Online captures live where raw update captures already live: the update-capture root for package installs and the checkout's `.artifacts` directory for Git installs. A run that ends before the capture under ownership adopts it drops it. A failed online capture drops the finished stores' server schemas one by one and keeps the directory if any schema cannot be dropped. When automatic restoration is unavailable and a package install keeps its online capture, `openclaw doctor` lists it with the other retained update snapshots.

Two files were split to stay under the 700-line cap: the online capture lives in `src/infra/update-database-backup-online.ts`, and `migrateDatabasePortSource` moved unchanged to `src/infra/database-engine/port-source-migration.ts`.

Maintainer decisions:

- `--wait-for-gateway-stop <seconds>` is a new public `openclaw update` option.
- PostgreSQL stores are now captured while serving on every update, including updates of a managed service. That adds one full capture while the Gateway serves (65 to 70 s for the 1.5 GB store below) and takes it out of the stop window (85 s to 11 s).
- Alternative: capture while serving only with `--wait-for-gateway-stop`, so managed-service updates keep the single capture after the stop.

## Evidence

- Regression tests, red on base and green with the change: `update-database-backup-engine.test.ts` "captures each PostgreSQL store while the Gateway serves, from its own capture snapshot" and "keeps an unchanged online capture and captures a written store again under ownership". Both fail on base with `PostgreSQL update capture requires exclusive ownership`, pass on the head, and fail again with the production change reversed (`git apply -R`).
- `doctor-update-snapshots.test.ts`: a retained online capture under the update-capture root is listed by Doctor, and an unreadable update-capture root warns even without an npm install ("warns about an unreadable update-capture root without an npm install"); each red without its fix.
- A capture under ownership that throws no longer orphans the online capture: the cohort hands it over only after that capture succeeds, so the run's cleanup drops it. No dedicated test for this one.
- Cleanup regressions in `update-command-database-backup.online-abort.test.ts`, each red without its fix: a run cancelled as the online capture finishes drops it; a failed online capture drops its finished stores one by one, skips the unfinished one, and lives under the update-capture root on package installs.
- PostgreSQL conformance (`node scripts/test-database-conformance.mjs --engine postgres`, PostgreSQL 17.11): `src/snapshot/postgres-generation.postgres.test.ts` 3/3, including the new digest case (stable, changes on a committed update, a sequence allocation and a `TRUNCATE`, unchanged after a rolled-back delete).
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, oxlint and oxfmt on the changed files: clean. `pnpm check:changed` against `origin/main` at `9a6a00e3e2bb`: every check passes except the dead export scan, which reports only exports outside this change; the scan also fails on `origin/main` itself. The assertion safety ratchet, which flagged one cast in the Doctor listing, passes after the follow-up commit.

### Runtime output

Real Git install on macOS with every store family on PostgreSQL 17.11 (private cluster): state store 3.5 MB, main agent store 1.4 MB, and an idle agent store with 1.5 GB of rows. The local credential and service stores stay SQLite. The Gateway runs in the foreground (`openclaw gateway run`), so the updater does not manage it. Each run updates between two real commits, the start commit and the same commit plus one docs line, pinned with the updater's detached dev target. Downtime runs from the Gateway stop to `/readyz` on the new build. Timestamped `HH:MM:SS` lines are the harness in UTC; `HH:MM:SS.mmm` lines are the update output in local time.

Base, stopped native update (`2516bca9fdb8` to `63d1c9a8e2da`):

```text
$ openclaw update --channel dev --yes --no-restart        # Gateway stopped first
18:10:45 gateway stopped; running the native update with the Gateway stopped
[... update output cut ...]
  ✓ database snapshot (84.79s)
[... update output cut ...]
18:26:18 update exit 0
18:26:26 gateway ready on 63d1c9a8e2da; down 941.0 s
```

Head, same install shape (`8a7da6d4b6ee` to `5beb516a80cf`; the later head only adds Doctor's snapshot listing, which update-time Doctor skips):

```text
$ openclaw update --channel dev --yes --no-restart --wait-for-gateway-stop 600
13:09:37.023   ✓ preflight-build (116.18s)
13:12:05.909   ✓ database snapshot (Gateway serving) (69.62s)
13:12:06.282 Update prepared while the Gateway served. Stop the Gateway through its owner now; waiting up to 600s for it to release state ownership (<redacted: holder detail>)
21:12:06 update asked for the stop after 506.2 s of preparation while serving
21:12:07 acknowledged write: automation occ-proof-between-capture-and-stop created through the Gateway
21:12:08 gateway stopped
13:12:32.810   ✓ git-checkout (5.27s)
13:12:44.453   ✓ database snapshot (11.29s)
[... Doctor output cut ...]
13:16:47.427 Warning: Kept the capture taken while the Gateway served: <state>/agents/probe/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite
13:16:47.492 UPDATE_EXIT=0
== gateway ready on 5beb516a80cf after 7.9 s start
== acknowledged write present: 1
```

The write lands after the online capture and before the stop. After the stop, the store it changed is captured again while the idle 1.5 GB store keeps its capture (`database snapshot (11.29s)` and the `Kept the capture` warning), and the write is present on the new build. The stop to update exit is 279.5 s; with the 7.9 s start, the Gateway was down about 287 s. The harness lost the exit code to a locale error after this run, so the last two lines come from a restart of the same install and state right after the update. Two earlier head runs on the same shape, before the cleanup fixes, were down 341.4 s and 303.0 s.

Head, forced Doctor failure after the stop (`8a7da6d4b6ee` to a target whose Doctor throws once the harness creates a flag file after the online capture):

```text
13:29:19.310   ✓ database snapshot (Gateway serving) (65.35s)
13:29:19.712 Update prepared while the Gateway served. Stop the Gateway through its owner now; waiting up to 600s (<redacted: holder detail>)
21:29:21 acknowledged write: automation occ-proof-between-capture-and-stop created through the Gateway
21:29:21 armed forced Doctor failure
21:29:21 gateway stopped
13:29:40.197   ✓ git-checkout (5.48s)
13:29:52.208   ✓ database snapshot (11.7s)
13:30:16.210   ✗ openclaw doctor (21.98s)
13:30:16.210     Failing check openclaw doctor (command-failed): proof: forced Doctor failure after the Gateway stopped
13:32:11.291   ✓ database rollback (114.75s)
[... update output cut ...]
13:32:46.252 Warning: Kept the capture taken while the Gateway served: <state>/agents/probe/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite
13:32:59.628 UPDATE_EXIT=1
21:33:07 gateway ready on 8a7da6d4b6ee; down 225.9 s
21:33:08 acknowledged write present after the update: 1
```

Doctor fails after the stop. The database rollback then restores every store, including the capture kept from before the stop; restore refuses a store whose live generation differs from the recorded one, so this also shows that the generation recorded inside the capture snapshot matches. The previous build `8a7da6d4b6ee` serves again, and the write acknowledged between the capture and the stop survives the rollback.

What remains in the stop window is mostly Doctor (three passes, about 3.5 minutes here), which this change does not touch. Both base and head successful runs also report `Automatic database restoration unavailable: databases changed after snapshot capture; the writer is unknown` after Doctor on this fresh install; it predates this change.

Upgrade from the latest stable release: blocked by #200357. `v2026.11.4` keeps shared state and agent stores on SQLite (PostgreSQL there is experimental and Workboard-only), so an all-PostgreSQL install cannot start from it. On a SQLite Git install at `v2026.11.4` (`d843d6af39a4`), the stable updater refuses the update to this head before changing anything, and the previous build serves again with a write made on stable intact. It refuses the update to this branch's base `2516bca9fdb8` the same way, so the refusal is not from this change: it is #200357, where the Git updater refuses targets after #198661 at `preflight-build`. Until that fix merges, no stable Git install can reach this head, so the base-to-head run in Data-model compatibility is the newest install that does. The stable-to-head Git cell will be run again once #200357 is fixed:

```text
22:21:13 hop 1: gateway stopped; d843d6af39a4 updates itself to 53c2e0710a01
  ✗ preflight-build (22s)
    Failing check preflight-build (command-failed): Error: Declaration input escapes checkout: [redacted-path]
⚠️ OpenClaw update failed: preflight-no-good-commit.
22:24:31 hop 1: update exit 1
22:24:40 hop 1: gateway ready on d843d6af39a4; down 207.2 s
22:24:41 hop 1: write made on stable present: 1
```

Not run: Linux and systemd, a managed service, a package install, a Gateway-initiated update.

### Local review

Local ClawSweeper, `--local-range` against a fresh `origin/main`, four rounds:

| Round | Head | Correctness | Ratings (overall / proof / patch) | Findings |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `70df3ac2a12c` | patch is incorrect | F / F / C | P2: online capture leaked when the run is cancelled as it finishes. Fixed. |
| 2 | `37d4b3e9e123` | patch is incorrect | C / D / C | P1: package-install capture outside the update-capture root. P2: failed-capture cleanup refused the whole batch. Both fixed. |
| 3 | `ec3111b6baa9` | patch is correct | D / D / B | P3: retained online snapshots on package installs were not listed by Doctor's update-snapshot check. Fixed. |
| 4 | `37a356b966e9` | patch is correct | F / F / B | P3: an online capture was orphaned when the capture under ownership threw. P3: the incomplete-inspection warning needed an npm install. Both fixed in `7da4339c06f7`. |

The proof rating reflects that a local range review has no PR body or attached output. After round 3 the head makes one helper private for the dead export scan and adds the Doctor listing for the P3, without a type assertion. Security: cleared in all four rounds. The round 4 fixes at `7da4339c06f7` have not had a local round of their own.

prs.title: fix(signal): unblock approvals while the requesting turn is waiting
prs.body:
Closes #194029

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Signal approval responses wait behind the turn they need to release. Once dispatched, UUID approvers can be rejected after command normalization, and a typed approval confirmation can cancel the waiting turn with a transcript conflict.

## User Impact

An authorized owner can approve a waiting command from Signal using `/approve` or a supported reaction. Ordinary messages and session-mutating commands retain their conversation ordering. Existing access, exact-target approval checks, and durable audit records remain enforced.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Route the existing narrow set of Signal controls and canonical approval-reaction candidates through a conversation-scoped control lane. Previously stored controls can move only from their exact original conversation lane to that conversation's control lane.
- Supply text-command facts for core active-run admission.
- Preserve UUIDs through Signal command/allowlist normalization instead of stripping their letters into phone-number-like values.
- Keep fast `/approve` exchanges visible in history but outside model context, using the existing context-free recorder contract. Their confirmations must not invalidate the transcript snapshot of the turn waiting for approval; the decision still reaches the model through the tool result.

The lifecycle type lives in the existing leaf types module, removing the review's import cycle. The existing routing helper moves unchanged into the context sibling to respect the oversized handler's growth guard. No schema, dependency, public SDK surface, or configuration option is added.

Related reviews: #175345 does not change Signal ingress; #191787 concerns native-approval capability metadata; merged #153829 supplies the Telegram control-lane precedent. The final recorder fix follows the existing context-free status mechanism from #192585.

## Conflict refresh — 2026-11-17

Merged upstream `edbc5bcea9b605a826cc722d298c784c6a8fef78` into the existing branch, preserving its four original commits. Updated head: `8ce7760f3ebe8ea065b5f00099fbc6c0448fafab`.

The only textual conflict was in Signal's inbound context helper: this branch relocates the existing routing helper, while upstream #200058 renders native mentions in quoted messages. The resolution retains both. Automatically merged changes preserve upstream response-prefix handling and restart tests alongside the approval fixes. The introduced PR diff remains 15 files, +269/-70.

- **176 focused cases pass in 10 files** on the resolved tree: 81 Signal cases (including upstream quoted-mention and group-mention tests), and 95 shared command/transcript cases. Signal wrapper wall time: 120.55 seconds; shared wrapper wall time: 98.78 seconds, including compilation.
- Production core and Signal package type checks, focused regression-test types, targeted lint, formatting, diff checks, pre-commit guard, and import-cycle check pass (0 runtime value cycles). The current test-line budget passes: +138 test lines, 400 allowance, 138 existing allocation credit; no baseline or allocation changes.
- Fresh independent read-only review of the public conflict-resolution bundle found no actionable merge regression. The initial agy review timed out without a result; the completed fallback review covered the manual resolution and overlapping automatic merges.
- The first sandboxed test attempt was stopped after process-identity/loopback restrictions caused fixture failures. The completed run used the required local process and loopback permissions. One type-check attempt overlapped lint's artifact ownership; it was rerun successfully after lint completed.
- Live Signal/model, stable-upgrade, and final-effect authorization receipts below remain evidence for the explicitly pinned earlier head `d24bc8ab8ccbd869accc368c9b6a595016e65055`; those external/live checks were not repeated for this conflict refresh. New-head GitHub CI is separate from the earlier passing runs. [CI run 43902495410](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43902495410) currently reports `action_required` with zero jobs; no new-head CI pass is claimed. GitHub reports the updated PR mergeable; maintainer review and the workflow action remain pending.

## Evidence from the earlier tested head

- Base used for local proof: `8b023da72a1a595450b3071782ec1d4940bd459f`. Previously live-tested candidate: `d24bc8ab8ccbd869accc368c9b6a595016e65055`.
- Red before repair: DM/group queue controls do not dispatch; command context is `normal` rather than `text-slash`; three UUID formats fail approval authorization after command formatting; the fast-approval recording boundary omits `contextFreeCommand`. Corresponding regressions pass after repair.
- **206 relevant cases pass across 11 test files**: 113 Signal cases and 93 shared command/transcript cases. The final consolidated fixture was also verified by rerunning its 74-case lifecycle suite. Signal validation took 63.80 seconds; shared validation took 103.85 seconds, including compilation. Existing authorization, wrong-target, ordinary FIFO, replay, and routing controls remain covered.
- Official production-core and extension type checks, focused changed-test type checks, type-aware lint, formatting, diff and pre-commit checks pass. Temporary test configurations extend the repository configuration; no compiler settings were committed.
- Final clean Linux CLI-startup build passed in **2m 10.7s**. This is the startup profile, not a full release/package/declaration build. Local architecture check reports **0 cycles**.
- Independent reviews of the cycle repair, UUID repair, and final recorder diff returned scoped-clean. The test fixture stays in its existing suite and shrinks by consolidating repeated values.

### Live Signal and model proof

Verified the exact clean candidate with a real agent, configured OpenAI model, and the registered Signal account through Signal Desktop. Approval mode remained gated; only allow-once decisions were used.

```text
candidate: d24bc8ab8ccbd869accc368c9b6a595016e65055
whoami request: pending
/status during the wait: replied; displayed d24bc8a
/approve <redacted> allow-once: allowed via channel policy
whoami final reply: stdout openclaw
separate printf signal-final-ok request: pending
thumbs-up on its native prompt: allowed via channel policy
final reply: signal-final-ok
ingress after both cases: completed=20, pending=0, claimed=0, failed=0
```

These checks exposed and reproduced both the UUID normalization refusal and the typed-confirmation transcript conflict before their repairs. The final run completed without those failures. Only sanitized decision metadata and receipts are included here; no private transcript, account identifier, credential, or screenshot is published.

### Actual stable upgrade

The installed stable core and official Signal plugin, both 2026.11.1, accepted real Signal events into a separate state directory. The stable journal contained an ordinary completion, a claimed typed approval, and a pending reaction in the original direct-conversation lane. After stopping stable, applying the supported offline Doctor migration to the test copy, and starting the candidate, all three records were completed, with the pending reaction reconciled to the control lane; no pending or failed ingress remained.

Account, account UUID, owner allowlist, agent/session filters, default model, and exec/elevated/filesystem policies were checked against the verified native backup and retained. The fixture uses a separate workspace and disables scheduled jobs. Native reaction tests explicitly use forwarding mode `session` with the existing private-session filter; `targets` alone does not start Signal's native approval handler. This demonstrates real packaged-state transport replay, not continuation of an already terminated process's exec call.

### Final-effect authorization proof

The follow-up security review requested rejection at the actual decision owner, beyond the identity helper. On the same exact built head, a separate credential-free Gateway loaded the real Signal plugin and approval capability. Its real exec tool requested a harmless file-marker command; no approval or execution callback was mocked.

For each public resolver used by Signal—legacy `exec.approval.resolve` for typed commands and canonical `approval.resolve` for reactions—both checks passed:

| Resolver | Refused actor | Approval after refusal | Decision waiter released | Command ran before current approval | Same command ran after current approval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `exec.approval.resolve` | Unlisted UUID | pending; no decision | no | no | yes |
| `exec.approval.resolve` | Queued, then revoked UUID | pending; no decision | no | no | yes |
| `approval.resolve` | Unlisted UUID | pending; no decision | no | no | yes |
| `approval.resolve` | Queued, then revoked UUID | pending; no decision | no | no | yes |

The unlisted UUID differs from the listed UUID only in letters, retaining the same numeric projection. In each revocation case, the old actor's control was first persisted with the real SQLite channel-ingress queue, and its pending row was checked. The Gateway's runtime configuration publisher then replaced the Signal approver policy while the original exec request remained alive. Only after publication was the unchanged queued control claimed and submitted to the real resolver. It was refused with `APPROVAL_NOT_FOUND`; `approval.get` still showed pending without a decision, the real decision waiter remained blocked, and the command's marker did not exist. A current listed actor then approved that exact request; the waiter returned allow-once and the real command created its marker. This positive control was repeated for all four cases.

This is an owner-boundary integration proof with synthetic identities and a test-controlled dispatch barrier, not another live Signal-network/model run. It deliberately submits to the final resolver rather than relying on earlier channel rejection. Runtime policy publication isolates the custody guard from file-reload scheduling; no authorization checks or process guards were bypassed. Separately, an attempted public `config.patch` policy reload was observed deferring Signal reload until active Gateway requests finish, so that timed-out attempt is **not** counted as revocation proof. The earlier exact-head live Signal/model proof remains the transport/user-flow evidence. The final isolated Gateway closed cleanly. No production source change was needed for this additional proof.

### Check boundaries

The local test-line guard against the historical base remains **25 lines over due to inherited debt**: base 6,533,876/6,533,851; candidate 6,534,014/6,533,989. The patch adds 138 counted regression lines and exactly 138 allocation credit. The shared baseline and unrelated tests were not changed.

The SQLite and HTTP fixtures were run on a qualified host with process-owner and loopback access. The exact candidate's [CI gate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42223925652/job/127915523030) and [architecture guard](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42223925652/job/127913150828) pass.

The candidate was used for bounded tests, and the normal stable service was restored. No permanent deployment or merge has been performed. Maintainer/security review remains required.
