prs.title: fix(logging): publish support bundles atomically
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves `openclaw sessions export-trajectory` can leave a half-written bundle at the requested output directory when a later write fails (disk full, cancellation, a transient I/O error). Because the directory already exists, retrying the same export fails with `EEXIST` and the partial bundle stays on disk with an authoritative-looking `manifest.json`. ## User Impact A failed export publishes nothing: the requested directory is left free, and the same command succeeds on retry. Successful exports are byte-identical and keep the existing `0700`/`0600` modes and layout. ## Why This Change Was Made `writeSupportBundleDirectory` created the final directory first and then wrote each file into it with `wx`. Build the bundle in a private sibling generation (`mkdtemp` beside the requested path), then publish it with a single `rename`; on failure only the owned staging directory is removed. This mirrors the staged sibling publication the ZIP sibling already uses through `writeExternalFileWithinRoot` (`src/logging/diagnostic-support-bundle.ts`). Refs #127432 (trajectory directory export publishes manifest-bearing partial output). The repair direction there also proposes a completion marker; this change deliberately keeps scope to ownership of the staging generation and does not add a marker file or a new publication API. Fix classification: behavior-completing (same output for successful exports, failed exports no longer occupy the target path). ## Evidence Proof ceiling: `shipped-run` for the built export loader with one injected `ENOSPC`; `producer-chain` for the physical disk-full trigger (not reproduced with a real full filesystem here). Nothing about the write chain is mocked: the real bundle writer, real redaction and real session parsing run. 1. Focused regression `src/logging/diagnostic-support-bundle.test.ts` → "releases the output directory when a bundle write fails partway" (remote secretless container, Node v24.22.1): - BASE `a8a7ce94eb54`: `1 failed | 5 passed` — `AssertionError: expected [ 'bundle' ] to deeply equal []` - HEAD: `6 passed (6)` 2. Built-loader before/after on the shipped export path (`dist/export-trajectory`, main @ `a8a7ce94eb54`), same synthetic session file and workspace, one injected `ENOSPC` on the transcript `.jsonl` write: | | BASE | HEAD | | --- | --- | --- | | first error | `ENOSPC` | `ENOSPC` | | files left at output path | `events.jsonl`, `manifest.json` | none | | retry outcome | `EEXIST` | success | | retry files | — | `manifest.json`, `events.jsonl`, `session-branch.json` | Probe and raw output: `.artifacts/cli-proof/` on the `fix/trajectory-atomic-export` branch. Not tested: an actual full filesystem (the failure is injected at the same `writeFile` boundary the CLI uses); export cancellation mid-run; concurrent exports to the same path (unchanged — the published rename keeps the existing `EEXIST`-for-existing-directory behavior). Cleanup: all runs used `mkdtemp` workspaces under `/tmp` with a synthetic session file; no Gateway, model, or user state was touched.
Why not extend writeExternalFileWithinRoot That helper publishes a file (or an archive) into a root; it does not prepare a directory tree with per-file modes and nested directories. Reusing it here would mean a new directory-publish API on the fs-safe owner, which is a larger change than the defect needs.

## What Problem This Solves

When a local plugin package changes during `openclaw plugins registry --refresh`, verification can refuse the refreshed registry. Text output hid the existing reason behind “The CLI command failed.” and a Doctor hint, although JSON already reported the plugin difference and retry instruction.

## Why This Change Was Made

Raise the same existing message as an `ExpectedCliError`. This uses the class already exported by `failure-output.ts`; that file and its exports are unchanged. No message text, JSON behavior, exit status, successful-refresh behavior, configuration, or persisted format changes.

The existing regression now checks the error name and human output together. It retains both text and JSON cases; synthetic paths and assertions are compacted without removing another test. Production: +2/-2, net 0. Tests: net 0. Contributor commits and credit are retained.

## Evidence

[Natural CLI reproduction and full source/test receipts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/198839#issuecomment-6878672891).

- A real local development plugin's valid manifest is atomically replaced while the real CLI refreshes. No mocks, injected inspection state, or database edits.
- Base `b4cc5654115b`: text failure prints only the generic error and Doctor hint; exit 1.
- Candidate: text prints the existing differing-plugin reason and retry instruction; exit 1.
- Both: clean refresh succeeds, exit 0. JSON failure envelopes match after normalizing only fixture roots, exit 1.
- Final regression: text case fails on base, JSON case passes. All 20 tests pass on candidate.
- Changed files pass targeted formatting and lint checks.
- Final head `379d4dce9838`: full declaration build and installed packed smoke both exit 0. [Receipts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/198839#issuecomment-6878789166).

The source-tier CLI receipts used contributor head `b07aae5b4b95`; subsequent commits only compact tests, leaving runtime bytes unchanged. Source and vitest-source checks ran on the host through ocx with task-owned homes and profiles. The diff passes the host-ocx isolation rule.

## Risk

Two-way door: reverting restores the prior error classification without a migration. Blast radius is only text-mode stale-registry refresh refusals. Successful refreshes and JSON output are unchanged.

prs.title: fix(onepassword): expire cached secrets on elapsed time
prs.body:
## Reopened

This PR reopens #193412 with the same patch and evidence. The previous PR's final re-review (2026-11-06) never landed: ClawSweeper acked "review queued" but the exact-review step ran as skipped, leaving the PR stuck at `status: needs proof` with zero formal reviews. The production code is byte-identical to the reviewed head (`d76c3b49efd`); only the base is refreshed so the test-line ratchet aligns with current `main`.

## What Problem This Solves

`OnePasswordBroker.get` caches a resolved secret for `cacheTtlSeconds` (default 300 s) so repeated reads do not hit `op`. Both ends of that window read the wall clock:

- freshness: `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()`
- write: `expiresAtMs: Date.now() + config.cacheTtlSeconds * 1000`

A backwards clock step on the Gateway host keeps the cached secret being served as fresh for the length of the step after a rotation, so an agent can keep using a rotated credential until the clock catches up.

## Why This Change Was Made

Secret-cache expiry now runs on elapsed time (`performance.now()`). The TTL, cache key (`slug`), target-fingerprint check, config-fingerprint invalidation, and audit rows are unchanged; behavior without a clock step is identical.

Standing grants and pending authorizations keep the wall clock on purpose: they are persisted safety windows (`grantTtlHours`), so an operator correcting the clock must not extend a persisted grant. Only this in-memory, per-process cache moves.

The module is a bundled extension and may only import `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*`, so it reads `performance.now()` directly. Bundled extensions ship with the host, so no compatibility path is needed.

This is **behavior-completing** for the elapsed-clock family (#191606, #192700, #193147, #193306).

## User Impact

A clock correction no longer extends a cached secret past its TTL. Without a clock step nothing changes: same TTL, same cache hits, same audits.

## Evidence

### Unit regression (mocked clocks and mocked `getItem`)

`extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts` via the repository's Vitest entry (`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts`) on Node v24.22.1:

| Test | BASE | HEAD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `expires cached secrets on elapsed time when the wall clock steps backwards` | **FAIL** — the second read is a cache hit (one `getItem` call) | PASS |
| `rechecks grant expiry with cache TTL 300` / `7200` (existing) | PASS | PASS |

The existing harness already fakes `Date.now`; it now fakes `performance.now` with the same counter so both clocks advance together, and `advance(ms)` drives both. The new test steps `Date.now` back an hour while `performance.now` advances past the TTL.

### Real-boundary proof — committed reproducible test (real broker + real op-client + real CLI execution)

ClawSweeper asked for real-behavior evidence through the op boundary rather than mocked clocks and a mocked `getItem`. This proof drives the **shipped production classes end to end**: `OnePasswordBroker.get` → real `OpClient.getItem` → real `resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli` trust validation → real subprocess exec of an `op` CLI. A fake `op` executable (owned by the current user, non-writable, absolute-node shebang — passes the same trust validation the product runs) stands in for the 1Password CLI and logs every invocation to a counter file. The wall clock is stepped back one hour by overriding `Date.now` (the same rollback the fix targets); the process-local `performance.now()` is the real clock and its value at the second read (≈14.5s) far exceeds the 1s cache TTL.

This was previously a one-off driver script; it is now committed as `re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step` in `broker.test.ts`, so it runs in CI. RED/GREEN verified locally:

```
# BASE (broker.ts reads Date.now)
 × re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step
   → expected '1\n' to be '1\n1\n' // Object.is equality
# HEAD (broker.ts reads performance.now)
 ✓ re-fetches a secret through the real op boundary after a backward clock step 1323ms
 # counter file reads "1\n1\n" — op called 2×, secret re-fetched
```

The counter-file discriminator makes the stale-cache defect directly observable: BASE serves the pre-rollback cached value and logs one `op` invocation; HEAD re-fetches and logs two. BASE/HEAD differ only in `broker.ts`'s clock read (`Date.now` vs `performance.now`); everything else (real op-client, real trust check, real exec, same fake-op binary, same test) is identical. No production Gateway, session, token, vault, or real 1Password credential was touched; all CLI targets are local fixtures. The test is `it.runIf(process.platform !== "win32")`-guarded because the trusted-node fixture relies on a POSIX shebang.

HEAD full suite:

```
 ✓ extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts (29 tests)
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  29 passed (29)
```

### Shipped-Gateway proof — real Gateway process, real plugin, real `op` subprocess, real wall-clock step

ClawSweeper asked for evidence through the isolated Gateway with a real agent and model rather than mocked clocks under Vitest. This run drives the **built `dist` for the reviewed head** (`d76c3b49efd`; this PR's head `9fd039bc3bc` has byte-identical production files — `broker.ts`, `broker.test.ts`, `openclaw.plugin.json`, `package.json` — the only delta is the refreshed base), and a base build that differs **only** in `broker.ts`'s clock read. It runs as a long-running Gateway and reaches the plugin's broker through the shipped `POST /tools/invoke` path — the same production entry the Control UI and channel adapters use:

```
Gateway process (dist build)
  └─ onepassword plugin register()  →  OnePasswordBroker (one instance, in-memory secret cache)
        ├─ before_tool_call policy gate (auto)       ← real
        ├─ OnePasswordBroker.get → cache lookup      ← the changed line
        ├─ OpClient.getItem → resolveTrustedOnePasswordCli
        └─ subprocess exec of a fake `op` CLI         ← real exec; logs every invocation
```

The fake `op` is a POSIX script owned by the invoking user, mode `0700`, with an absolute-node shebang, inside a `0755` directory chain — it passes the **same** `resolveTrustedExecutablePath` trust validation the product runs (an untrusted fixture is rejected with `1Password CLI executable is not trusted`, so the trust check is live, not bypassed). A Gateway token, no channel, no real vault, no real 1Password credential, no outbound endpoint: the fixture host is local.

Sequence, identical on both builds: **read #1** (populates the cache, TTL `cacheTtlSeconds: 1`) → step the host wall clock **back 1 hour** with `date -s` → wait **2 s** so elapsed time passes the 1 s TTL → **read #2**. The discriminator is the number of `op` subprocess invocations.

**HEAD (elapsed clock) — GREEN: the cache expires and the secret is re-fetched**

```text
[gateway] http server listening (2 plugins: memory-core, onepassword; 11.8s)
=== [HEAD] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [HEAD] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:46:33Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:46:33Z

=== [HEAD] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [HEAD] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [HEAD] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 2 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:46:33.309Z
2026-11-06T03:46:35.748Z
```

**BASE (production file restored to `Date.now()`) — RED: the backwards step keeps the stale cache alive**

```text
[gateway] http server listening (2 plugins: memory-core, onepassword; 12.6s)
=== [BASE] read #1 (populates the secret cache) ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}
op subprocess invocations after read #1: 1

=== [BASE] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour ===
before: 2026-11-06T04:28:23Z
after:  2026-11-06T03:28:23Z

=== [BASE] waiting 2s so elapsed time passes the 1s TTL ===

=== [BASE] read #2 ===
{"ok":true,"result":{"details":{"ok":true,"slug":"demo","value":"proof-secret-value","itemTitle":"Demo Item","fieldLabel":"credential"}}}

=== [BASE] RESULT: the op subprocess ran 1 time(s) ===
--- op invocation transcript ---
2026-11-06T04:28:22.624Z
```

BASE returns the **cached** secret on read #2 with **one** `op` invocation: after the host clock moved back an hour, `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()` is still true, so a rotated credential keeps being served. HEAD returns the same value but **re-fetches it** (two `op` invocations separated by exactly the 2 s wait and the clock step), because `performance.now()` advanced past the 1 s TTL regardless of the step.

Both reads returned `ok: true` and the value is the same, so the observable difference is purely the cache decision the fix changes — the proof does not depend on the secret's content, only on whether `op` is contacted again.

### Model-driven agent-turn proof — full agent loop, real Gateway, real plugin, real `op` subprocess, real wall-clock step

The previous review asked for the same cache discriminator driven by a **real agent turn** rather than `POST /tools/invoke`. That is now done: a real isolated Gateway runs the agent `main`, and each turn goes user-message → model `tool_use` → onepassword tool executes the real `op` subprocess → `tool_result` returned to the model → model reply. The full tool loop is observable over the Gateway WS API (`agent stream=item` events with `name: onepassword`, `phase: start` → `phase: end`, `status: completed`; core `audit_events` rows `tool.action.started`/`tool.action.finished` with `status: succeeded` for `tool_name=onepassword`).

The model is **real**: the local model endpoint (`deepseek-v4-flash` via the local compatibility proxy) actually generates the `tool_use` and the final reply; the agent turn, plugin, policy gate, and `op` subprocess are all real. One transport detail is disclosed: that model endpoint's stream mode returns `stop_reason: end_turn` even for tool calls (verified directly; non-stream returns the correct `tool_use`), which would stop OpenClaw's embedded runner before it executes the tool. A thin protocol bridge on the model port converts the streamed request to a non-stream request and re-emits the model's real response as spec-correct SSE (`stop_reason: tool_use`). The model output is real; only the transport framing is adapted so the real agent loop, real plugin, real policy gate, and real `op` subprocess run end to end.

Sequence, identical on both builds: **turn #1** "read demo" (agent invokes `onepassword`; cache populated, TTL `cacheTtlSeconds: 1`) → step the host wall clock **back 1 hour** with `date -s` → wait **2 s** so elapsed time passes the 1 s TTL → **turn #2** "read demo" again. The discriminator is the number of real `op` subprocess invocations.

**HEAD (elapsed clock) — GREEN: the cache expires and the secret is re-fetched**

```text
=== [HEAD] turn #1 ===  RESULT: op invoked 1 time(s)   (cache miss, fetch)
=== [HEAD] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour (17:43:18 → 16:43:18) ===
=== [HEAD] turn #2 ===  RESULT: op invoked 1 time(s)   → op count 1 → 2 (refetch)
op subprocess invocations total: 2
```

**BASE (production file restored to `Date.now()`) — RED: the backwards step keeps the stale cache alive**

```text
=== [BASE] turn #1 ===  RESULT: op invoked 1 time(s)   (cache miss, fetch)
=== [BASE] stepping the wall clock backwards 1 hour (17:49:37 → 16:49:37) ===
=== [BASE] turn #2 ===  op count stayed 1; onepassword plugin audit row: "outcome":"cache-hit"
op subprocess invocations total: 1
```

BASE serves the **cached** secret on turn #2 (`outcome: cache-hit` in the plugin's audit store): after the host clock moved back an hour, `cached.expiresAtMs > Date.now()` is still true, so a rotated credential keeps being served. HEAD re-fetches on turn #2 because `performance.now()` advanced past the 1 s TTL regardless of the step.

### Proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `9fd039bc3bc`; the shipped-Gateway dist proof above ran on `d76c3b49efd`, whose production files are byte-identical (`git diff d76c3b49efd HEAD -- extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts extensions/onepassword/src/broker.test.ts` is empty; `dist/extensions/onepassword/index.js` contains `cached.expiresAtMs > this.secretNow()`)
- RED baseline: same tree with **only** `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` reverted to `Date.now()` (two lines), rebuilt and run identically
- Production entry: shipped Gateway `gateway run` from `dist`; tool reached via `POST /tools/invoke` → `onepassword` plugin tool → `OnePasswordBroker.get`; model-driven proof reaches the same broker via the real agent turn (model `tool_use` → onepassword tool → `OnePasswordBroker.get`)
- Recorder: fake `op` CLI appends one timestamp line per invocation; the line count is the discriminator
- Acceptance RED: BASE → 1 `op` invocation across the two reads after a −1 h clock step (both via `tools/invoke` and via the agent turn; the agent-turn BASE run records `outcome: cache-hit` in the plugin audit store)
- Acceptance GREEN: HEAD → 2 `op` invocations across the same sequence (repeated on a second HEAD build with the same result, both via `tools/invoke` and via the agent turn)
- Control: both builds return `ok: true` and the same secret value on both reads; the only variable is the cache-expiry decision
- Cleanup: the Gateway is stopped after the run and the host clock is restored immediately after read #2 (`restored:` timestamp in each log); the fixture op binary, token file, and state live under a private `0700` home directory and touch no real vault, channel, or credential

### Impact surface

| File:line | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:183-184` | Elapsed clock for the secret cache only |
| `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts:537,558` | Cache freshness read and write; grant/pending windows untouched |

### Not tested

- **Model transport is adapted, model output is real.** The model is the local `deepseek-v4-flash` endpoint (real output). Because its stream mode reports `stop_reason: end_turn` for tool calls, a protocol bridge converts the request to non-stream and re-emits the real response as spec-correct SSE. No model output is fabricated; only the stream framing is translated. A maintainer can re-run the identical turns against a hosted model by pointing the provider at it — same recipe as the Shipped-Gateway proof.
- No live 1Password account: the CLI boundary is a local fake `op` binary that passes the product's own trust validation. The proof exercises the cache decision, not the `op` HTTP client.
- Local `pnpm tsgo:core` cannot run on this contributor host (bundled `tsrs` needs GLIBC 2.29+); type checking is left to CI.

### Cleanup

Work happened in a detached worktree off `origin/main`; no user Gateway, session, token, or user config was touched. The proof's Gateway used an isolated state/config dir under a private `0700` home, was stopped after the run, and the host clock was restored immediately after read #2.

### Maintainer options

<details>
<summary>Land-ready or alternatives</summary>

Narrow single-owner change in one broker method pair plus its test; land as-is if the elapsed-clock direction is what you want here.

Alternatives rejected: moving grants and pending authorizations to the elapsed clock (persisted windows should follow the wall clock an operator sets); clamping instead of switching clocks (leaves existing entries frozen).

Scope: `extensions/onepassword/src/broker.ts` and its test file.

</details>

prs.title: fix(knowledge): report discrawl export errors without a traceback
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`discrawl-normalize.mjs` crashes with a raw Node traceback for every rejected export — channel-name resolution, guild mismatch, bad `--threads`, bad timestamps, `discrawl status` failure — because the run rejects out of the top-level `await` with no CLI boundary catch. The sibling script `chat-transcript.mjs` in the same skill already reports the same class of input errors as a single clean line (#197307 open; merged siblings #196398, #196440).

The output stream ordering had the same validate-after-open shape as #196440: `createWriteStream(output)` ran before channel/guild/threads validation, so a rejected export raced the stream open against process teardown for the user's previously preserved JSONL.

Precedent: #197307 (same file family, same "reject without a traceback" shape; this PR covers the Discrawl normalizer), #196440 (validate before touching output).

## Why This Change Was Made

- `run()` gained the same CLI boundary catch as `source-manifest.mjs`/`#197307`: print only `error.message`, `process.exitCode = 1`. No stack, same exit code.
- Destination creation moved after every input validation and after `database.prepare`, so a rejected export never opens (and truncates) the output file — the #196440 ordering.
- The `finally` now destroys a non-stdout destination so a rejected export cannot leave the open stream holding the event loop (without this, the new `exitCode`-only exit would hang on validation errors).

No new validator, option, config, or policy. Valid exports take the identical code path apart from stream creation happening after validation instead of before.

Production LOC is +11/-4 (1 file); test +75/-0 (1 new file).

Classification: `behavior-completing` (completes the reject-without-traceback shape for the Discrawl normalizer; same boundary pattern as the sibling scripts).

## User Impact

A rejected Discrawl export now prints one diagnostic line (e.g. `Channel name resolved to 0 rows; supply --channel with the stable channel ID`) and exits 1, instead of a multi-frame Node traceback. A pre-existing preserved `messages.jsonl` can no longer be truncated by a rejected run. Valid exports are byte-identical before and after (control run below).

## Evidence

### Exact-head proof receipt

- Product head SHA: `c5cf853931feaa51f9be651a2535103368c34de2` (branch `fix/knowledge-discrawl-validate-first`)
- Current-main RED baseline: `91db919f2de1675ec62da6524f3bda0415f9f8b9` (discrawl-normalize.base.mjs = `git show origin/main:…/discrawl-normalize.mjs`)
- Production entry: `node discrawl-normalize.mjs --config x --channel nope --since 2026-10-01T00:00:00Z --before 2026-10-02T00:00:00Z --output <pre-existing file>` (script file itself; node:sqlite builtin)
- Canonical owner exercised: `run() in extensions/knowledge/skills/knowledge-source-ingest/scripts/discrawl-normalize.mjs`
- Recorder/readback boundary: exit code / stderr line count / pre-existing output file bytes
- Cleanup: isolated tmp dirs only; no Gateway/session/token/config touched

### Inspectable RED -> GREEN terminal trace

Shipped script file in docker `lexiflow-all:latest`, Node v24.22.1, fake `discrawl` CLI on PATH returning a fixture archive. Base = current-main file, head = this branch. Full harness output:

```text
== RED (base, invalid channel, pre-existing output) ==
base  exit=1 stderr_lines=12 traceback=true preserved=true
base  stderr: "file:///ws/discrawl-normalize.base.mjs:84\n        throw new Error(\n              ^\n\nError: Channel name resolved to 0 rows; supply --channel with the stable cha"
== GREEN (head, invalid channel, pre-existing output) ==
head  exit=1 stderr_lines=1 traceback=false preserved=true
head  stderr: "Channel name resolved to 0 rows; supply --channel with the stable channel ID"
== control (valid channel, base vs head byte-compare) ==
base  exit=0 rows=1 summary={"provider":"discord","source_key":"discord:9:100",...,"item_count":1,"watermark":"7",...}
head  exit=0 rows=1 summary={"provider":"discord","source_key":"discord:9:100",...,"item_count":1,"watermark":"7",...}
control_identical=true
```

Note on the original truncation claim: with a small fixture archive the stream-open vs process-teardown race on current main does not truncate within the measurement window (5/5 runs preserved); the deterministic, reproducible defect is the traceback, which the boundary catch fixes. The reordering removes the race class entirely (open cannot precede validation) and is required so the `exitCode`-only exit cannot hang on the dangling stream — the test suite's preserved-file assertion guards the ordering.

### Verification

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/knowledge/src/discrawl-normalize.test.ts extensions/knowledge/src/source-manifest.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` — 4 passed (clean-error RED here; successful-export coverage stays in source-manifest.test.ts per review)
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/knowledge/src/chat-transcript.test.ts extensions/knowledge/src/source-manifest.test.ts extensions/knowledge/src/skill-packaging.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` — 7 passed (sibling scripts unaffected)
- `node scripts/check-test-lines-ratchet.mts` — OK; `node scripts/check-line-cap-ratchet.mjs` — OK
- Not tested: `--output` into a missing directory still surfaces a stream-level error (pre-existing behavior, separate concern); mid-iterate DB errors keep their existing crash class.

### Scope and risk

- Production LOC: +11/-4 (1 file)
- Test LOC: +121/-0 (1 new file)
- Existing-solutions preflight: mirrors the `source-manifest.mjs` boundary pattern cited in #197307; no new helpers
- Config/default, protocol/schema, authorization, storage, migration, upgrade impact: none

prs.title: fix(knowledge): report malformed chat export rows without a traceback
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A chat export containing a malformed JSON line makes `chat-transcript.mjs` crash with a raw `SyntaxError` stack trace instead of naming the offending row. The neighboring input validations (UTF-8 decode in #196398, UTC `occurred_at` in #196440) throw a one-line `Error` identifying the row; `JSON.parse` was the remaining unguarded read.

Precedent: #196398, #196440 (same file, same "reject malformed chat exports with a clean error" shape; this PR covers the JSON parse step)

## Why This Change Was Made

`readRows` parsed each JSONL line with `JSON.parse` in a `.map()` and let any `SyntaxError` escape as a full Node traceback. The parse now runs in a loop that numbers physical lines (before skipping blanks) and throws a one-line `Error` naming the row, and the CLI boundary catches it — mirroring `source-manifest.mjs` — so the process prints only `error.message` and exits 1 instead of a Node stack trace. No validator, option, config, or policy change.

Production LOC is +11/-2, net +9 (1 file); test: +17/-1 (1 file).

Classification: `behavior-completing` (completes the reject-without-traceback shape for the JSON parse step)

## User Impact

A damaged chat export now fails with `Row N of the export is not valid JSON` as the only stderr line (exit 1, no traceback) before any output is written. The row number is the physical line of the malformed JSON even when blank lines precede it. Valid exports are unaffected.

## Evidence

### Inspectable RED -> GREEN terminal trace

Shipped `chat-transcript.mjs` CLI with synthetic JSONL (Node v24.13.1). `RED` is the current-main file; `GREEN` is this branch.

```sh
printf '{"id":"m1","occurred_at":"2026-11-09T10:00:00Z","payload":{"author_id":"1","author_name":"A","content":"hi"}}\n{invalid-json}\n' > malformed.jsonl
node extensions/knowledge/skills/knowledge-source-ingest/scripts/chat-transcript.mjs --input malformed.jsonl --output-dir out --channel '#t'
```

RED (current main) — raw `SyntaxError` traceback, exit 1:

```text
<anonymous_script>:1
{invalid-json}
 ^

SyntaxError: Expected property name or '}' in JSON at position 1 (line 1 column 2)
    at JSON.parse (<anonymous>)
    at file:///.../chat-transcript.mjs:48:27
    at Array.map (<anonymous>)
    at readRows (file:///.../chat-transcript.mjs:48:8)
```

GREEN (this branch) — one line naming the row, no traceback, exit 1:

```text
Row 2 of the export is not valid JSON
```

Blank-line case — a blank first line before the malformed row reports the physical line 3:

```text
Row 3 of the export is not valid JSON
```

Legal control — valid export still succeeds, exit 0, expected files written:

```text
{"days":1,"chunks":1,"messages":1}
2026-11-09.jsonl 2026-11-09.txt chunks.json
```

### Committed regression

`extensions/knowledge/src/chat-transcript.test.ts` gains a subprocess case: a valid row, a blank line, then `{invalid-json}` exits 1, prints `Row 3 of the export is not valid JSON`, emits no stack frame (`at ` absent from stderr), and writes no `chunks.json`. It fails on base (raw `SyntaxError` traceback) and passes with the fix.

```sh
pnpm vitest run extensions/knowledge/src/chat-transcript.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```

### Scope and risk

- Production LOC: +11/-2 (1 file); test: +17/-1 (1 file)
- Existing-solutions preflight: reuses the neighboring rows' `throw new Error(...)` style; no new validator/option/config
- Config/default, protocol/schema, authorization, storage, migration, upgrade impact: none
- Cleanup: synthetic fixtures under `/tmp/chat-a-probe/`; no production Gateway, session, token, or config touched
- Not tested: multi-byte/Unicode malformed bytes are covered by #196398's fatal UTF-8 decoder; this PR only changes the JSON parse step

prs.title: fix(sessions): keep the canonical abort outcome when compaction is interrupted
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`sessions compact <key>` intentionally has no default client timeout, but did not forward the command's cancellation signal. Ctrl+C acknowledged the interrupt while the CLI continued waiting for `sessions.compact`.

## Change

Forward the existing async-work signal to the Gateway transport, then preserve its canonical abort outcome before rendering ordinary failures. No new options, helpers, or message text. The original contributor commit is retained.

The regression is folded into the existing lifecycle command suite. Existing genuine-failure and option coverage remains; there is no new test file or allocation record.

## Evidence

A real isolated Gateway trimmed a synthetic 100,001-event transcript with `--max-lines 200`. Each run cloned the same golden state; there was no proxy, held request, provider mock, or injected fault.

- Base: still waiting two seconds after SIGINT; the subsequent SIGTERM terminated it with exit 137.
- Candidate: exit 130 within 225 ms of SIGINT, with no failure banner.
- Uninterrupted controls: exit 0 on both, keeping the same 200 events.
- The server finished the trim after either interrupted client stopped. All four resulting transcripts had identical hashes. This change cancels the client wait, not an accepted server mutation.

## Risk and rollback

Two-way door: reverting restores the previous client wait behavior. Blast radius is the `sessions compact` CLI interruption path. Server compaction ownership, explicit timeouts, normal output, storage, configuration, and protocol are unchanged.

Detailed commands, red/green tests, natural-path receipts, packaging proof, and limits: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/199050#issuecomment-6882800321

prs.title: fix(cli): show the gateway health reason in status --deep
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw status --deep` prints only `The CLI command failed. For help, run openclaw doctor.` when the Gateway is unreachable, hiding the actual health reason. The reason (`Gateway is unreachable`, or the probe error from a failing health check) was only visible with `--json`.

## User Impact

User impact: `status --deep` now prints the real health reason plus a diagnostic recovery step (`Run openclaw gateway status --deep for gateway diagnostics.`) instead of the generic failure line, with the same exit code 1. The step is a diagnostic command that the service owner never refuses and that applies to local and remote targets alike. `--json` output keeps the stable probe-error message and the exit code is unchanged; no new wording in machine output.

## Why This Change Was Made

The deep status path surfaces a failed gateway health probe by throwing a bare `Error`, which the CLI failure handler classifies as unexpected and replaces with the generic line in human output. Throwing an `ExpectedCliError` instead lets the human output carry the health reason plus a recovery step, matching the actionable-error contract and what the JSON path already reports. The step is deliberately a diagnostic command rather than a lifecycle command: `gateway start`/`gateway install` can be refused by the service owner (for example under an external supervisor), so deriving eligibility from the gateway mode or installation snapshot would recommend commands that are not reliably available. A diagnostic next step needs no such policy and is never refused.

## Evidence

Discriminating regression (`src/commands/status.scan-failure.test.ts`, `status --deep gateway health failures > reports the gateway health reason with a diagnostic recovery step`):

- **BASE** (throw `new Error(health.error)`): both local and remote cases fail — rejection is a plain `Error`, not an `ExpectedCliError`.
- **HEAD** (this change): 8/8 tests in the file pass for both a local and a remote unreachable target.

Real CLI proof through the **supported shipped launcher** (`node openclaw.mjs`, built dist, Node 24, isolated HOME, no Gateway running), same build with only the throw changed:

Before (base):
```
$ openclaw status --deep; echo $?
[openclaw] The CLI command failed.
[openclaw] For help, run `openclaw doctor`.
1
```

After (head):
```
$ openclaw status --deep; echo $?
Gateway is unreachable
Run `openclaw gateway status --deep` for gateway diagnostics.
1
```

`--json` machine output is unchanged (the probe error alone, `{ "ok": false, "error": { "type": "cli_error", "message": "Gateway is unreachable" } }`).

The new first-party audit mock carries a mock-isolation annotation explaining why the real security audit must stay outside this fixture (the deep-status regression only asserts the gateway health failure path).

Test-line budget: 61 added lines, allocated in `config/test-lines-allocations/status-deep-health-reason.txt`.

### Maintainer options

<details>
<summary>Scope and alternatives</summary>

This is a narrow single-file change plus its regression test; the TTL-free behavior, JSON schema, and exit codes are unchanged.

Alternatives considered:
- Keeping the bare throw: leaves the health reason hidden in human output.
- Wrapping at the CLI boundary: the `ExpectedCliError` contract already exists for exactly this and is what sibling commands use.
- Human-only recovery text: kept the machine output as the stable probe error so JSON consumers see no wording change.
- Recommending `gateway start`/`gateway install`: rejected because those commands can be refused by the service owner (external supervisor, no installed service), so the hint must not assume either is permitted; a diagnostic command needs no eligibility policy.
</details>

prs.title: fix(cli): name the operator's spelling for an unknown --channel
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw directory` reports `Unsupported channel: undefined` for any `--channel` value it cannot resolve. A user who types `slak` for `slack` gets:

```sh
$ openclaw directory self --channel slak
Unsupported channel: undefined
```

The name they typed is gone from the message, and the placeholder does not say which command to run next. The same input already gets a usable answer from a sibling command in the same CLI:

```sh
$ openclaw channels remove --channel slak
Unknown channel "slak". Run `openclaw channels list --all` to see configured and installable channels.
```

This is not a regression of #199616. That PR changed this guard's error classification from a plain `Error` to `throwExpectedCliError` and deliberately kept its message; its stated scope was that `directory --json` hides the remedy on **stderr**. The message content is a separate defect that #199616 did not cover, and it reproduces identically before and after that change.

## User Impact

The operator's own spelling reaches the terminal in both text and `--json` mode, so a typo is self-evident. Nothing else changes: the guard still fires on the same condition, the exit code stays `1`, the non-explicit branch keeps its existing message, and no configuration, default, or channel capability is touched.

## Why This Change Was Made

`resolveInstallableChannelPlugin` returns no `channelId` when it cannot resolve an explicit name (`src/commands/channel-setup/channel-plugin-resolution.ts`), so on the explicit branch `selection.channel` is `undefined` and `String(selectedChannelId)` interpolates the empty placeholder.

Report `explicitChannel` when the operator supplied one, and keep `selectedChannelId` on the non-explicit branch:

```ts
throwExpectedCliError(`Unsupported channel: ${String(explicitChannel ?? selectedChannelId)}`);
```

The non-explicit branch still passes the resolved channel id, so the existing `Unsupported channel: unavailable` contract asserted in `src/cli/directory-cli.test.ts` is unchanged. The shared `formatUnknownChannelMessage` owner is **not** used here: its "Run `openclaw channels list --all`" wording belongs to `channels`, and adopting it would rewrite the message this guard already owns in both branches. Keeping the interpolation is the smaller change and preserves #199616's test.

Fix classification: behavior-completing (same guard, same exit code; only the reported name changes).

## Evidence

1. Focused regression `src/cli/directory-cli.test.ts` → three new cases (`self`, `peers list`, `groups list`) asserting the operator's spelling on the explicit branch, run on Node v24.22.1 with the repo's `scripts/run-vitest.mjs`:
   - BASE `9a6a00e3e2bb` (production change stashed, new tests kept): `3 failed | 21 passed (24)`
   - HEAD `f75738f24a8b`: `24 passed (24)`
   - The pre-existing `preserves the JSON-mode remedy when the selected channel has no plugin` case passes on both, confirming the non-explicit branch is untouched.
2. Shipped CLI, built `dist` at each commit, isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` + synthetic config, no Gateway and no user state:

| | BASE `9a6a00e3e2bb` | HEAD `f75738f24a8b` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `directory self --channel slak` | `Unsupported channel: undefined` | `Unsupported channel: slak` |
| `directory self --channel bogus` | `Unsupported channel: undefined` | `Unsupported channel: bogus` |
| `directory peers list --channel slak` | `Unsupported channel: undefined` | `Unsupported channel: slak` |
| `directory groups list --channel slak` | `Unsupported channel: undefined` | `Unsupported channel: slak` |
| `directory self --channel slak --json` | `"message": "Unsupported channel: undefined"` | `"message": "Unsupported channel: slak"` |
| exit code | `1` | `1` |

Control on the same BASE build, unchanged by this PR: `channels remove --channel slak` → `Unknown channel "slak". Run \`openclaw channels list --all\` to see configured and installable channels.`

Formatting: `oxfmt --check` clean on both files; `git diff --check` clean.

Not tested: a live channel plugin that resolves but exposes no `directory` capability, non-`en` locales, macOS/Windows, and an installed upgrade. The `--channel` value used here is a plain unknown name, which is the reported shape.

Cleanup: every run used a `mkdtemp` state directory under `/tmp` with a synthetic `{"agents":{"entries":{}}}` config. No Gateway, model, session, token, or user state was touched.

## Why This Change Was Made

Forward the existing command signal through the Gateway status read and credential-required probe, stop interrupted reads before offline diagnostics, and reject an interrupted fallback probe even when it resolves normally with an aborted result. The original fix and commit by @wangmiao0668000666 are preserved.

The additional commit deliberately narrows the pre-action catch: cancellation is rethrown, rather than treated as an unavailable guard. That prevents bootstrap or the credential command from starting without a guard verdict after interruption. Ordinary warning, refusal, and unavailable-guard outcomes and their text are unchanged. No production message strings changed.

## User Impact

Interrupted guarded commands exit 130/143 without a late state-directory refusal. Existing top-level CLI-failure/doctor guidance still appears on the tested source runtime. Matching paths and Gateway-down operation still proceed; mismatched paths still refuse with the same text.

## Evidence

[Proof and redacted receipts](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/199353#issuecomment-6887788748).

- Natural live Gateway startup, not held replies or fault injection: main twice and candidate twice. After SIGINT/SIGTERM, main printed late refusals and exited after 1.611/2.603 s; candidate printed no refusal and exited after 1.110/0.956 s with 130/143.

The added resolving-probe case separately fails on pre-fix `d43cec1` (returns allow); final head has 14 passes and 2 platform skips. Final Vitest duration: 89.82 s including cold worker preparation. - Touched-file formatting and lint passed. Full `ocx build --dts` and prepared-pack/extracted-entrypoint smoke passed. Packed smoke links candidate workspace dependencies; it is not a fresh dependency-install test.
- All execution used host ocx after the protected-path admission check. No Worktrunk/Git hooks ran; unchanged install/build/pack lifecycle scripts ran through ocx.

## Scope and Risk

Production +11/-0 across two files. Tests +57/-57 (net 0) across two files: consolidated setup/table coverage and an export-preserving runtime mock, no allocation file. Removed only the obsolete runtime-mock baseline exception (-1 config line). The command lifecycle remains the cancellation owner; no new state, schema, API, flags, or messages.

Two-way door: reverting restores the previous cancellation behavior without a migration. Blast radius is limited to interruption while a guarded local CLI command checks Gateway state paths.

prs.title: fix(audit): stop interrupted audit reads when the CLI is cancelled
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw audit` keeps waiting for a pending Gateway reply after Ctrl+C, then prints a misleading RPC timeout error. The read-only audit queries (`audit.activity.list`, legacy `audit.list`, `audit.run.inspect`) do not forward the command signal, so an interrupted read stays open until the launcher kills the process.

## User Impact

Interrupted audit queries promptly release their read connection and exit with the normal SIGINT/SIGTERM code, without printing a late error or an upgrade-state reply the user no longer wants.

## Why This Change Was Made

Forward the existing command signal through both read-only audit query helpers, keep aborted reads quiet, and skip output when the read was cancelled. This mirrors the same read-only CLI cancellation pattern as the recently merged external contributions #198076 (`tools usage status`) and #198083 (`hooks status`), at the separate `audit` entry point. The legacy `audit.list` fallback keeps its existing unsupported-method discovery; an aborted read returns before that fallback instead of falling through.

## Evidence

**Shipped CLI proof** — real `openclaw audit --json` executed from the source tree (`node --import scripts/tsx.mjs src/entry.ts audit --json`) inside an isolated state/workspace, driven against a synthetic loopback WebSocket gateway peer speaking the real OpenClaw wire protocol. The peer completes the real `connect.challenge` / `connect` / `hello-ok` handshake (protocol 4), then holds the real `audit.activity.list` request pending while SIGINT (Ctrl+C) is delivered to the controlling PTY.

| Revision | exitCode | SIGINT→exit | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BASE `d5d77e181a2e` (unfixed) | **-9 (SIGKILL)** | **2068 ms** | Read is NOT cancelled. The process hangs in the pending `audit.activity.list` read after Ctrl+C and is killed by the harness timeout instead of exiting on its own. |
| HEAD `378deb30e85a` (fixed) | **130 (SIGINT)** | **238 ms** | Read is cancelled. The CLI exits normally with the SIGINT code ~9× faster; no late audit output is printed. |

The decisive difference: BASE holds the pending read after interruption and is killed; HEAD cancels the pending read and exits promptly with the canonical SIGINT code. BASE stderr: `Command interrupted by SIGINT. Waiting for cleanup before exiting.` then SIGKILL; HEAD stderr: the same notice, then normal cleanup and exit 130.

[Evidence](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wangmiao0668000666/openclaw/2d8059e2ea4b/proof/audit-read-cancel/EVIDENCE.md) · [BASE receipt](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wangmiao0668000666/openclaw/2d8059e2ea4b/proof/audit-read-cancel/base-receipt.json) · [HEAD receipt](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wangmiao0668000666/openclaw/2d8059e2ea4b/proof/audit-read-cancel/head-receipt.json) · [BASE stderr](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wangmiao0668000666/openclaw/2d8059e2ea4b/proof/audit-read-cancel/base-stderr.txt) · [HEAD stderr](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wangmiao0668000666/openclaw/2d8059e2ea4b/proof/audit-read-cancel/head-stderr.txt) · [driver](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wangmiao0668000666/openclaw/2d8059e2ea4b/proof/audit-read-cancel/drive.py) · [synthetic peer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wangmiao0668000666/openclaw/2d8059e2ea4b/proof/audit-read-cancel/drive-peer.mjs)

**Red/green focused regression** (`src/commands/audit.test.ts`): a held Gateway read that rejects when the passed signal aborts.


- **BASE (red):** two new tests fail — an interrupted activity read and an interrupted run-inspection read both keep the held read pending and surface `held read never released` instead of exiting quietly:
  - `FAIL |commands| src/commands/audit.test.ts > audit command interruption > drops an interrupted activity read without falling back` — `promise rejected "Error: held read never released" instead of resolving`

- **HEAD (green):** 27 passing tests across the file (`25 existing + 2 new`) in 4.86s: `pnpm vitest run src/commands/audit.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`. Aborted activity reads return before the legacy fallback (`callGateway` called once); aborted run inspections return undefined.

**Controls preserved:** all 25 existing cases pass unchanged — ISO/ms timestamp conversion, invalid-filter rejection, legacy `audit.list` fallback only with legacy-compatible filters, message-filter refusal on old Gateways, opaque-cursor recovery, `audit.run.inspect` rendering, upgrade-state reporting. The unsupported-method fallback and error rendering are untouched.

**Checks:** `oxlint`, `oxfmt`, and `git diff --check` pass on the two touched files. `check-test-lines-ratchet`: net +54 test lines within the 400-line allowance, no allocation record needed.

Precedent: #198076, #198083 (same read-only CLI cancellation shape).

prs.title: docs(thinking): document the subagent spawn thinking precedence
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`agents.entries.<id>.thinkingDefault` is documented as the per-agent default thinking level, and its bullet links to
[thinking resolution order](/tools/thinking#resolution-order), but that section never covered subagent spawns. A reader
therefore expected `thinkingDefault: "off"` on a specialist to apply when `main` spawns it with `sessions_spawn`, and the
child silently ran at the caller's level instead. The full spawn precedence order was written down nowhere.

## Why This Change Was Made

This takes the report's second option — keep the behaviour, document it — because the inheritance is intentional:
`docs/tools/subagents/tool-reference.md` already states that native sub-agents inherit the caller's turn and that only ACP
spawns apply the target's `thinkingDefault`.

New `Subagent spawns` subsection under the resolution order in `docs/tools/thinking.md` lists every step of the chain,
checked against `src/agents/subagents/spawn/subagent-spawn-thinking.ts`:

1. an explicit `sessions_spawn.thinking` argument;
2. the requester's `agents.entries.*.subagents.thinking`;
3. the target's `agents.entries.*.subagents.thinking`;
4. `agents.defaults.subagents.thinking`;
5. the caller's own selected level, only when that level was chosen explicitly (`callerThinkingExplicit !== false`).

It also records the two consequences the report needed: the first resolved value is saved on the child session as its
initial `thinkingLevel`, so it outranks the child's own `thinkingDefault` on later turns; with none of the five, the child
uses its own model default. ACP spawns additionally apply the target's `thinkingDefault` then its per-model
`params.thinking`. The section names both entry points (`subagent-spawn-plan.ts` for native,
`acp-spawn-runtime.ts` for ACP) so a future change to the chain has an obvious doc to update.

The `thinkingDefault` bullet in `docs/gateway/config-agents/entries-and-multi-agent.md` now says which case it does *not*
cover and links to the new section, and names the target-side `subagents.thinking` workaround — including the caveat that
a requester-side `subagents.thinking` still wins.

## User Impact

Docs only; no behaviour change. Someone configuring a specialist agent now sees why the child ignored
`thinkingDefault`, what to set instead, and every condition of the chain that decides it.

## Evidence

- `pnpm format:docs:check` → `Docs formatting clean (1421 files)`.
- `pnpm lint:docs` → `Summary: 0 issues in 0 files`.
- Every step, the persistence consequence and both entry points are quoted from
  `src/agents/subagents/spawn/subagent-spawn-thinking.ts:12-30` and its callers (`subagent-spawn-plan.ts:21,175-188`,
  `acp-spawn-runtime.ts:103-117`) rather than from the report.

## AI Assistance

This PR was prepared with AI assistance from the issue report; the author reviewed the change and its evidence.

prs.title: fix: show multi-question reply format
prs.body:
Closes #173760

AI-assisted. Substantially follows the shared-guidance and regression shape from #173845 by @D41910; the commit credits Winoren as co-author.

## Summary

- Show one bounded, copyable multiline example in the initial multi-question prompt and invalid-answer recovery notice.
- Document the same accepted reply format.
- Derive the regression's successful reply from the displayed example so guidance and parser behavior cannot drift.

## Issue

Closes #173760.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: messaging-channel users can be told to answer every `ask_user` question by number or id without being shown that each answer needs its own keyed line.

## User Impact

User impact: after an incomplete grouped answer is rejected, the user sees a concrete two-line reply template and can fill it in while the same question remains open.

## Root cause

The multi-question parser already accepts one keyed answer per line, but the shared prompt owner and rejection notice exposed only abstract wording. A normal one-line prose reply fills question 1 and leaves later required questions empty, so the recovery path repeated guidance that did not demonstrate the required shape.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared prompt guidance is the canonical owner for this format. Reusing one bounded constant in the initial prompt and rejection notice fixes both user-visible paths without changing parsing, validation, authorization, custody, or question lifecycle. #190513 remains complementary parser/numbering work; #193400 remains complementary correction-delivery work.

## Verification

- Exact upstream base: `c61a7c0cf6b72f9c35ad8acdc432e132f4d86a50`; the five touched files were unchanged from the reproduced `95363ce54afd893d89cc6bd6645578dba52888d0` snapshot.
- Before source oracle: exit 1. A one-line two-question answer populated `where`, left `game` empty, and found no copyable example in prompt, rejection, or docs.
- After the same oracle: exit 0. It extracted `1: <answer for question 1>\n2: <answer for question 2>`, filled it as `1: Lisbon\n2: 2000`, and mapped both keyed answers while confirming the rejection notice and docs use the same format.
- `node --experimental-strip-types --check` passed for all four touched TypeScript files.
- `node scripts/docs-list.js` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Exact-head GitHub Actions at `b53ab9bf4816e1b41767192072e59dbf914d5750` passed `openclaw/ci-gate`, dependency review, and security-sensitive review. Job `128927468471` ran `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.question-custody.test.ts`: 17/17 tests passed, including `reports an incomplete multi-question answer and keeps the question open` in 24 ms.
- Production delta: `+6/-2` (net +4); tests `+13/-6`; docs `+10/-3`.

## Before/after

Before:

```json
{"answers":{"where":"either is fine, and lets do X","game":""},"hasExample":false,"docsExplain":false,"reproduced":true}
```

After:

```json
{"example":"1: <answer for question 1>\n2: <answer for question 2>","completeAnswer":"1: Lisbon\n2: 2000","answers":{"destination":"Lisbon","budget":"2000"},"correctionUsesShared":true,"docsExplain":true,"fixed":true}
```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** Multi-question text prompts and invalid-answer recovery now show the keyed multiline reply shape the existing parser accepts.
- **Real environment tested:** Exact current OpenClaw source snapshot on macOS with Node 22.22.3; source-level behavior oracle plus syntax/docs/diff checks; exact-head GitHub Actions on Linux.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** Node source oracle reading the production prompt, rejection, parser contract, and docs; `node --experimental-strip-types --check` on the four TypeScript files; `node scripts/docs-list.js`; `git diff --check`.
- **Evidence after fix:** The oracle derived `1: Lisbon\n2: 2000` from the displayed example, resolved both keyed answers, confirmed both runtime messages share the guidance, and exited 0. Exact-head CI also ran the owning custody regression file: 17/17 tests passed, including the changed incomplete-answer case in 24 ms.
- **Observed result after fix:** The user-visible recovery text now contains a copyable answer that satisfies both questions without changing parser or lifecycle semantics.
- **What was not tested:** No live Telegram account, deployed Gateway, or external model/API. Focused Vitest was not run locally; the exact-head GitHub Actions job ran the owning regression file successfully.

## Risk and scope

Low. This changes shared bounded guidance, one recovery string, one documentation paragraph, and assertions around the existing custody flow. No config, schema, protocol, persistence, parser, validation, authorization, or delivery lifecycle changes.

## Not tested

No live Telegram account, deployed Gateway, or external model/API was tested. Local focused Vitest and autoreview were unavailable in the original publication environment. The exact current head is now covered by GitHub Actions run `42544696697`: `openclaw/ci-gate`, dependency review, and security-sensitive review passed, and job `128927468471` ran `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.question-custody.test.ts` with 17/17 tests passing; the changed incomplete-answer regression passed in 24 ms.

prs.title: fix(subagents): a child result committed to the requester transcript is never lost or replayed
prs.body:
## What was wrong

A requester wake commits the child result to the parent transcript before it calls the model. If that turn then failed (for example the provider returned 529), the subagent row recorded `delivery=failed`, `disposition=permanent_failure`, next to its own `requesterDelivery: consumed` fact. The result was in the parent's transcript, but the row said it was lost.

- Only private (`completionTarget: "parent"`) completions counted a consumed input as delivered.
- A yielded batch carries the `yieldedFinalDeliverable` marker (written on every yielded batch, `subagent-registry-requester-yield.ts:580`). It was excluded even when its turn failed before it answered, so it settled as a failure.
- A result that never reached the transcript was given up after three attempts on a 30 s / 120 s ladder.

Measured on base `2435c1faa791` (real Gateway, real model, provider down for the parent model): `delivery=failed disposition=permanent_failure consumed=true` (table below).

## The rule

- A result committed to the requester transcript is never dispatched again.
- If the turn failed before it answered, the result is delivered. This applies to yielded batches too. The turn's own error is visible in the chat, and the next turn reads the result from the transcript.
- If the requester answered but its channel send failed, or the turn ended for a recorded policy reason, the outcome stays a failure, and its existing notice path still runs.
- A result that no turn committed stays owed. It has no attempt limit, ladder or expiry, per the class rule "a failed turn does not touch a result; wake is a function of stored state".

## What this deletes

- The private-only and yielded-final exceptions in the consumed check. A committed input that is followed by a turn failure is delivered.
- `REQUESTER_SETTLE_WAKE_MAX_ATTEMPTS`, the retry-delay ladder, `resolveRequesterSettleRetryState` and the exhaustion settle.

No storage, schema or protocol change, and no new module. Production code: **+57 / −69 (−12)**. The additions are the turn-failed-before-answer rule (`subagent-delivery-state.ts`) and the missed-channel marker on the direct response.

## What triggers a retry, and why it cannot spin

- Only two things trigger the next attempt for an uncommitted result: the subagent sweeper tick (every 60 s, `subagent-registry-sweeper.ts`) and the Gateway restart restore.
- A conflict that keeps happening cannot loop. The wake commits the input before it calls the model, so a later conflict only loses the answer. The result is then consumed, so it is delivered.
  - Probe: real Gateway, mock provider, a writer that appends to the parent transcript on every synthesis request, and the real sweeper ticked 6 times.
  - Result: **1 attempt in 6 ticks**, row `delivered`, child input in the transcript once.
- A down provider does not loop for the same reason. The requests counted below come from that one turn's own runner backoff.
- Known limit: a failure before the commit (preparation or admission refused) is evaluated again once per sweeper tick. That attempt makes no model call. I did not change it.

## E2E (real Gateway from source, `claude-opus-5-5` parent and `claude-sonnet-5-5` child via cliproxy; a local proxy returns 529 for the parent model while "down"; isolated state, service env stripped, unique random ports)

| Journey | Base `2435c1faa791` | Head `10cfa70da2b2` |
|---|---|---|
| Provider down 300 s while the yielded parent wakes for its child | `delivery=failed disposition=permanent_failure consumed=true`. 7 refused requests, all within 62 s of the wake. | `delivery=delivered consumed=true` while still down. 7 refused requests, all within 67 s of the wake, then **0** for the remaining ~4 min. No "couldn't be delivered". |
| Next human turn after the provider returns | answers with the child result (it is in the transcript) | answers `parent-got child-final …` |
| `kill -9` the Gateway after the child ended and before the wake (parent busy) | `pending` → after restart `delivered consumed=true`; the parent replies with the child result | `pending` survives the kill → Gateway back in ~45 s → `delivered consumed=true`; the parent replies `parent-got child-final …` ~2 min after restart, once, with no duplicate |

An intermediate head (`39e5a58`, production identical to `ab9ab16`) still showed `failed/permanent_failure` on the provider-down journey, the same as base. That run found the yielded-marker exception fixed in `10cfa70`.

Tests: `subagent-requester-delivery.test.ts` adds yielded private finals ("failed before answering" → delivered, red before the fix; "missed its channel" → failed). `server.subagent-transcript-conflict.test.ts` now pins the new contract: a conflicted, uncommitted result stays owed and is due at once, and the 4th wake after 3 conflicts delivers it.

Local ClawSweeper review (`gpt-6.1-sol`, normal speed) of `10cfa70`: patch is correct, 0 findings. Its maintainer question ("retry indefinitely without the attempt budget?") is answered by the class rule above: no attempts, ladders or expiry. The cost of retrying is bounded by the probe and the outage counts.

CI: the earlier red `checks-node-changed-*` jobs were `[MISSING_EXPORT] resolveIdentityPathViaExistingAncestor` from `main` (the same failure on #200247: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43948463342/job/133585463142), fixed by #200242. The later red `server.subagent-transcript-conflict.test.ts` asserted the deleted ladder and was updated in `39e5a58`.

Follow-ups (same class, separate PRs): `/new` before a pending result is consumed shows that result in the fresh conversation's runtime context; and "subagent source lifecycle changed before completion delivery" drops a finished result when the parent's run has moved on.

prs.title: fix(ui): measure boot assets with the shipped gzip level selection
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: the Control UI performance gate reports boot JS gzip growth that the shipped build does not have, because it recompresses hash-normalized boot assets at libdeflate level 12 only while the build ships the smallest of levels 10, 11 and 12.

## User Impact

No user-visible change. Maintainers and contributors get a performance gate whose normalized boot gzip numbers follow the same compression policy as the shipped sidecars, so a change that shrinks shipped gzip no longer fails boot budgets because of compressor-level noise. Budgets, hash normalization, identity fallback, Brotli settings and code splitting are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

`createControlUiPrecompressedAssetVariants` (ui/vite.config.ts) picked the smallest gzip of levels 10/11/12 for boot assets and level 12 for deferred assets. `measureControlUiBudgetAsset` (ui/config/control-ui-asset-compression.ts) received `compression.boot` but always used level 12 when normalization changed the text, and the served sidecar size when it did not, so the measured policy depended on whether normalization touched the asset. Both paths now call one selector, `gzipControlUiAsset(body, boot)`.

Observed on #200145 (4be2dde vs b307684, two identical paired Studio builds): shared boot JS raw +53 B, shipped gzip **-384 B**, normalized budget gzip **+729 B**, with identical chunk and module inventories. #200145 depends on this PR.

## Evidence

- **Fail-first parity test** (`ui/src/app/vite-precompression.node.test.ts`): measures a hash-normalized fixture where level 10 beats level 12 and asserts boot, deferred and ineligible (identity) measurements equal what the build ships. On main sources it fails with `expected 5460 to be 5432` (level-12 measurement vs shipped boot sidecar); with this change it passes. Reproduced locally and in the container below.
- **Local** (rebased onto main `48cd549b1c48653061ec312e35fef62d13df62cf`): `pnpm test ui/src/app/vite-precompression.node.test.ts ui/src/app/vite-config.node.test.ts test/scripts/control-ui-performance.test.ts` → 102 tests passed; with main's `ui/config/control-ui-asset-compression.ts` and `ui/vite.config.ts` the parity test fails again (`expected 5460 to be 5432`).
- **Crabbox container proof, current head** (Mac Studio, provider `local-container`, image `node:24.22.1-trixie` runtime_image_id `sha256:f1e034976f948cf212ef1f659c12e5dd58ac7eab947831813e81a62401ca38be`, Node v24.22.1, 8 CPU / 24 GiB, `--no-hydrate`): lease `cbx_f3fafd504399` (run_bc538d6712fc108889e25da14415f77d), HEAD `9d34a02905360ee3e104b6c2b18a49009d3d4209`, command `corepack pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --store-dir .pnpm-store; corepack pnpm test ui/src/app/vite-precompression.node.test.ts; corepack pnpm ui:check-performance:base 48cd549b1c48653061ec312e35fef62d13df62cf` → parity test 2/2 passed, gate **exit 0**, total 3m34s, lease stopped. Chat boot JS 1,323,907 → 1,323,751 B (−156; limit 1,324,691), new-page boot 815,710 → 815,554 B (−156; limit 816,160), largest JS 558.5 KiB (limit 559.0), startup JS and CSS unchanged.
- **Earlier proof, previous head `7b9674ac`** (same image and recipe): lease `cbx_2cc06ff303e6` showed the parity test passing on the branch and failing with main's sources, and `ui:check-performance:base 9e66164c` exit 0. Lease `cbx_10eff13acc0d` ran #200145's `3e7e9f0` plus this fix (scratch branch `scratch/ocf-552-perf-parity-3e7e9f0`, HEAD `bc2aad92`): `ui:check-performance:base b307684` → **exit 0**. That pair previously failed (+729 B normalized; over the largest-JS, chat and new-page caps by 205, 234 and 142 B). With the fix: chat boot JS 1,312,699 → 1,313,109 B (+410; limit 1,313,246), new-page boot 815,218 → 815,628 B (+410; limit 815,806), largest JS 558.6 KiB (limit 558.7).

<details><summary>Review notes</summary>

Independent review found no P0–P2 issue in this diff. It noted a pre-existing, separate gap: the gate derives boot assets from `index.html` only, while the build also treats login-only chunks (`routes.login`, deliberately absent from the HTML) as boot for compression. Those chunks are not part of the chat/new boot totals; aligning that classification needs the gate to learn the login route set and is left as a follow-up rather than widened into this fix.

</details>

prs.title: feat(slack): show streamed reasoning as task rows and roll long native streams into continuation messages
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Slack's presentation of streamed reasoning (`agents.defaults.reasoningDefault: "stream"`) is broken on `main`, and this PR replaces it rather than adding an alternative:

- **Narration keeps only the head of each reasoning burst.** `formatReasoningProgressDisplayLine` → `compactProgressText` keeps the start of the buffer (`chars.slice(0, end) + "…"`), so once a burst passes ~118 characters every later delta yields the same line and nothing further reaches Slack. The code calls it a rolling row; in practice it shows the burst's opening sentence. A recorded run on `main` sent 3,047 characters of reasoning to Slack as two ~120-character rows. The same compacted line is the native path's narration.
- **The fallbacks disagree.** With `nativeTransport: false` the frozen head rows stay on the card after the turn; when Slack refuses native streaming for a channel the fallback card is deleted after the answer, so reasoning shown during the turn disappears.
- **Long turns lose their stream.** Slack documents that "a streamed response has a time limit of 10 minutes" ([agent design guide](https://docs.slack.dev/ai/agent-design/)), and it holds regardless of appends (measured: appends every 20 s rejected ~605–611 s after `chat.startStream`; idle appends accepted at 8 min, rejected at 12 min). After that both `appendStream` and `stopStream` fail with `message_not_in_streaming_state`. `main` has no rollover, so any native turn past ~10 minutes, reasoning or not, loses its progress message.
- **Answers were lost on `msg_too_long`, and a late boundary could stop the stream under the answer.** Fixed on `main` by #199849 (merged); this PR builds on it.

Slack's `plan` block is the structure built for this: collapsible rows with per-row details, rendered in the web client and the iOS app (both checked), and accepted in ordinary `chat.postMessage` / `chat.update` messages as well as streams. So no client or transport needs the text form, and this PR has no presentation setting.

## User Impact

- **Streamed reasoning renders as 🧠 task rows** on the native progress card, interleaved in order with tool rows and collapsed under `Thought for <n>s, <k> tool calls` when the turn ends. The compacted reasoning narration line is removed. Model commentary (visible text between tool calls) is unchanged. With reasoning off, the card shows tool rows exactly as on `main`.
- **Every native progress turn becomes a chain of messages when it needs one.** The current message is sealed (`Thinking, continued below`, open rows completed) and the turn continues in a new message in the same thread when the next update would exceed the size budget, 50 rows (Slack stops showing rows past 50), or 8 minutes of stream age (ahead of Slack's 10-minute close). A plan of any size spreads over as many messages as it needs, every step exactly once. Short turns stay on one message: every exact chunk sequence in `dispatch.preview-fallback.test.ts` passes unchanged.
- **The answer always arrives.** It goes under the cards on the last message when it fits, otherwise in its own message; if Slack still rejects it, it is posted through the normal reply path and the stream is closed (#199849).
- **The quiet card (`toolProgress: false`) shows reasoning rows but no tool rows.** `reasoningDefault: "stream"` and `toolProgress: false` are separate choices, so a user who asked for reasoning and not tool rows gets exactly that; with reasoning off the quiet card is unchanged from `main`.
- **`progress.maxLines`, when set, is the per-message row cap** for native cards (at most 50). A card never shows more rows than configured; instead of evicting rows, the overflow continues in a new message. Unset, native messages hold up to 50 rows (the draft-card default window of 8 is not applied as a cap, so default turns are unchanged).
- **No new configuration.** The schema, types, UI hints, plugin SDK surface and generated config files are identical to `main`.

Other visible effects for turns that roll or show reasoning: native cards no longer evict rows (a message that cannot hold more rolls instead), so running rows are not painted complete early and errored rows keep their title. A tool still running when its message seals is shown complete there and continues on the next message, since a row cannot move between Slack messages.

## Commits

1. `feat(slack): render streamed reasoning as task rows on the native progress card`
2. `feat(slack): roll long native progress streams into continuation messages`

The two delivery fixes that used to lead this branch landed as #199849; the branch is rebased onto `main` on top of them.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Rows (commit 1):** reasoning is merged through the compositor's existing merge, split into segments of about 240 characters at word boundaries and pushed as task rows (`reasoning:<n>`, complete except the newest). A tool call or the end of a reasoning phase seals the open segment before the tool row is admitted. Row titles are capped at 250 characters, our own cap below the 256 Slack documents (the API does not enforce 256). The compositor option it uses (`reasoningLine`) stays internal; there is no new public plugin SDK export.
- **Size model (commit 2), measured against Slack:** `chat.startStream` / `chat.appendStream` reject a message with `msg_too_long` once the plan block, serialized as Slack stores it (compact JSON, non-ASCII as `\uXXXX`), plus the markdown text exceeds 13,200 units, and markdown alone is capped at 12,000 characters. Markdown costs one per character except emoji, which cost their `:shortcode:` length (`:+1:` 4, `:brain:` 7, `:white_check_mark:` 18). Row titles, `details` and `output` share that limit; a row adds a fixed ~46 plus its id, each `details`/`output` field a one-off 132; the plan title is not counted. The ledger (`stream-size.ts`) mirrors that model and rounds up where Slack's cost varies (every row counted as in progress, an emoji in markdown as 20, in `details` as 80), so it can only overcount; a test checks that every measured boundary message counts at or above Slack's ceiling. Budgets sit about 20% under: 10,500 total, 9,600 text, 7,000 rows (at least 3,500 left for an answer), plus 50 rows and 8 minutes of age (`SLACK_STREAM_MESSAGE_MAX_AGE_MS`).
- **Message chain (commit 2):** when the next update would not fit, or the message is expiring, the message is sealed and a new stream continues in the thread, and the chain keeps rolling while plan steps remain that have not appeared as currently rendered (title, status, details). A step whose status or title changes after a roll is shown again, on the current message when it fits there. It builds on `main`'s `rotateInterruptedStream` (one `sealStream` operation for human interruptions and rollover; the thread is kept as `interruptedThreadTs`) and keeps `main`'s `nativeFinalThreadTs` / `canFinishNativeFinal`, snapshot reset and rotation paths.
- **Stop:** a Stop during a roll leaves the stopped session current, so nothing new starts, as `main` already does for a turn-level Stop.

Follow-ups, separate because they touch other transports: rows on the Block Kit fallback card via `chat.update` (also ending its delete-after-turn inconsistency) and in the final message when streaming is off.

### Measurements behind the design (real Slack, 2026-11-15/16)

- Stream lifetime: two streams appended every 20 s were rejected at ~605 s and ~611 s after start (with and without recipient fields); idle streams accepted appends at 4, 5, 6 and 8 minutes and rejected at 12. `chat.stopStream` after the close fails the same way.
- Size limit: exact boundary searches (n accepted, n+1 rejected) on `chat.startStream` and `chat.appendStream`: 12,000 characters of ASCII or of a 3-byte character are accepted alike (so not UTF-8 bytes); emoji cost their shortcode length (3,300 × `:+1:`, 1,885 × `:brain:`, 942 × `:technologist:`, 733 × `:white_check_mark:`, each totalling ~13,200); rows plus text sum to exactly 13,200 at 1, 3,000, 6,000, 8,172 and 11,000 characters of text; a single 20,000-character title and a 20,000-character plan title are accepted.
- `plan` block outside streams: the block a finished stream stores (`plan` with `tasks[]`, `details`, `output`) is accepted by `chat.postMessage` and `chat.update`, and renders as the same collapsible card in the web client and the iOS app (rows open in a sheet; a tool row's details and output expand).
