prs.title: fix(postgres): chat history slows under concurrent reads
prs.body:
Closes #188956
Related: #197313, #190001 (#197313 tracks the repeated read snapshots inside each history page, which #190001 addresses)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: on PostgreSQL, `chat.history` requests queue behind two history workers when several clients load history at once, so tail latency grows with concurrency while the CPU sits mostly idle.

## User Impact

User impact: concurrent `chat.history` on PostgreSQL waits much less for a history worker. Re-measured on current `main` (medians of 8 interleaved runs per build): at 8 concurrent clients p50 drops from 19.6 to 12.02 ms, p99 from 54.31 to 31.76 ms, and throughput rises from 378.1 to 622.95 requests/s; at 32 clients p99 drops from 163.13 to 103.1 ms. Single-client p50 is unchanged; single-client p99 rose from 15.08 to 17.07 ms over all runs (14.87 to 15.13 ms in the quieter block). SQLite keeps its current lane size.

Cost, measured on the same runs (medians of 8 runs per build):

- Memory: during concurrent history reads the Gateway runs up to two more transcript isolates (about 57 MiB of heap each). Peak transcript-worker heap rose from 334.1 to 453.6 MiB and peak Gateway RSS from 2,764.9 to 3,153.1 MiB. The extra isolates retire after the pool's existing idle timeout: 45 s and 100 s after load both builds ran the same number of transcript isolates with about the same heap (45 s: 229.4 vs 242.8 MiB; 100 s: 223.8 vs 227.8 MiB). RSS at 100 s was 2,106.1 vs 2,324.7 MiB.
- PostgreSQL connections: backends for the runtime role peaked at 23 on base and 25 with the change; both were back to 13 after 100 idle seconds. Each extra history isolate can retain up to two idle transports for three minutes; the documented budget (`isolates × (active + 2)`) now notes up to four history isolates.

**Decision for review:** should PostgreSQL history use up to four workers, accepting the cost above? This revises the two-worker reader cap from #167295 and #169110 for one lane on one engine.

- (a) Accept four workers for PostgreSQL history (this PR). Cost: up to two more isolates (about 120 to 124 MiB of worker heap and about 320 to 390 MiB of peak RSS across the two benches below) and two more peak backends, only while history load is concurrent; single-client p99 from 15.08 to 17.07 ms over all runs (14.87 to 15.13 ms in the quieter block). On a host whose CPU is already saturated by other work, the extra workers did not help p99 (see Evidence, block 1).
- (b) Keep two workers. PostgreSQL history keeps queueing: 5.57 ms of queue wait per worker request at 8 clients, 13.34 ms at 16.
- (c) Make the larger lane opt-in with a setting. No default cost, but it adds a config surface for an internal pool size, and the default keeps the queueing.
- (d) A cap of eight. Measured on an older `main` (see Evidence): lower queue wait at 16 clients, at about two and a half times the extra memory and with more backends.

Recommended: (a). The extra workers exist only on PostgreSQL agent stores and only under concurrent history reads, they retire through the existing idle timeout and cleanup owners, and SQLite, transcript search and every other lane keep the current cap. The memory bound stays fixed (at most four history isolates on any host), and the latency it buys is the symptom #188956 reports.

## Why This Change Was Made

On PostgreSQL a history worker spends most of a request blocked in `Atomics.wait` on bridge replies, so sizing the lane like a CPU-bound reader leaves requests queued while CPU is free. The history lane on PostgreSQL agent stores now gets two workers per CPU above one, capped at four (two on a two-CPU host). Transcript search, the other transcript lanes, and every SQLite lane keep the existing reader size from #167295 and #169110. No new setting.

The database engine is installed during boot, after the lane module is imported, so the history pool now resolves its size on first use instead of at import. Production code: +47/-7 lines ignoring whitespace (the pool options block is re-indented inside the first-use constructor); tests +117; docs +9/-4.

Scope: this closes #188956 (the queueing in front of the history workers). The transaction round trips inside each page are #197313, addressed by #190001; the two touch different files and are measured separately.

## Evidence

Evidence files: https://github.com/etzelm/openclaw/tree/assets/pg-r2-l3d-history-reader-lane-evidence/current-main-2026-11-07 (paths below are relative to it; method, host and store in `README.md`). The earlier bench on `31866655fd6` stays at the root of the same branch.

Acceptance rule: through a running Gateway on PostgreSQL, at 8 or more concurrent clients, queue wait per worker request and p50 drop, throughput rises and p99 at 8 clients drops; single-client latency holds; the memory and backend cost is reported, and the extra isolates retire once history load stops.

- **Tests** on this head merged into current `main` `078033289a3`: a per-engine sizing table (`src/infra/worker-pool-sizing.test.ts`) and a lane test that installs the engine after importing the lane, as boot does (`src/config/sessions/session-history-lane-sizing.test.ts`: PostgreSQL 4, SQLite 2, search 2). Both pass, as do the consumer suites for the transcript lanes, the search worker, reconcile readiness, the chat history worker and worker-pool preparation: 12 files, 161 tests (`tests/unit-head.log`). On `main` the sizing table fails because the resolver does not exist, and the PostgreSQL lane case gets 2 instead of 4 while the SQLite case passes (`tests/unit-base-red.log`). `pnpm check:changed` on the merged head passes every check except two repo-wide audits that fail the same way on plain `main` `078033289a3`: changelog attributions (bot credits in `CHANGELOG/` files) and the dead export scan (`scripts/lib/control-ui-gesture-probe.ts`, `src/process/command-reservation-census.ts`) (`tests/check-changed.log`, `tests/base-changelog-attr.log`, `tests/base-deadcode.log`). CI on `987348094eb` was green.
- **After merging `main` `4a0e45492b8`** (head `3e55cf3ef68`): `main` dropped the history worker's `prewarmHistory` option (#198512), so the lazy pool no longer passes it; sizing is unchanged. The sizing table, the lane test and the consumer suites above plus the prewarm and history worker lifecycle suites pass: 14 files, 169 tests. One test in `session-transcript-worker-lanes.test.ts` (`releases pressure subscriptions after native settlement and rearms reopened lanes`, added on `main` by #197510) fails on this head and on plain `main` `4a0e45492b8` alike, 3 of 3 runs each on a macOS arm64 host. `pnpm check:changed` passes every step except the dead export scan, whose findings are all in files this PR does not touch.
- **Closed-loop `chat.history` bench on current `main`**: base `main` `078033289a3` vs this head merged into it, both built with `pnpm build`. A fresh Gateway on PostgreSQL 17.11 per run, seeded through its own RPCs with 200 sessions (170 sessions across 6 agents with 2 to 4,675 messages each, plus 30 imported Claude CLI sessions with tool rows hidden between visible turns). Limit 100, 45 s per arm, 16 runs (8 per build) in two interleaved blocks (base head head base base head head base). No run was dropped. Medians over all 16 runs (`bench/block-all/medians.tsv`; every run in `bench/block-all/arms.tsv`; raw scrapes in `bench/runs/`):

| arm | p50 / p95 / p99 ms | p99 range | requests/s | queue wait per worker request | handler mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 client, base | 6.09 / 10.69 / 15.08 | 12.85 to 51.11 | 156.4 | 0.0 ms | 5.19 ms |
| 1 client, fix | 6.00 / 11.02 / 17.07 | 11.9 to 106.71 | 154.4 | 0.0 ms | 5.27 ms |
| 8 clients, base | 19.6 / 31.82 / 54.31 | 28.99 to 161.47 | 378.1 | 5.57 ms | 19.46 ms |
| 8 clients, fix | 12.02 / 19.64 / 31.76 | 20 to 230.82 | 622.95 | 1.23 ms | 10.1 ms |
| 16 clients, base | 37.66 / 54.15 / 88.16 | 58.52 to 200.55 | 411.8 | 13.34 ms | 37.21 ms |
| 16 clients, fix | 24.6 / 42.92 / 66.77 | 45.72 to 499.74 | 606.65 | 6.73 ms | 23.41 ms |
| 32 clients, base | 71.04 / 96.61 / 163.13 | 90.84 to 421.36 | 431.7 | 28.54 ms | 72.43 ms |
| 32 clients, fix | 48.48 / 84.22 / 103.1 | 66.74 to 578.74 | 634.25 | 17.02 ms | 47.23 ms |

Queue wait is `openclaw_worker_queue_wait_seconds{kind="sessionTranscript"}`; handler mean is `openclaw_gateway_rpc_handler_seconds{method="chat.history"}`. The host is shared, and the wide p99 ranges come from runs under other load, so the two blocks are also reported separately:

- Block 2 (`bench/block-b2/`, started only below a 1-minute load of 12; arms at load 4 to 25): p99 at 1, 8, 16 and 32 clients 14.87 / 30.47 / 68.2 / 115.94 ms base vs 15.13 / 25.1 / 64.69 / 88.53 ms fix; p50 at 8 clients 18.11 vs 11.73 ms, throughput 431.6 vs 651.05 requests/s. At 16 clients p99 is about even while p50 drops from 35.98 to 24.6 ms.
- Block 1 (`bench/block-b1/`, load 6 to 55): p50, throughput and queue wait improve at 8, 16 and 32 clients as above, but p99 does not improve consistently: 69.65 vs 73.11 ms at 8 clients, 147.19 vs 113.72 ms at 16, 198.87 vs 281.24 ms at 32. The worst fix tails are `pg-head-r1` (the highest 1-minute load in the bench, 37 to 55) and `pg-head-r2` (load 25 to 33, started with 25% of host memory free); the other two fix runs in the block have p99 21.7 and 36.16 ms at 8 clients. When the host's CPU is already saturated, extra workers add little.

- **Moved the wrong way**: memory and backends (see User Impact: +120 MiB peak transcript heap, +388 MiB peak RSS, +219 MiB RSS 100 s after load, +2 peak backends); single-client p99 15.08 to 17.07 ms over all runs (14.87 to 15.13 ms in block 2; p50 6.09 to 6.00 ms over all runs, 5.71 to 5.94 ms in block 2; single-client p95 10.69 to 11.02 ms over all runs) and 19.35 to 33.27 ms in block 1 (driven by `pg-head-r2`, single-client p99 106.71 ms); single-client throughput 156.4 to 154.4 requests/s over all runs (163.6 to 155.65 in block 2); and in block 1, under the heaviest host load, p99 at 8 clients 69.65 to 73.11 ms and at 32 clients 198.87 to 281.24 ms. In the pair bench on current `main`, single-client p95 12.75 vs 10.47 ms (+22%), p99 21.33 vs 12.85 ms and throughput 136.4 vs 159.0 calls/s (-14%) (`pair-bench/medians.tsv`). These are part of the decision above.
- **Memory and connections** (`bench/block-all/memory-medians.tsv`, per run in `memory.tsv`): see User Impact. Heap and isolate counts come from the Gateway's worker metrics, sampled by the 30 s diagnostic heartbeat; RSS and backend counts are sampled every 2 s.
- **SQLite**: the lane size is unchanged by construction (the resolver returns the existing reader size for every non-PostgreSQL agent engine; covered by the sizing table and lane test). The earlier bench on `31866655fd6` measured SQLite p50, throughput and transcript isolates unchanged; not re-measured here.
- **Cap of four vs eight** (earlier bench on `31866655fd6`, 3 runs each, `bench/medians.tsv` and `bench/memory-medians.tsv` at the branch root, rows `base-a`, `fix4` and `fix8`): eight gave 0.07 ms queue wait at 8 clients and 1.66 ms at 16, at +325 MiB peak transcript heap, +974 MiB peak RSS and 27 peak backends over `base-a`, against +120 MiB heap, +382 MiB RSS and 25 peak backends for four (`fix4` over `base-a`).

- **Pair bench on current `main` `82210a2bbdb0`** (`pair-bench/`): four builds from one `main` (`main`, `main` + #190001, `main` + this PR, `main` + both), four runs each in interleaved order, PostgreSQL 17.11, closed-loop `chat.history` at 1, 8, 16 and 32 clients. Gate results on the same `main`: unit 12 files / 162 tests pass with this PR (the new sizing and lane tests fail on plain `main`); with both PRs unit 28 / 386 and PostgreSQL conformance 15 / 165 pass. Medians of 4 runs, this PR vs `main`: at 8 clients p50 13.84 vs 19.65 ms, p99 26.26 vs 46.48 ms, 555 vs 385 calls/s, queue wait per worker request 1.06 vs 5.28 ms; at 16 clients p50 29.21 vs 41.94 ms, 507 vs 362 calls/s; at 32 clients p50 58.09 vs 79.41 ms, p99 88.81 vs 199.78 ms, 545 vs 372 calls/s. At 1 client p50 is 6.31 vs 6.01 ms and p99 is noisier (12.12 to 60.43 ms across runs vs 11.74 to 23.23 ms on `main`; the two highest runs had the highest arm-start load of this build's four runs, 13.1 and 17.9 in `pair-bench/arms.tsv`). Cost: peak Gateway RSS 2789 vs 2468 MiB (+321 MiB), peak transcript worker heap 456 vs 332 MiB (+124 MiB), peak transcript workers 8 vs 6, peak PostgreSQL backends 23 vs 21; 100 s after load, 4 workers vs 3 and the same 13 backends. With #190001 as well, p50 is the same at 16 and 32 clients (29.57 and 58.06 ms) but p99 is higher (81.27 vs 67.81 ms, 128.55 vs 88.81 ms). At 8 clients the pair has p50 15.21 ms, p99 55.06 ms and 480.2 calls/s: p99 is above this PR alone (26.26 ms) and also above `main` (46.48 ms), and throughput is below this PR alone (555.25 calls/s) in all four paired runs (`arms.tsv`), so host load does not explain it. The cost comes from #190001 on this dense-page store (history worker time per request 3.741 vs 3.229 ms at 8 clients, `pair-bench/worker-time.tsv`) and is reported there.

### Gaps

- The bench store is synthetic, written through the Gateway's own RPCs, because `main` does not admit a `pg_restore` of a production store. Its shape follows the production bench in #188956.
- Shared host: the p99 tails in block 1 are dominated by other load (per-arm load in `arms.tsv`). Two fix runs (`pg-head-r2` in block 1, `pg-head-r8` in block 2) started while another job held most host memory; both are kept.
- At 16 clients and above the four-worker lane queues again (6.73 ms per worker request at 16, 17.02 ms at 32). A cap of eight removes most of that at a higher memory cost.
- Memory figures needed one measurement-only line, applied identically to both builds: the diagnostic heartbeat publishes its memory sample every 30 s instead of only after agent activity (`scripts/instrument-*.diff`). Isolate counts and heap cover every transcript lane, not only history, and 30 s sampling can miss the exact peak. RSS was watched for 100 s after load here; the earlier 300 s pair on `31866655fd6` (`bench/runs/pg-*-idle-r1` at the branch root) showed no lasting RSS difference with the same isolate count (1,676 vs 1,745 MiB at 300 s).
- Transcript search on PostgreSQL also blocks on bridge replies and keeps its two-worker cap; not measured here.
- The bench host is shared (1-minute load 4.2 to 13.8 at run start, `pair-bench/run-order-and-load.txt`, and 3.8 to 22.2 at arm start, `pair-bench/arms.tsv`). Tails at 1 and 8 clients move with that load; medians at 8 or more clients do not. Idle retirement past 100 s was not sampled in the pair bench; the earlier bench above covers it.

prs.title: feat(plugins): let an operator run a memory plugin beside the memory slot owner
prs.body:
Closes #198445

## What Problem This Solves

A memory plugin that does not own `plugins.slots.memory` is disabled before it registers anything, so an operator cannot keep memory-core and also run an external memory plugin.

## User Impact

An operator can set `plugins.entries.<id>.memory.sidecar: true` to load that memory plugin beside the slot owner. The mode is an explicit operator opt-in. The plugin keeps its hooks, tools and corpus supplements. The slot owner keeps `memory_search`, the memory runtime, the recall grant and memory lessons. A turn now carries a host-minted memory audience when a loaded sidecar can use it, so a sidecar that routes recall and retain by audience works next to memory-core. Configs without the setting load and behave as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

The registrar already strips slot-owner fields from a memory capability registered by a plugin that is not the owner (the dreaming sidecar relies on this), so the missing piece was the load decision. The setting is per plugin entry, so an operator accepts the cost of a second memory system for each install. `openclaw plugins enable` keeps the current slot for a sidecar entry, so enabling one does not replace memory-core.

Every sidecar lookup reads `plugins.entries` through the canonical policy id, so a manifest id such as `MiXeD-memory` matches its lowercase entry `mixed-memory`. Root help admits a sidecar only when the normalized memory slot is not `none`.

Memory audiences are minted by the host, not by plugins. The embedded runner minted one only when the slot owner was a native provider, so next to memory-core (a legacy runtime) a sidecar saw no audience and skipped recall and retain. The gate is now: native slot owner, or at least one loaded memory plugin that is not the slot owner and has `memory.sidecar: true`. The audience comes from the same `resolveMemoryAudienceFromEntry` call with the same owner, sender and lineage checks, so it grants nothing a native owner would not. A config with no sidecar entry returns before any registry read, so legacy-only turns still take no session lease and read no lineage. The other native-only paths (project memory bootstrap, post-compaction refresh, memory flush) talk to the slot owner's provider and are unchanged.

Config surface: `plugins.entries.*.memory` and `plugins.entries.*.memory.sidecar` are counted once per plugin entry, so the generated plugin path count in `docs/.generated/config-baseline.counts.json` rises from 5080 to 5454. No other config paths change.

<details>
<summary>Changes</summary>

- `PluginEntrySchema`: `memory.sidecar` (boolean), with label and help text.
- `normalizePluginsConfig`: `entries[id].memorySidecar`; `isMemorySidecarEnabled` reads it by canonical policy id.
- `resolveMemorySlotDecision`: `sidecar` parameter; enabled and not selected when the slot names another plugin; still disabled for `slots.memory: "none"`; a case variant of the owner id is not a sidecar.
- Callers: runtime loader, config validation, CLI root descriptors, plugin root contributions.
- `applySlotSelectionForPlugin`: drops the `memory` kind for a sidecar entry, so enable does not move the slot.
- `hasLoadedMemorySidecar` (`src/plugins/memory-state.ts`): true when a loaded `memory` plugin other than the slot owner has `memory.sidecar` on; never loads a plugin.
- `resolveEmbeddedAttemptMemoryAudience`: mints when the owner is native or `hasLoadedMemorySidecar` is true.
- docs/plugins/manifest.md: one line on the setting.

</details>

## Evidence

Builds: main `4cffd43ee04`, this branch before the audience change (`a3fca384bdb`) and with it (`e4597199264`), built from source. The external plugin is `@etzelm/openclaw-memory-hindsight` 0.9.0 from npm (manifest id `hindsight-native`, kind `memory`, `slotMode: sidecar`). `hindsightApiUrl` points at a loopback mock that logs every request and answers recall with one canned memory (`PROOF-CANARY-7731: the operator's test color is teal.`); no real credentials.

The head `44125d5382a` merges main (`4a0e45492b8`) on top of `e4597199264`, with one import reordered for the current formatter. On that merged tree, the 94 tests in the changed test files pass and `pnpm config:docs:check` is OK.

Chat turns: each build ran as an isolated scratch Gateway (own HOME, state dir, config, loopback port and token) with the repo's QA mock-openai server as the model, `plugins.slots.memory: "memory-core"`, and two `chat.send` turns on `agent:main:main`.

| Run | `plugins inspect hindsight-native` | `tools.catalog` | `memory.status` provider | Requests at the Hindsight mock | Canary in the model prompt |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| main, plugin enabled, no `memory.sidecar` | disabled: `memory slot set to "memory-core"` | `memory_search`, `memory_get` | `memory-core` | none | no |
| `a3fca384bdb`, `memory.sidecar: true` | loaded | + `hindsight_recall`, `hindsight_reflect`, `hindsight_retain` | `memory-core` | none (`auto-recall skipped: this session has no memory audience`) | no |
| `e4597199264`, `memory.sidecar: true` | loaded | + `hindsight_recall`, `hindsight_reflect`, `hindsight_retain` | `memory-core` | per turn: `POST .../memories/recall` and `POST .../memories` (retain) | yes, both turns |

```

```

No `no memory audience` lines appear. The `hindsight_*` tool factories return null only for the sessionless `tools.catalog` call, which has no audience by design, and not during the turns. The model sees a compact tool list in this setup (`tool_search`, `tool_describe` and core tools), so neither `memory_*` nor `hindsight_*` tools are listed directly and no tool call was exercised.

Upgrade from the latest stable release (npm `openclaw@2026.11.3`), one scratch HOME and state dir:

- Stable: `onboard --non-interactive`, `plugins install` and enable of the 0.9.0 plugin, slot kept on memory-core, `config validate` passes, Gateway starts healthy with `memory.status` provider `memory-core`, `doctor --non-interactive` exits 0.
- Branch on the same state and config, without `memory.sidecar`: `config validate` passes with the config unchanged. The state written by stable needs `doctor --fix` before the Gateway serves sessions (the agent database schema moved on main), and `doctor --fix` exits 0. After it, `doctor --non-interactive` exits 0, the plugin stays disabled (`memory slot set to "memory-core"`), and the Gateway starts healthy with `memory.status` provider `memory-core` and no `hindsight_*` tools.

- Stable 2026.11.3 refuses the same state dir afterwards because the branch (main) state database is at schema 40 and stable supports 22.

Tests (`pnpm test` on the changed test files): 84 passed across `loader.memory-sidecar`, `config-state`, `slot-selection` and `plugin-root-contributions`. The case-variant slot check asserts a literal decision (`{ enabled: false, reason: 'memory slot set to "mixed-memory"' }`). Audience gate: `attempt-memory-audience.sidecar.test.ts` (native owner granted; legacy owner without sidecar none, with no lineage read or lease; legacy owner with a loaded sidecar granted; sidecar setting off or plugin not loaded none; a turn the owner checks deny stays denied) and `memory-state.sidecar.test.ts`. The new tests fail on `a3fca384bdb` (3 failed: `expected undefined to deeply equal { kind: 'owner-private', ... }` and `hasLoadedMemorySidecar is not a function`) and pass with the change; with the neighbouring audience and memory-state suites, 93 passed.

prs.title: fix(ai): keep provider checkpoints across model switches
prs.body:
## Problem

A session that changes models drops its own server compaction checkpoint, resends the full raw history, and falls back to client summarization. Model changes happen through fallbacks, per-turn overrides and model alternation within one session.

The provider replay check compared the model id. After #200063 removed the credential-path check, the model check was the other common cause. On the host that reported the original incident, model changes accounted for 357 of 800 dropped-checkpoint turns, mostly a session alternating between `gpt-6-astra` and `gpt-6.1-sol`.

## Fix

- The replay check is now provider API, endpoint and session. The model id stays in the stored record but is no longer compared.
- Providers accept their own replay items across models. I checked this with raw API calls before changing anything:
  - **OpenAI compaction items:** `gpt-6-astra` ↔ `gpt-6.1-sol` and `gpt-5.4-mini` → `gpt-5.4` are accepted, and the model recalls a fact that is only in the compacted history.
  - **OpenAI encrypted reasoning:** the same pairs are accepted.
  - **Anthropic compaction blocks:** `claude-sonnet-4-6` → `claude-opus-4-8` is accepted and recalls the compacted fact. These blocks are plaintext summaries.
- An item a provider cannot use is still rejected server-side (`invalid_encrypted_content` / `item_conflict`), and the existing replay recovery handles it.

The production change is one comparison removed. The tests that asserted the model check are replaced with positive cases.

## Evidence

**Regression test:** `openai-responses-compaction-replay.test.ts` › "replays a checkpoint written by another model in the same session". It fails on the old check and passes with the fix.

**Real-model E2E** (isolated state; each arm built from its own source):
- Three seed turns on `openai/gpt-5.4-mini` with server compaction, then a final turn on `openai/gpt-5.4` in the same session with the same key.
- Request shapes come from `OPENCLAW_DEBUG_MODEL_PAYLOAD=summary`.

| arm | final-turn request | items | text chars | answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| base | messages only; `compactionItems=0` | 11 | 113,090 | correct |
| fix | `compaction, message:user, message:developer`; `compactionItems=1` | 3 | 656 | correct |

**Checks:**
- The touched replay suites pass (100 tests).
- `check:changed` passes except the dead-export scan. That scan reports unused exports in files this PR does not touch, which come from the current `main` tree.

## Scope

Encrypted reasoning from a different model is still dropped on a model switch. The generic cross-model history transforms (`transcript-transform.ts`, `transport-message-transform.ts`) and `dropStaleOpenAIReasoning` strip it before the replay check runs. That costs one turn of reasoning context, not the session's history, so it is left for a separate change.

## Follow-up

The context meter still estimates from the full transcript when a checkpoint is present. That fix is a separate PR.

prs.title: fix(update): finish managed updates when readers race the old updater's database capture
prs.body:
Related: #197083
Related: #200022

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a managed update from 2026.11.3 or 2026.11.4 can leave the Gateway stopped and report "data at risk" when an `openclaw update status` call, or another reader, is running while the updater snapshots the databases.

## User Impact

User impact: such updates now finish on the new version instead of stopping the Gateway. Automatic database restoration is still unavailable for that update, and Doctor now says so in a warning.

## Why This Change Was Made

Published updaters record database fingerprints that include SQLite's WAL-index change counter. If readers keep the WAL index alive past the updater's last ledger commit, the next native open after they exit rebuilds that index. The counter resets, even though no data changed. The target Doctor then refused its first attributed write with "SQLite migration source changed after update capture". The parent refused rollback because its own comparison failed the same way. The parent's forward recovery then migrated with the target Doctor, could not read the migrated data, and kept the Gateway stopped.

Doctor now recognizes that one shape at its first admission. A database that differs from the parent's capture is adopted only if its WAL index was rebuilt over retained frames: the WAL is non-empty, iChange is zero and the last frame checksum is non-zero. Any commit after the rebuild would raise iChange again. In that case Doctor:

- keeps reporting `unchanged: false`, so the parent still refuses restore;
- warns that SQLite rebuilt the index and restoration is unavailable;
- attributes its own writes from the admitted state, so the update finishes forward.

Any other change before admission, such as a foreign shared write, still refuses at the first attributed write, as before. Writes after admission also still refuse.

Old updaters (11.3 and 11.4) take this target-side path, so this fixes 11.x → next-release hops. A 2026.11.4 *target* (#200022, 11.3 → 11.4) is not changed by this PR.

## Safety and Scope

**What is adopted.** Only databases whose difference matches the rebuilt-index shape are adopted. A real write before admission reaches that shape only if it commits frames and then every connection leaves without a checkpoint, so that the next open rebuilds the index. In practice this needs the last writer to crash, or a read-only connection to close last. Even then no data is lost: every parent's restore gate re-compares the live generations to its capture and refuses, because a restore would discard that write. The pre-fix flow also migrated the same bytes forward, through the parent's forward recovery. The existing foreign-shared-write refusal (`client-credential-update.test.ts`) and the 2026.9.34 changed-data cases still refuse unchanged. Content identity cannot be compared directly: the fingerprint a published parent sends is sha256 over [dev, ino, birthtime, content digest, iChange, frame checksum], and the rebuild has already erased the old iChange.

**Main as the parent.** Main's own generation reader is just as sensitive to rebuilds. In a local check, a capture taken while a reader holds the index, then a reader exit and a non-writing reopen, changed the committed generation both with and without a TRUNCATE checkpoint. With this PR, a main → future hop that loses that race completes forward, but automatic restore is unavailable for it. Making the fingerprint survive rebuilds is planned as a follow-up: compare against the generation with iChange normalized, since the frame checksum and content digest already record the writes. That follow-up changes how parents and targets interpret the same value across versions, so it is kept out of this fix.

**What this does not fix.** A later Doctor failure under an 11.3 or 11.4 parent still ends in "rollback refused → forward recovery → that parent's own settlement cannot open the migrated data → Gateway stopped". That code ships in the parent and hands off to the new driver only after Doctor succeeds, so the target cannot change it. On the installed new version, `openclaw update repair` recovers, as confirmed in #200022. A fix for the parent would need an 11.4.x patch release, which is a maintainer decision.

## Evidence

- Crabbox AWS reproduction, 11.4 → main `f6d0c3ea69a` (1 GB state DB, two `openclaw update status` pollers), monitored with auditd and a 100 ms watcher on the SQLite family. The run stranded: `openclaw doctor` failed with "migration source changed", rollback was refused, settlement failed with "cannot open your existing data", and the Gateway was left inactive. At the end of capture the readers exited, and the 11.4 driver's next native open rebuilt the WAL index. `-shm` went from iChange `0x7d` to `0`, while the frame checksum, WAL bytes and DB bytes were unchanged.
- New regression test `migrates after a no-write WAL index rebuild while the parent's restore stays refused`. It fails on base with the same error and passes with the fix.
- Existing refusals are unchanged: the 2026.9.34 changed-data cases, the outside-commit tests, the after-admission predecessor-stop case and the client-credential foreign-shared-write test all still pass.
- `tsgo:core` and `oxlint` pass on the touched files.
- autoreview at P2: one finding, declined and named in a code comment. A commit after capture that only read-only connections outlive, followed by a rebuild, matches the adopted shape (see Safety and Scope). A re-review with that context came back scoped-clean. An independent `codex exec` review of the narrowed diff found nothing.

prs.title: build(release): stop releases shipping a Codex plugin floor that admits broken plugins
prs.body:
Refs #181619

The immediate `startedAtMonotonicMs` failure was fixed by #182995. This PR adds a release-time compatibility check to catch future stale runtime floors; it does not replace that runtime fix.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a release can ship with a Codex plugin floor (`minimumCompatibleVersion` in `src/plugins/official-runtime-plugins.ts`, #168930) that still admits plugin releases the new core breaks. Nothing checks the floor against the release, so it falls behind silently. #181619 is the result: 2026.10.6 made the Codex execution deadline require `startedAtMonotonicMs`, the floor stayed at `2026.9.7`, and a left-behind `@openclaw/codex` 2026.10.5 loads and fails every turn after 1 ms instead of being refused with the repair command. 2026.10.7 ships the same floor.

## User Impact

User impact: none at runtime. Release tooling only. `release-check` now fails when a version-bound runtime's floor no longer type-checks against the release being cut, and names the fix (raise the floor). Users then get the existing refusal with `openclaw update repair` / `openclaw plugins update codex` guidance instead of silently failing turns.

## Why This Change Was Made

The floor is the existing owner for this (#168930): a hand-kept literal, bumped "when a Plugin SDK subpath used by this runtime is removed". Two kinds of change slipped past it:

- a newly required argument: `startedAtMonotonicMs` (#155801, included in 2026.10.6);
- removed exports: `sanitizeToolArgs` (#169063) and `HEARTBEAT_RESPONSE_TOOL_NAME` (#180106) on main.

The Codex runtime imports these private-local SDK pieces lazily and declares an open-ended `pluginApi`, so a stale floor only shows up as failing turns after an update.

`scripts/check-official-runtime-floor.mts` checks the floor itself: for each version-bound runtime it takes that runtime's source at its floor release tag and type-checks it inside the checkout being released (root `tsconfig.json`, so the core's SDK is read from source). A type error in the old runtime means the floor admits a runtime this release breaks. It catches both removed exports and changed arguments. It reuses the release checkout's install for third-party dependencies.

- `release-check` calls it before packing. It reads the floors from the release checkout (`process.cwd()`), not from the trusted tooling checkout the npm preflight runs from, so each release line is checked against its own floor.
- A missing floor tag fails if the floor is older than the release candidate. Only an unreleased floor equal to the candidate version is skipped.
- A floor above the release version admits no older runtime. It is skipped when the checked release also admits its own runtime version (#195255's exact-pair rule, read from the release checkout, not from the tooling), and fails when that release would refuse the runtime published with it. Main between releases is the common case: its version string stays at the last stable (`2026.11.2`) while the floor is `2026.11.5-beta.1`.
- Release checkouts are shallow and tagless, so the check fetches only the floor tag.

Also: the floor comment now covers exports and required arguments, and points to the check; `docs/help/testing-updates-plugins.md` describes the step next to `release:check`.

Not changed: the floor values themselves. In the historical v2026.10.7 checks below, raising the floor to `2026.10.6` passed the missing-argument check. On the tested main build `a3a5add7136`, older published plugins also failed on removed exports. These are reproductions of the original compatibility gaps, not a claim that today's release needs those exact floor values; #182995 subsequently fixed the original missing-argument failure. Release owners still choose the appropriate floor for each release.

Open for release managers: whether this check should block release qualification or stay a command run by hand. This PR makes it a blocking step; that choice is theirs.

## Evidence

Proof artifice: the CLI regression creates a local Git tag, a minimal synthetic plugin and SDK, and an intentionally missing tarball; the compiler is real. Historical release-checkout runs used released source with floor values deliberately changed for the failing and passing comparisons. Published-package model runs are separate evidence for the original incident, not proof of the new CLI test.

Test lines are net +204 against `main`: 118 lines cover the new planner (including the above-release exemption), diagnostic classification and release-checkout ownership; 86 reuse the existing CLI fixture and native compiler helpers to catch missing tags and real compiler incompatibility at the release gate. Planner-only tests cannot prove that release-check invokes the guard before package inspection.


Unit tests (`test/scripts/check-official-runtime-floor.test.ts`, 10): released floor is checked; an unreleased candidate-version floor is skipped; a floor above the release fails when the checked release refuses its own runtime version and is skipped when it admits it; non-version-bound/no-floor/no-source runtimes are ignored; runtime errors are separated from setup errors; a compiler run that fails without diagnostics is a broken check, not a pass; the floors are read from the checked checkout, and a checkout without floors reports none.

November 1 repair: the existing `release-check` CLI integration suite now creates a local Git release tag and uses the real TypeScript compiler. It verifies that a missing older tag and a newly required SDK argument both stop release checking before package inspection. Making that argument optional lets the floor check pass and reach the intentionally missing tarball. The regression fails on the original base because release checking reaches the tarball without checking the floor. The missing-tag case also fails against the previous PR implementation.

Before integrating current main, the repaired patch passed 64 tests across the four release/script suites on the Linux proof bench, plus scripts and tooling-test typechecks, targeted lint and formatting checks. Docs lint passed. The main integration preserves both imports in the release-check test; it does not change the repair's behavior.

Current PR CI: `openclaw/ci-gate` passes on `c04b5d342ab` (58 checks passed, none failed). Required release-manager review is still outstanding.

Historical end-to-end runs on real release checkouts (proof bench, Linux), `checkOfficialRuntimeFloors` against each core, 15 to 65 s per run. The following results were captured for the original investigation, before the later runtime fix in #182995; references to main describe the tested checkout, not today's main:

| Core checkout | Floor | Result |
|---|---|---|
| v2026.10.7 | 2026.9.7 (as released) | fails: `run-attempt-turn-state.ts(173,65): Property 'startedAtMonotonicMs' is missing` |
| v2026.10.7 | 2026.10.6 | passes |
| v2026.10.10-beta.3 | 2026.9.7 | fails: `startedAtMonotonicMs` missing; no exported member `sanitizeToolArgs` |
| v2026.10.10-beta.3 | 2026.10.10-beta.1 | passes |
| main with this change | 2026.9.7 (as on main) | fails: no exported member `HEARTBEAT_RESPONSE_TOOL_NAME`, `normalizeHeartbeatToolResponse`, `isSilentReplyPayloadText`; heartbeat tool options gone |

### Live run: the check on real release checkouts

Proof bench (Linux, Node 26), output as captured. The v2026.10.7 runs use the npm preflight's shape: this branch's script run directly from a separate tooling checkout (`TSX_TSCONFIG_PATH=<tooling>/tsconfig.json node --import <tooling>/scripts/tsx.mjs <tooling>/scripts/check-official-runtime-floor.mts`) with the release checkout as the working directory. The main run is this branch's script run directly in this checkout.

v2026.10.7 with its released floor (`2026.9.7`), then with the floor raised to `2026.10.6`:

```text
official-runtime-floor:
codex 2026.9.7 no longer type-checks against OpenClaw 2026.10.7; raise its minimumCompatibleVersion in src/plugins/official-runtime-plugins.ts to the first release that does:
  .artifacts/official-runtime-floor/codex/extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt-turn-state.ts(173,65): error TS2741: Property 'startedAtMonotonicMs' is missing in type '{ startedAtMs: number; timeoutMs: number; settlementTimeoutMs: number; ...
exit=1

official-runtime-floor: codex 2026.10.6 type-checks against OpenClaw 2026.10.7.
exit=0
```

v2026.10.10-beta.3 with floor `2026.9.7`, then `2026.10.10-beta.1`:

```text
official-runtime-floor:
codex 2026.9.7 no longer type-checks against OpenClaw 2026.10.10-beta.3; raise its minimumCompatibleVersion in src/plugins/official-runtime-plugins.ts to the first release that does:
  .artifacts/official-runtime-floor/codex/extensions/codex/src/app-server/run-attempt-turn-state.ts(173,65): error TS2741: Property 'startedAtMonotonicMs' is missing in type ...
  .artifacts/official-runtime-floor/codex/extensions/codex/src/app-server/tool-progress-normalization.ts(2,3): error TS2724: '"openclaw/plugin-sdk/agent-harness-runtime"' has no exported member named 'sanitizeToolArgs'. Did you mean 'sanitizeToolResult'?

official-runtime-floor: codex 2026.10.10-beta.1 type-checks against OpenClaw 2026.10.10-beta.3.
```

main with this change (floor `2026.9.7`), first lines:

```text
codex 2026.9.7 no longer type-checks against OpenClaw 2026.10.7; raise its minimumCompatibleVersion ...:
  .../src/app-server/event-projector-assistant.ts(3,10): error TS2305: Module '"openclaw/plugin-sdk/reply-chunking"' has no exported member 'isSilentReplyPayloadText'.
  .../src/app-server/heartbeat-tool-fallback.ts(3,3): error TS2305: Module '"openclaw/plugin-sdk/agent-harness-runtime"' has no exported member 'HEARTBEAT_RESPONSE_TOOL_NAME'.
```

Floor above the release (11 Nov, after #195255): this branch's script against today's main (version `2026.11.2`, floor `2026.11.5-beta.1`, has the exact-pair rule), then against the real `v2026.11.2` release (no exact-pair rule) with its floor deliberately set to `2026.11.5-beta.1`:

```text
official-runtime-floor: SKIP codex floor 2026.11.5-beta.1 is above OpenClaw 2026.11.2; no older runtime is admitted and the matching version is exempt.
EXIT=0

official-runtime-floor:
codex: floor 2026.11.5-beta.1 is newer than OpenClaw 2026.11.2; the matching codex release would be refused
EXIT=1
```

The previous head of this branch failed the first case. The new planner case and CLI step fail on that head and pass here (25/25 in the two touched suites).

The original `release-check` has no runtime-floor step. These examples show the compatibility gap that the new step detects; they do not claim that every other release check passed on those checkouts.

Release-workflow shape (trusted tooling from main, working directory = the v2026.10.7 checkout): with the release's floor at 2026.9.7 it fails on `startedAtMonotonicMs`; with the release's floor set to 2026.10.6 and the tooling's floor left at 2026.9.7 it passes, so the floors are read from the release.

Earlier prototype of the same method (old plugin source type-checked against a newer core): plugin 2026.10.5 on 2026.10.6 and 2026.10.7 and plugin 2026.9.6 on 2026.9.7 (#168748's removed `agent-harness-task-runtime`) are flagged; plugin 2026.10.6 on 2026.10.7, 2026.10.4 and 2026.10.3 on 2026.10.5, and matched pairs show no errors.

Live, released npm packages, real model (#181619 comments): core 2026.10.6 + plugin 2026.10.5 fails both turns; `openclaw doctor --fix` refreshes the plugin to 2026.10.6 and both turns answer. The reporter confirmed the same on 2026.10.7: a plain npm upgrade left the plugin at 2026.10.5 with no warning, and `openclaw plugins update codex` fixed it.

Pre-PR lanes on the proof bench, run in parallel: `tsgo:core`, `tsconfig.scripts.json`, type-aware oxlint (4 configs) on the changed files, format check, `lint:docs`, and `test/scripts/check-official-runtime-floor.test.ts`, `test/scripts/release-check.test.ts`, `test/release-check.test.ts`, `test/package-scripts.test.ts`. `pnpm check:changed` itself stalled on its SQLite ratchet step in the bench container (unrelated to this change), so those lanes were run individually.

Limits: it checks the floor release only, assuming newer plugin releases are at least as compatible; behaviour changes that keep the same types are not caught; it needs network access to fetch the floor tag.

Related: #194184

## What Problem This Solves

Talk configuration does not explain that unsupported thinking settings can be normalized, including when `off` enables thinking on a model that requires it.

## User Impact

Users can see that the setting is a preferred thinking level: unsupported choices are mapped to a supported level, and `off` can still enable thinking when the model requires it. Leaving the setting unset preserves normal session/model behavior. No runtime behavior, configuration schema, or defaults change.

## Why This Change Was Made

This is the small documentation follow-up discussed during the review of #194184, kept separate so it did not disturb that PR’s reviewed branch. Align the Talk documentation, configuration reference, and configuration help text with the merged behavior.

## Evidence

- Compared the wording with the merged admission logic and existing thinking-selection policy.
- Docs index sanity, focused MDX validation (3 files), TypeScript syntax check, scoped formatting/lint, configuration-doc baseline validation, and `git diff --check` passed.
- No new tests or runtime code paths; the change replaces four descriptions and regenerates the required configuration-doc baseline hash.

Requested by Sally. AI-assisted documentation update.

prs.title: fix(cli): preserve Bash login settings when installing completion
prs.body:
Closes #200194

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: installing Bash completion makes new login shells ignore the user's existing `.bash_login` or `.profile` when neither `.bashrc` nor `.bash_profile` exists.

## User Impact

Users keep their existing login settings and PATH additions after enabling completion during setup or through the CLI. Completion remains available, and reinstalling or removing it preserves the user's profile content.

## Why This Change Was Made

Bash loads the first login file in its precedence order. The completion installer previously created `.bash_profile` whenever `.bashrc` was absent, unintentionally hiding either lower-precedence file.

The existing profile resolver now keeps the `.bashrc` preference, then selects an existing login file in Bash order, and creates `.bash_profile` only when none exists. Status, installation and cleanup use that same selection. A hook written to shared `.profile` loads the Bash cache only in Bash, so other shells can still read the profile.

This prevents new shadowing; it does not remove an already-existing `.bash_profile`, whose contents and ownership may be intentional.

## Evidence

Reproduced on base `4a0e45492b89` and replayed on the fix using the real `runCli` dispatcher, core command registration and cache generation for `completion --shell bash --write-state --install --yes`, followed by native `/bin/bash --login -c` in fresh homes. macOS 27.0.1, Bash 3.2.57, Node 26.12.1; no model, provider or live Gateway involved.

The actual generated cache registers `_openclaw_completion`. Sanitized output excerpts:

```text
# Base, existing .profile
Profile not found at <isolated-home>/.bash_profile. Creating a new one.
setting=unset
complete -F _openclaw_completion openclaw

# Base, existing .bash_login
Profile not found at <isolated-home>/.bash_profile. Creating a new one.
setting=unset
complete -F _openclaw_completion openclaw

# Fixed, existing .profile
Installing completion in <isolated-home>/.profile...
setting=preserved
complete -F _openclaw_completion openclaw

# Fixed, existing .bash_login
Installing completion in <isolated-home>/.bash_login...
setting=preserved
complete -F _openclaw_completion openclaw
```

The existing `.bash_profile` control preserves the setting on both versions. Fixed runs also checked status, byte-identical reinstallation, cleanup preserving user settings, and sourcing `.profile` in Zsh without loading the Bash cache.

Committed regressions exercise real Bash login shells with literal state paths containing spaces, quotes and dollar signs. The two affected layouts fail on the base; the existing-profile control passes. The existing state-directory replacement test also covers the new shared-profile hook.

- **71 focused tests passed**, five Windows-only cases skipped on macOS: completion runtime, quoting, Doctor and setup.
- Focused TypeScript, type-aware lint and formatting checks passed.
- Source command-dispatcher replay uses core-only completion generation. The development launcher separately stopped at its Gateway-offline build guard in the isolated environment; a packaged-launcher/full-onboarding run and broad CI are not claimed.

<details>
<summary>Focused test command and implementation scope</summary>

```sh
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  src/cli/completion-runtime.test.ts \
  src/cli/completion-runtime.windows.test.ts \
  src/cli/quote-cli-arg.test.ts \
  src/commands/doctor-completion.test.ts \
  src/wizard/setup.completion.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```

The change replaces the two-file Bash selection, extends existing hook recognition/removal, and moves the unchanged completion-path quoting helper into the existing CLI quoting module to keep the runtime within its lint size limit. No new profile manager or configuration surface. Production delta: +38/-23 lines; test delta: +39/-4 lines against the base.

The separate Unix installer's PATH fix in #124779 does not change this completion resolver. Its normal `.bashrc` creation means this is not a claim that every `install.sh` run is affected.

</details>

AI-assisted implementation and investigation; the author reviewed the source, patch and native-shell evidence.

prs.title: fix: keep retryable subagent completions scheduled
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes completed subagent results becoming stranded when a retryable requester completion loses its scheduled wake after cancellation, timeout, preparation invalidation, or conflict.

Related: #200020, #200005, #200165.

## User Impact

Retryable requester completions keep the existing bounded retry schedule. After three attempts, the registry records a terminal failure with the existing visible failure notice instead of leaving a retryable label with no scheduled work. Successful parent `NO_REPLY` or empty settlement remains intentionally quiet.

Already-stranded rows whose older build retired the wake and suppressed delivery require explicit recovery; upgrading does not resurrect those wakes. Runs with committed or unknown effects remain failed for explicit recovery rather than replaying their work. No configuration or schema changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The delivery classifier already owns retryability, but the scheduler applied a second reason allowlist. Typed timeout and preparation failures could therefore lose their wake. Predispatch cancellation also returned an unclassified `path: none`, while exhausted retryable outcomes retained that disposition in storage.

One typed error map now classifies these interruptions using admission and execution-owned replay-safety facts. The scheduler consumes the disposition directly, and the persistence owner records exhaustion for previously failed/retryable rows. This removes the duplicate allowlist and unbounded preadmission retry branch. Production delta is +39 lines; the growth carries the typed interruption and replay-safety distinctions. Test delta is +154 lines, with +10 documentation lines. Ordinary completion delivery retains its existing frozen result and stable idempotency identity; the stricter replay-safety checks apply to fresh requester-settle attempts.

## Evidence

The table regression failed on the exact parent for eight intended cases; the separate SQLite regression reproduced a retired wake retaining a retryable disposition. Focused proof covers cancellation, returned timeout, worker timeout, preparation invalidation, conflict, bounded redelivery/exhaustion, unsafe replay rejection, and visible notices across database reopen. The final CI-repair run passes 203 cases across the yielded-settle, lifecycle retry-grace, requester-settle dispatch, direct-delivery, and delivery suites. The prior focused proof also includes the real SQLite wake/exhaustion cases. Full-candidate Codex autoreview is clean through P2 on final head `6030ca8f09105`.

CI on the preceding head exposed two real repair needs: stale typed timeout/abort assertions and an overbroad policy change that made ordinary frozen-result retries permanent. Both were reproduced locally and fixed; the lifecycle fixtures remain unchanged to protect that existing behavior. Final-head [CI passed](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43927598450). Landed as `aa4d490a848b4d96801fd7afcdea6cc01cc80d6e` after the pinned auto-merge request; no CI bypass was used for this follow-up. ClawSweeper revision 2 reviewed `6030ca8f09105` with zero findings and zero open items; all three previous items have a numbered source-and-proof response.

Final-head `pnpm build` and the built-Gateway reproduction passed (167.14 seconds including transform/setup). An isolated built Gateway with a real agent and synthetic Responses provider passed the foreground-interruption reproduction: exactly two settle attempts, one foreground turn, and the recovered child result visible through `chat.history`. No production data was used; this is not an external-provider proof.

Final committed-head `pnpm check:changed --base 4a0e4549` passes every gate except inherited dead exports: production types, all core test typechecks, lint, formatting, import/SQLite guards and ratchets pass. All 111 unique dead-export findings reproduce on the exact parent (116 baseline; no candidate-only finding). The earlier 106 count omitted five aliased labels. Owner history attributes them to #198943 (45), #198936 (36), #198933 (18), commit `472cd0a2f542` (8), #198133 (1), #200056 (2), and #200073 (1). These remain main regressions; this PR does not hide or baseline them. No changed module is imported by the Control UI.

A/A/B synthetic classifier measurements (5,000 contexts; 100,000 calls per sample) show cancellation-envelope wall time 0.168/0.160/0.189 µs, CPU 0.478/0.481/0.526 µs, sampled allocation 802/799/1,423 bytes per call. Healthy and quiet paths are broadly unchanged; no speedup is claimed. This owner performs no database or workspace scan.

prs.title: fix(facetime): build the paired audio driver with a supported deployment target
prs.body:
Related: #165206

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: the paired FaceTime audio driver cannot be built with Xcode 27, because the pinned BlackHole 0.7.1 project declares `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET = 10.10` for the BlackHole target and Xcode 27 rejects a target below 12.0 as a hard error instead of a warning.

## User Impact

User impact: `facetime.installDriver` completes on a current Xcode, so `OpenClaw-Mic` and `OpenClaw-Feed` are installed and the FaceTime carrier's audio path is reachable. Without this, the driver install fails outright on macOS 27 hosts with Xcode 27, and `facetime.setup` never reaches a usable state. The deployment floor of the installed driver moves from 10.10 to 12.0, which stays below the macOS 14.4 the FaceTime plugin already requires, so no supported host loses the driver.

## Why This Change Was Made

`install-driver-root.sh` invokes `xcodebuild` against the pinned BlackHole project without overriding the deployment target, so the build inherits `10.10` from the vendored project and fails on Xcode 27. This pins `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=12.0` on the `xcodebuild` invocation instead of editing the vendored project, keeping the pinned tarball and its checksum untouched.

The privileged wrapper checksums the installer it is about to run, so `expectedInstallerDigest` in `install-driver.applescript` is updated to match the modified installer. Without that, every install would abort on the digest comparison before reaching the build.

A new test fails if the installer stops pinning a deployment target of at least 12.0, and fails if `expectedInstallerDigest` no longer matches the installer. Those two drift apart silently otherwise: the digest mismatch only surfaces at install time, as an administrator-prompted failure with no indication which file changed.

## Evidence

### 1. The build, before and after

Same Xcode 26.6, same pinned BlackHole 0.7.1 tarball (sha256 `e9de179da54ed55ff27876990f3a2dcfefa66e6bd6cfcba448a8564eabdf3e89`), same `xcodebuild` flags apart from the added build setting.

Before, with the inherited target:

```
base build exit=0
base deployment-target diagnostics:
  /.../BlackHole-0.7.1/BlackHole.xcodeproj: warning: The macOS deployment target 'MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET' is set to 10.10, but the range of supported deployment target versions is 10.13 to 26.5.99. (in target 'BlackHole' from project 'BlackHole')
base built minos:
    version 10.10
      minos 11.0
```

After, with the target pinned to 12.0:

```
patched build exit=0
patched deployment-target diagnostics:
  (none)
patched built minos:
      minos 12.0
      minos 12.0
```

### 2. The digest pin the wrapper checks

`install-driver.applescript` copies the installer into its protected directory and compares the copy's checksum against `expectedInstallerDigest` before running it. Reproducing that comparison against the modified installer:

```
pinned=060835a26dfe8870e1736b47673eaf5e91ed63d0e7a808b23a8f8bb478dd41a8
actual=060835a26dfe8870e1736b47673eaf5e91ed63d0e7a808b23a8f8bb478dd41a8
MATCH
```

### 3. The new test is red on the base installer and green here

```
$ sh extensions/facetime/scripts/test-driver-deployment-target.sh
install-driver-root.sh does not pin MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET
exit=1

$ sh extensions/facetime/scripts/test-driver-deployment-target.sh
driver deployment target 12.0 and installer digest pin agree
exit=0
```

The same test also catches the digest drifting out of sync, which is the failure mode the pin exists to prevent:

```
$ printf '\n# drift\n' >> extensions/facetime/scripts/install-driver-root.sh
$ sh extensions/facetime/scripts/test-driver-deployment-target.sh
expectedInstallerDigest does not match install-driver-root.sh
  pinned: 060835a26dfe8870e1736b47673eaf5e91ed63d0e7a808b23a8f8bb478dd41a8
  actual: 0b3707d1b25a0a3a34ec14032a36f4313e26b3330c5ee9082ad3b31030999923
exit=1
```

### 4. The rest of the plugin's script suite still passes

```
$ for t in test-driver-deployment-target test-driver-transaction test-uninstall-inventory test-xcode-trust; do sh extensions/facetime/scripts/$t.sh; done
test-driver-deployment-target         PASS
test-driver-transaction               PASS
test-uninstall-inventory              PASS
test-xcode-trust                      PASS
```

Package inspection is unchanged: `npm pack --dry-run` ships no native source, generated driver, dylib, `.build`, or BlackHole artifact.

### Gap

This host has Xcode 26.6, where the stale target is a warning and the build still exits 0, so the hard Xcode 27 error is not reproducible here. What the local build does prove is that the pinned target removes the diagnostic entirely and produces a driver whose floor is 12.0. The Xcode 27 acceptance path itself needs a host with Xcode 27, or CI.

No SIP, developer-tools, or macOS privacy setting is touched by this change.

prs.title: fix: keep cold credential reads responsive on slow filesystems
prs.body:
Related: #200136

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: cold credential reads can block Gateway requests on synchronous database identity and inspection-budget filesystem probes before reaching the read worker.

## User Impact

Credential reads remain responsive while filesystem metadata is slow. The existing worker still validates the complete captured file identity before opening the database and transferring credentials. Runtime retirement and same-root usage ordering remain enforced. No configuration, schema, durability, or dependency changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Team 25c97908 incident on 2026-11-16 at 05:02 PST exposed a 1.97 s main-thread btrfs transaction wait in catalog lock creation and a 2,002 ms event-loop stall. #200136 deleted that redundant lock. This follow-up repairs the cold credential-read boundary uncovered by the same audit.

The existing async identity owner now prepares the reader's physical file facts; the existing SQLite worker owns complete key/birthtime validation. Redundant host probes and reverse lookups of already-known agent identities are deleted. All internal reader-factory callers await preparation. Unresolved agent discovery participates in the existing read-resource lifetime before yielding, so retirement cannot deliver credentials or admit fresh file/cache state. Usage requests reserve the existing preparation queue before async work, preserving ordering.

Inspection budget preparation also becomes async in the existing session and one-shot read owners. Captured runtime context and accepted-work settlement survive that await. Production grows by 37 lines across 22 modules: async discovery and resource lifetime replace duplicate checks. No new cache, queue, protocol, or authority owner.

## Evidence

Final focused proof passes 78 tests across eight files, including actual credential reads, candidate stores, source checks, usage admission, and the broker consumer. Additional OAuth settlement/concurrency proof passes 22 cases. A real read-child regression rejects a wrong captured birthtime that the parent incorrectly accepted. Cold registry-retirement and post-retirement admission regressions fail before their repairs and pass afterward. Existing main-thread FS observation verifies the cold read flow.

The canonical check:changed entry point (`node scripts/check-changed.mjs --base HEAD`) completed. Task-owned mock/type findings were repaired; final touched core/services/agents type graphs, lint, format, and diff checks pass. Structural SQLite worker, import, schema, and line gates passed. Unchanged dead exports reproduce on exact parent 6670297776a00 and originate in 24385a20428a / #200056: a confirmed main regression, not a baseline waiver. The whole check command is not claimed green.

Three isolated Codex passes completed. One P2 was rejected after checking both production callers: usage admission occurs before entering the reservation owner, and its unconditional cleanup releases the reservation. The other passes had no findings; no accepted/actionable findings remain.

Twenty serialized fresh Node 26.12.1 processes exercised a real synthetic 37,641,338,880-byte database containing 5,000 session rows and one synthetic auth row. Each sample verifies returned credentials and disposal. Four identical-baseline controls, four zero-delay A/B pairs, and four A/B pairs with one injected 2,000 ms target metadata delay all completed. No Team data was used. The surrounding 62,000-file workspace is not scanned by this owner.

| Median | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| No-delay owner time | 4.758 ms | 4.724 ms |
| No-delay main-thread CPU | 1.968 ms | 1.943 ms |
| No-delay parent-process CPU | 8.344 ms | 7.868 ms |
| No-delay main-isolate allocation | 868,468 bytes | 630,268 bytes |
| Delayed owner time | 2,014.252 ms | 2,008.244 ms |
| Delayed maximum heartbeat gap | 2,010.365 ms | 8.814 ms |
| Scoped synchronous metadata calls | 7 | 0 |

Candidate delayed heartbeat maximum across all four samples was 15.553 ms. A/A owner median was 4.288 ms, range 3.746–5.951; main CPU 1.876 ms. No-delay latency/CPU differences are within process spread. Allocation controls varied substantially, so the lower candidate allocation median is not claimed as an improvement. During the injected delay, the responsive candidate executes heartbeat/runtime timers for two seconds while baseline blocks them: its measured CPU/allocation includes that extra instrumentation work and does not isolate owner overhead.

These are APFS fault-injection measurements, not direct btrfs measurements. Each measured target has cold application identity/file-state/row-cache admission and an explicit known agent ID; a separate clone warms module/read-worker startup. OS page cache and unknown-directory discovery are not claimed cold. Parent CPU excludes the spawned SQLite child's CPU.

Two earlier native-staging cancellation cases exceeded their original 10 s deadlines. Exact-parent isolated replays passed; a diagnostic replay of the same three files passed 56/56 without changing barriers or deadlines. That does not establish their cause, a fix, or inheritance. Diagnostic-only edits are excluded, and the uncertainty remains for exact-head CI.

Diagnostic/legacy source reads, unknown-directory generic writes, source cohort comparison, and secrets activation/rollback remain separate audited boundaries. No global zero-sync claim. Changed modules have no runtime Control UI import; no Node import was added to a browser-facing module.

Initial CI 43921173131 found a missing consumer migration in the auth-watch benchmark added by #186370 after this lane's base. Main was integrated for this named type failure; fixture setup now awaits the async identity owner before its unchanged assertion. Scripts types, targeted lint/format, and fresh Codex review pass. No production change or compatibility alias was added.

The actual small benchmark smoke separately fails with zero intercepted watch callbacks instead of 64. That identical failure reproduces on exact CI main parent 4a74c61ae7c438587bc272840d180d16f7c5a283. #197445 / 36afa92b2370c23bfd64d3f4a6f1b3aab68fd300 moved all directory watches into the existing child host, while this benchmark still intercepts the parent's fs.watch. This is a confirmed main benchmark regression for follow-up; the smoke is not claimed passing and an unrelated benchmark redesign is excluded.

Final-head CI [43924604188](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43924604188) succeeded on2ed553960fde3a48eb5206aecd8f5b8aacf388ad. Final ClawSweeper review6924641156 has zero open items; native review and preparation are complete. Landing is pending.

prs.title: fix(gateway): store-backed gateway token failures hide the real secret provider error
prs.body:
> **AI-assisted: yes**

Closes #200175

## What Problem This Solves

- Fixes a problem where any Gateway-authenticated CLI command (for example `openclaw cron list`) fails with "gateway.auth.token is configured as a secret reference but is unavailable in this command path" and advice to replace credentials, when the real cause is that the configured `store` secret provider could not be read (for example inside a read-only sandbox where the state directory is not writable). Agents and operators following the printed "Fix: set OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN..." line conclude their credentials are broken instead of requesting sandbox escalation or restoring provider access.
- **Related:** #196160 (same function, unset env templates — handled separately by #196164); #151944 (bootstrap deadlock, distinct); fix signal labels `clawsweeper:source-repro` / `clawsweeper:fix-shape-clear` / `clawsweeper:queueable-fix`.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Intended outcome:** when a provider-scoped secret resolution failure (such as `SECRET_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE` from the store provider) is the reason a Gateway SecretRef cannot be resolved, the surfaced error keeps the provider error as `cause` and the message names the provider failure and points at restoring provider access. When no provider failure is involved, the existing message (including the credential advice) is unchanged.
- **Out of scope:** making a read-only `store` SecretRef resolution not require write access to the state directory (a separate storage-lifecycle investigation), and the database-engine-selection wrap site (no typed cause exists there today).
- **Highest-risk area:** `GatewaySecretRefUnavailableError` message consumers; all existing catch sites key on the error class, not the message text, and the default message is byte-for-byte unchanged.
- **How is that risk mitigated?** Regression tests pin both message shapes, and the full gateway test surface (credentials, credentials-secret-inputs, client-bootstrap, probe-auth, gateway-rpc runtime) passes.

## User Impact

- **Success criteria:** with a store-backed `gateway.auth.token` and an unavailable store provider, the CLI now prints `Secret provider "store:default" could not be read: Secret store database is unavailable.` and a fix line pointing at restoring provider access, and no longer suggests `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN`/`--token`. The underlying typed provider error is preserved as `error.cause` for programmatic diagnostics.
- **What should reviewers focus on?** `src/gateway/credentials.ts` (message construction and cause preservation) and `src/gateway/credentials-secret-inputs.ts` (one-line cause pass-through); regression tests in `src/gateway/credentials.test.ts` (`GatewaySecretRefUnavailableError` describe block) and `src/gateway/credentials-secret-inputs.test.ts` ("preserves the provider failure instead of suggesting credential replacement").

## Evidence

- **Real environment tested:** isolated worktree of this fork at commit base `origin/main` (2026-11-16), Node v26.12.1, real resolution stack driven directly (`resolveGatewayCredentialsWithSecretInputs` → `materializeSecretInput` → `resolveSecretRefString` → `resolveStoreRefs` → state read) with a synthetic state directory whose `state/openclaw.sqlite` is unreadable, mirroring the sandbox case where the store read path cannot complete under the state directory.
- **Exact steps or commands run after this patch:**
  ```bash
  # regression tests (RED on base, GREEN with the patch)
  node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/gateway/credentials.test.ts src/gateway/credentials-secret-inputs.test.ts \
    src/gateway/client-bootstrap.test.ts src/gateway/probe-auth.test.ts src/cli/gateway-rpc.runtime.test.ts
  # format + lint + typecheck via the repo's targeted validation entry
  pnpm exec oxfmt --check <changed files> && pnpm exec oxlint <changed files> && pnpm tsgo:core
  # runtime proof (script in evidence dir): store-backed gateway.auth.token + unavailable store provider
  node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs runtime-proof.mts   # run once on base files, once with the patch
  ```
- **Evidence after fix:**
  ```json
  {
    "errorName": "GatewaySecretRefUnavailableError",
    "message": "gateway.auth.token is configured as a secret reference but is unavailable in this command path.\nSecret provider \"store:default\" could not be read: Secret store database is unavailable.\nFix: restore access to that secret provider, then retry this command with the same configuration.",
    "causeName": "SecretProviderResolutionError",
    "causeCode": "SECRET_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE",
    "suggestsCredentialReplacement": false,
    "namesProviderFailure": true
  }
  ```

prs.title: fix(matrix): report unreadable homeserver reads instead of a missing m.direct mapping
prs.body:
Closes #195973

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a Matrix send to a user target reports `No direct room found for <user> (m.direct missing)` when the homeserver read actually failed, so operators are pointed at a mapping that is intact.

## User Impact

User impact: during a homeserver outage, timeout, or 5xx the send error names the failed read, the underlying homeserver error, and a recovery step instead of blaming a missing `m.direct` mapping. The successful discovery/fallback path and the CLI JSON contract are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

`inspectMatrixDirectRooms` swallowed both lookup failures (`.catch(() => ({}))` and `.catch(() => [])`), so "could not read" and "read succeeded, no mapping" collapsed into the same empty result and `resolveDirectRoomId` always reported `(m.direct missing)`.

The inspection result now carries `directReadError` and `joinedRoomsReadError`, and resolution reports:

- `Could not read m.direct for <user> from the homeserver: <error>. Retry after homeserver access recovers.`
- `Could not read joined rooms for <user> from the homeserver: <error>. Retry after homeserver access recovers.`
- `No direct room found for <user> (N mapped room(s) could not be verified as direct). Run \`openclaw matrix direct inspect --user-id <user>\` to review the mapping.`
- the existing `(m.direct missing)` message only when both reads succeeded and there is genuinely no mapping.

Review follow-up in this revision:

- **CLI projection type:** `MatrixCliDirectRoomInspection` is derived with `ReturnType`, so the two new internal diagnostics made `toCliDirectRoomInspection`'s explicit object unsatisfied. Both fields are now omitted from that projection, restoring the production and test type graphs and keeping the CLI JSON output identical.
- **Recovery guidance:** every new diagnostic now names the next step.
- **Test-line allocation:** `config/test-lines-allocations/196020-matrix-direct-read-error.txt` (30 lines).

Non-goals: no retry policy, no admission change, no change to mapping writes, no change to the joined-room fallback.

## Evidence

prs.title: fix(infra): ignore a malformed GIT_CONFIG_COUNT when appending git config
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: every git command that inherits a malformed `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT` fails with `fatal: unable to parse command-line config`, because the app re-emits that value instead of validating it. A valid count with a leading `+` was also discarded by the first revision of this patch, which overwrote the caller's first entry.

## User Impact

User impact: agent worktree git operations keep working when the ambient environment carries a malformed `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`, and inherited caller configuration (for example `safe.directory`) survives a valid `+1` count instead of being replaced.

## Why This Change Was Made

`appendGitConfig` computed its start index with `Number(env.GIT_CONFIG_COUNT ?? 0)` and re-emitted the result. Git parses `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT` with `strtoul(..., 10)`: a leading `+` is valid, while `abc`, `1.5`, `0x10`, and `-1` make every git command fail.

```
$ GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=NaN git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree
error: bogus count in GIT_CONFIG_COUNT
fatal: unable to parse command-line config
```

The start index is now parsed like git does: trim, accept an optional leading `+`, require the rest to be digits, and fall back to `0` for anything git would reject. Valid counts (including `+1`) keep the existing append behavior, so caller entries are preserved.

Review follow-up in this revision: the digits-only check from the previous head rejected `+1` and reset the index to zero; that is fixed and covered by a regression that asserts the caller entry survives.

## Evidence

Behavior proof through the shipped worktree helper (`runGit` from `src/agents/worktrees/git.ts`), not unit assertions only. The script drives real `git` with the environment this helper builds:

after (this branch):

```
malformed count abc: OK gc.auto=0 caller-entry=<absent>
leading plus +1: OK gc.auto=0 caller-entry=caller-value
```

before (main): the helper emitted `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=NaN` (asserted by the new unit test) and git rejected the environment:

```
$ GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=NaN git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree
error: bogus count in GIT_CONFIG_COUNT
fatal: unable to parse command-line config
```

Unit tests, same file, source reverted for the "before" run:

```
# before
Tests  7 failed | 2 passed (9)
# after
Tests  10 passed (10)
```

Command: `node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run src/infra/git-maintenance-env.test.ts`

Test-line allocation: `config/test-lines-allocations/196050-git-config-count-guard.txt` (50 lines).

`git diff --check` is clean.

Proof boundary: the proof runs the shipped helper and real `git` on this platform (Windows), not a live agent worktree checkout end-to-end.

prs.title: fix: backup restore accepts a symlinked --target for PostgreSQL archives
prs.body:
Closes #197779

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw backup restore --target <dir>` refuses to restore a PostgreSQL archive with "PostgreSQL recovery configuration must be inside the restored archive." when any ancestor of the target directory is a symlink (for example `ln -s /Volumes/data/work ~/work`), even though the recovery configuration really is inside the freshly extracted archive.

## User Impact

Restoring a PostgreSQL backup into a directory reached through a symlink now works instead of aborting before any data is written. No configuration change, migration, or extra flag is required, and archives whose configuration genuinely escapes the restore target are still rejected.

## Why This Change Was Made

The containment guard compared two different spellings of the same location: `targetPath` kept the caller's spelling, which still contains the unresolved symlinked ancestor, while only the configuration path was run through `fs.realpath`. Once the ancestor resolved, the canonical configuration path was no longer lexically inside the unresolved target, so a legitimate archive was rejected. Both sides now go through the repo's containment canonicalizer (`canonicalizePathForContainment`) before `isPathInside`, so the comparison is between two canonical spellings while the existing escape rejection is preserved.

## Evidence

- [x] Regression test red→green: `accepts a recovery configuration below a symlinked restore target` (in `src/commands/backup-restore.test.ts`). With the previous guard restored, the test fails with `Error: PostgreSQL recovery configuration must be inside the restored archive.` (`1 failed | 19 skipped`); with this change it passes (`1 passed | 19 skipped`, 435ms). Command: `node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.commands.config.ts src/commands/backup-restore.test.ts -t "symlinked restore target" --reporter=verbose`.
- [x] Targeted suite: `src/commands/backup-restore.test.ts` → `18 passed | 2 skipped (20)`. The two skips are pre-existing `it.skipIf(process.platform === "win32")` cases, unrelated to this change.
- [x] Lint/format on the touched files: `oxlint` reports `0 warnings and 0 errors`; `oxfmt --check` reports `All matched files use the correct format.`
- [x] Scope: only `src/commands/backup-restore.ts` (the guard is now one exported helper, `assertRecoveryConfigInsideRestore`) and its test file changed. Extraction, manifest verification, and PostgreSQL restore orchestration are untouched.
- [x] Honest boundary: this proves the symlinked-ancestor false negative is gone and that a configuration outside the target still throws. It does not exercise a full PostgreSQL restore (no database engine is started); the guard runs before any engine work, so the test asserts the guard contract directly.
